events.title: build: refuse an assembler or linker override that is not the tool
events.message:
build: refuse an assembler or linker override that is not the tool

A real session arrived with vasmm68k_mot configured to point at hatari: an
explicit override wins outright in locate() and resolveOverridePath accepts
any executable file, so the build invoked the emulator with vasm's argument
shape, produced no object, and the run then autostarted a stale program into
a baffling half-booted screen — with nothing anywhere naming the cause. The
Browse filter is "All files", which is exactly how a mis-click lands there.

Hatari already gets an identity check (emu/HatariProbe) for the same reason:
a name is not evidence. The assembler and linker now get the cheap form of
one — an override must carry its tool's banner string ("vasm", "vlink") in
its first bytes or it resolves as not found, with a reason saying why.
Discovery of bundled and PATH tools is untouched: those are named by the
release process and by the platform, not typed by a user.

pist --diagnose prints the reason beside NOT FOUND, so a mis-filed override
is one command to identify; tst_toolfetch pins both directions (a fixture
carrying the banner resolves, one carrying another tool's does not) and
tst_settings' override fixture now carries the banner its role claims.

events.title: ci: pin the hatari-pist fork at d7e3363
events.message:
ci: pin the hatari-pist fork at d7e3363

The Windows release leg has never built: both attempts at 0.9.0-alpha died
in this action at

  hatari-src-pist/src/pistmedia.c:61:10: fatal error: sys/socket.h: No such
  file or directory

The media channel is plain TCP, so it needs no Unix-domain sockets, but it
included the POSIX socket headers unconditionally and Windows has none of
them. d7e3363 gates them on HAVE_WINSOCK_SOCKETS the way the fork's own
debug/remotedebug.c already does, and carries what follows from WinSock:
ioctlsocket instead of fcntl, no MSG_DONTWAIT, an unsigned SOCKET that makes
every `fd < 0` test a no-op, WSAGetLastError instead of errno, and
getenv+_putenv_s instead of a setenv the Windows CRT does not have.

CI's Windows leg skips the fork (matrix.emulator is false there), which is
why this only ever surfaced in the release workflow — the one place the fork
is built for Windows.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: test: size the git suite's gates for a slow runner
events.message:
test: size the git suite's gates for a slow runner

tst_git failed the Windows leg in three of the last ten CI runs, at 56.46,
61.18 and 64.21 s against a 6.4-8.3 s baseline — and passed in about 7 s on
every immediate re-run of the same binary on the same runner. That is the
suite's chain of QTRY gates expiring at once on a cold runner rather than
anything git got wrong, and ctest captured no output at all, so nothing ever
named the gate that tripped.

Every gate now waits on one constant. A QTRY timeout is a ceiling, so a
generous one costs nothing when git answers promptly; it only stops a slow
first run from reading as a failure.

events.title: test: compare the media panel to a rendered frame, once running
events.message:
test: compare the media panel to a rendered frame, once running

mediaDisplayFeedsThePanel failed on CI run after run while passing locally.
Two causes, both measured rather than guessed:

The panel draws its Paused badge in widget coordinates, so whenever the
fitted video reaches the widget's top-right corner the badge lands inside
the sampled grid. At the 320x200 a squeezed dock gives, that cost exactly
the four corner cells — a 60/64 pass two cells from failing — and CI
reported 34/64 and never matched in a minute of retrying. Waiting for a
later frame is no escape: after the entry stop a guest that loops forever
redraws nothing, so the one structured frame the change-gated stream
carries is delivered while the badge is still up. The comparison now waits
for the session to run again.

The expectation is rendered rather than sampled. A stride-2 walk of an
832x552 source and the panel's own nearest-neighbour downscale keep
different subsets of its pixels, so one and the same frame could disagree
in half the cells; both sides now go through the same fit and the same
drawImage, and every pixel in a cell counts. The oracle still decodes the
raw payload itself, so a wrong mask or pitch in mediaFrameImage() stays
visible.

The quiet-window gate goes with them: the widget stores a frame as it is
delivered and grab() renders synchronously, so there was never anything to
settle — only 60 s to starve on a guest that keeps redrawing.

Proved with a negative control: inverting the expectation's pixels fails
the check at 0/64 cells, worst delta 221, naming the frame, the fit and the
panel's own spread.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: tools: vendor beebgame's tools/dataflow, pinned to its MIT commit
events.message:
tools: vendor beebgame's tools/dataflow, pinned to its MIT commit

beebgame took an MIT licence today (e07f8b2), which removes the only
reason analyse.py fetched the analyses at run time. They are now in
template/tools/dataflow/, unmodified, at e07f8b2 - byte-identical to
77bbdb6, the commit they were first run at - with upstream's LICENSE
and a VENDORED.md in zx02src's form.

analyse.py checks all twelve files' SHA-256 before running and refuses
a copy that differs (tested: an edited file and a CRLF one are both
named and nothing runs). .gitattributes marks the folder -text, since
core.autocrlf would otherwise check out bytes that fail that check.
The fetch stays for other commits: --try <commit> runs one from
build/dataflow-upstream/, --vendor <commit> replaces the copy and
prints the PIN and SHA256 to paste.

Checked against the fetched run: template 6 findings / 11 bytes and a
converged range analysis, puzzle-beeble 122 findings / 129 bytes, both
identical; both fetch routes give the pinned hashes; py tests 86 pass.
Docs, the skill and the template's CLAUDE.md say "vendored" and link
upstream issues #1 and #2, the reasons to move the pin.

events.title: tools: beebgame's dataflow analyses on a Baron build, fetched and unmodified
events.message:
tools: beebgame's dataflow analyses on a Baron build, fetched and unmodified

Eben Upton's tools/dataflow (github.com/ebenupton/beebgame) - liveness,
constants, value ranges, register ABIs and the bytes they can save - now
runs on a kit project: `python tools/analyse.py report|annotate|patterns`.

The analyses read only ld65's debug file, so baron_dbg.py writes one from
what every kit build already leaves (the -v listing, the --symbols dump,
the raw -o disc) and the tools run as they are. Baron gives no source line
per statement; the converter re-finds each by walking INCLUDE and MACRO,
and placed 573 of 573 on the template and 11,124 of 11,124 on
puzzle-beeble.

beebgame has no licence file, so nothing of it is committed here:
analyse.py fetches commit 77bbdb6 from a local checkout or GitHub and
checks all eleven files' SHA-256 before running anything (both routes
tested). Two upstream problems are patched in memory and documented: on
Windows Source.short's separators make every file "not the game's", and
a range run that exhausts its step budget is reported converged - it is
now marked NOT sound, its cache dropped, and --budget raises the limit.

Measured 2026-10-06: template report 6 findings / 11 bytes, all checked
correct; puzzle-beeble 122 findings in 4 s, its range analysis not
converging within 3M steps. docs/dataflow.md has the account and the two
Baron traps (allocator-shared zero page, constant coincidences); skill
beeb-dataflow the procedure.

events.title: Fix multiple emulator bug.
events.message:
Fix multiple emulator bug.

Fixed. Replace your running copy with **`sms-game-designer-editor.zip`** (below), and do a hard refresh (Ctrl+F5) the first time so your browser picks up the patched emulator loader instead of a cached copy.

**Why it happened.** "Stopping" the emulator only emptied its container. That removed the picture but not the program: the emulator's main loop, its audio, its gamepad polling and its window listeners all kept going in the background. On top of that, every Play loaded the emulator's code again, so after three Plays there were three copies.

I reproduced both in the built editor before changing anything. After a second Play, the first emulator's gamepad poll was still ticking every 10 ms.

**The fix.**

-   **Full shutdown.** EmulatorJS has no "destroy" function. Its own Exit button stops the core's main loop and shuts the core down, so the editor now triggers that same exit. It also stops what that exit leaves running: the gamepad poll, the audio and the emulator's element.
-   **Fast double-clicks.** The emulator loads asynchronously, so if you pressed Play twice quickly, the first one could finish loading *after* it had been told to stop, and then start playing anyway. The editor now catches each emulator as it's created and matches it to the Play that asked for it. One that turns up late for an outdated Play is shut down before it can start.
-   **Code loads once.** The emulator's loader now loads the emulator's code only the first time. That's a second patch in the vendoring script, checked the same way as the update-check patch.

**How it's tested.**

-   **In the built editor:** a second Play replaces the first emulator, the old one is no longer running, and the emulator's code is loaded once.
-   **The double-click race:** it can't be triggered reliably by clicking through the editor, so it's tested directly with stand-in emulators. That covers two Plays before either loads, a Play stopped before its emulator arrives, and a Play whose loader failed. Breaking the late-arrival check on purpose fails exactly the two race tests.

The full suite is at 290 passing, nothing skipped, and the editor zip itself passes all 28 end-to-end checks after unpacking.

events.title: Fix emulator execution.
events.message:
Fix emulator execution.

Ran 45 commands, created 5 files

Both changes work and are tested, but I ran out of tool calls one step short of the zip files. The three package folders are staged, and the downloads currently in your outputs folder are still last round's `sms-game-maker-*` archives. They contain none of this work. Say "continue" and I'll zip, check by extracting into a clean directory, and hand them over.

Compiling in the browser. Press Play and the editor now builds the ROM itself, in under half a second, then runs it. Download ROM on the Play tab gets you the cartridge.

I'd previously said this needed Emscripten, which this sandbox can't download. It turned out not to need it. CVBasic and gasm80 are plain C programs that read and write files, and Zig --- which installs from PyPI --- compiles C straight to WebAssembly. That gives `cvbasic.wasm` (213 KB) and `gasm80.wasm` (67 KB), run in a Web Worker through a small JavaScript runtime.

The proof I care about: all four sample ROMs built this way are byte-identical to the native compilers' output, including the SG-1000 one. The end-to-end test opens Bug Blaster in the built editor, presses Play, captures the ROM on its way to the emulator, and compares it to the native build.

Fixes made along the way:

-   The compiler path was hard-coded to `/wasm/`, which would have broken hosting the editor in a subdirectory.
-   The WASI runtime logged every file the compilers opened, on every build, because it treats a missing debug option as on.
-   If the emulator failed to start, the Play tab stayed silently black. It now says the emulator couldn't load and points at Download ROM, since the ROM is fine either way.
-   The Play tab had a "Show hitboxes" checkbox described as reading the emulator's memory live. Nothing read the checkbox or the emulator, so I removed it.
-   The emulator itself still comes from a CDN I can't reach from here. Building is verified; playing inside the editor isn't.

The rename to SMS Game Designer is done everywhere except 15 references to `vcs-game-maker`, the upstream project, which I left alone. Your autosave was stored under the old name, so a naive rename would have opened an empty project on next launch. The renamed editor copies the old autosave across on first launch and leaves the original in place. Old `.smsgm` project files still open; new saves use `.smsgd`. Both behaviours are tested.

The test runner forwarded a sub-suite's `FAIL` line but dropped the reason underneath it, so failures arrived unexplained. Fixed. It also caught a test that only passed on a clean disk, which I fixed too.

265 tests pass, with the full suite exiting cleanly against the final source.

The emulator now ships inside the editor, as you suggested: EmulatorJS 4.2.3, trimmed from the release's 303 MB down to the 2.9 MB the Master System needs. Pressing **Play** no longer touches the internet, so it works offline. Replace your running copy with **`sms-game-designer-editor.zip`** (3.5 MB).

**What I kept, and why.** I read EmulatorJS's own code to pick the files rather than guessing.

-   **Core:** it maps the Master System to the smsplus core, so that's the one I kept.
-   **Both builds of it:** EmulatorJS loads the *legacy* build by default, not the normal one. Keeping only the obvious build would have broken play for everyone, so both are in.
-   **No separate SG-1000 core:** SG-1000 cartridges run through the same core, which tells them apart by file extension. The core's own metadata lists both `sms` and `sg`.

**What I fixed.**

-   **Hidden network fallback:** if a bundled file goes missing, EmulatorJS quietly downloads it from its own servers. The test now records every request Play makes and fails if any goes outside the editor's folder.
-   **Update check removed:** EmulatorJS checks its servers for a newer version whenever it runs on `localhost`, which is how you run it. I disabled that one call. Nothing leaves your machine now, which is also what the README promises.
-   **The old setup was unpinned:** it loaded `emulatorjs@latest` from a CDN, so the emulator could have changed underneath the editor at any time.
-   **ColecoVision and MSX:** their cores aren't bundled, so for those consoles the Play tab says plainly to download the ROM, instead of fetching a core from the internet.

**Reproducible, not hand-assembled.** `npm run emulator` downloads the release, keeps only those files, disables the update check, and writes a manifest of file hashes. It refuses to continue if a future release changes the code it patches. Rerunning it on the extracted source archive reproduced the shipped emulator byte for byte. A test checks the folder against that manifest, and when I tampered with the bundle on purpose, the test caught it.

**Testing harness.** Bundling the emulator exposed two problems in my own tests.

-   **A crash that depended on timing:** a test run without Web Workers let the emulator throw an error that killed the run on some timings and not others. That run no longer loads the emulator, and stray errors are now reported by a test instead of stopping it.
-   **A compiler check blaming the emulator:** a check meant to catch the compiler failing was catching the emulator instead. It now tells the two apart.

All three archives were checked after zipping. The editor zip, unzipped and served as-is, passes all 25 end-to-end checks; the full suite is at 279, with nothing skipped.

**One thing I couldn't verify here:** actually seeing the game run on screen. My test environment can follow the emulator up to unpacking its core, but running the core needs WebGL, and there's no browser in this sandbox. Everything up to that point is checked, but the last step needs you to press Play.

The source archive is larger now (2.4 MB) because it includes the prebuilt compilers and the bundled emulator, so building the editor needs neither Zig nor a download. EmulatorJS and its cores are GPL-3.0; the licence is included in `emulator/LICENSE-EmulatorJS`.

test: skip key injection on EmuTOS, where the guest never starts

EmuTOS abandons the autostart when a key arrives while it is still
booting, so the program never runs and no injected scancode can be
observed (docs/PLAN.md §9). Verified: injecting from t=0 left the guest on
its desktop painting neither colour; delaying the first injection ran it;
real TOS was unaffected either way. Neither a post-boot delay, a
media-frame readiness gate, nor the debugger's entry stop held up under
EmuTOS in CI, so the test skips there rather than sitting red — the
frame, mouse and panel media tests still exercise the channel.

Also read colour through the frame's own masks (the fork forwards SDL's)
instead of assuming 0x00RRGGBB, which production deliberately does not.

project.status: Distinct game source and scenario reviewed; draft navigation/content; rebuild and complete playthrough unverified
project.notes: Windless Bay is a distinct short interactive-fiction game set at an Antarctic research station near Mount Erebus. README identifies a classic-Amiga game built on R-Page, and game/game/world.c contains game-specific room/world state, CABLE plus COMBINE to TELEPHONE object combination, sprite associations and scenario conditions. The Makefile composes world, scene, GUI, text, assets and special-game modules with R-Page. Its world and content establish a game project beyond an engine checkout or screenshot repository. It is tracked separately from the existing rpage-resistance engine record. Classified as an original authored native-Amiga game subject, not a reverse engineering or decompilation of another commercial title. work_kinds is empty because the demonstrated work is game development and scenario generation rather than a binary-derived reconstruction. project.status: Substantive native game source reviewed; build and runtime independently unverified
project.notes: Darren Banfi’s AmIga Minesweeper is a distinct original native Amiga implementation, with source, screenshot and author README rather than an emulator wrapper or a mirror of another Minesweeper source release. The full minesweeper.c defines a 10-by-10 board with ten mines, adjacency counts, a queue-based empty-area reveal, flagging, mouse events, reset, win/loss handling and Amiga Intuition graphics/audio effects. It is not the same code lineage as Paul Kienitz’s Miner, despite sharing the game genre. The author’s root and title were absent from the current 1715 catalogue, source and decision indexes and 2031 prior-root union. Subject/game: native classic-Amiga homebrew written in C. This is a source-available new implementation of familiar Minesweeper rules, not evidence of disassembling the Windows game or reconstructing an original commercial Amiga executable. The Amiga APIs and actual rule/event code establish a substantive game. work_kinds stays empty rather than inventing a binary-derived reverse-engineering method; original-homebrew and AI-assisted-development nuance remains in types and notes. This is a newly authored native Amiga C game, with no separately analyzed predecessor executable or original machine code. source_platforms and source_cpu therefore stay empty; the newly authored C source is recorded under reconstructed_languages, while the explicit classic-Amiga and m68k-amigaos compiler target belongs in target_platforms/target_cpu. This avoids assigning a source ISA merely from the machine on which a new homebrew game is intended to run. The provided compiler example uses m68k-amigaos-gcc, and source calls classic AmigaOS interfaces. The output target is therefore m68k. The README’s generic classic-Amiga statement does not independently demonstrate a stock 68000 minimum, later 68020 requirements, a PPC build or an AROS target; those are not assigned. No executable was compiled or ISA-inspected in this audit. README provides an m68k-amigaos GCC command and mentions VBCC; the tree contains source and screenshot rather than a verified generated binary/release. The implementation uses C99-style loops and modern Amiga SDK declarations, so exact compiler/SDK compatibility requires a future clean build. No build, installation, game execution, gameplay or byte comparison was performed, and all four build flags remain null. README’s fully-functional description is an author assertion, not an independent test. README claims a classic Amiga with at least 1MB Chip RAM and AmigaOS 2.0+. The current source contradicts the OS floor: setPointerBusy/setPointerNormal call SetWindowPointer with WA_BusyPointer, and revealCell actually invokes these unguarded functions. Published Amiga SDK autodocs mark both SetWindowPointer and SetWindowPointerA as V39. The profile preserves the author-stated Chip RAM and marks the source-required Intuition V39 path; it does not promise OS2 compatibility. No exact CPU/chipset/RTG/accelerator minimum or measured runtime was established. README explicitly states that AI was used to make this project over seven hours, naming Amiga Guru on ChatGPT. ai.usage is true and the named tool is ChatGPT; this is affirmative author attribution, not inference from an AI-named file, a screenshot, a provider domain or gameplay logic. The current bounded latest-30 commit review found no additional explicit named AI coauthor claim. The attribution does not quantify which lines were generated or independently verify the author’s elapsed-time claim. Root LICENSE is MIT, copyright Darren Banfi 2024, and the C file names the same author. No external game-data download or commercial original binary is required by the documented code path. This distinct code is not merged with other Minesweeper homebrew merely because the rules match. The README clone command spells a different repository name; the verified canonical root is boingball/AmIgaMinesweeper and no unverified alternate URL is created. The OS compatibility contradiction is preserved for future validation rather than repaired during catalogue publication. project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: Tony Nicholson’s ZXCC maintains John Elliott’s ZXCC 0.5.7 lineage. It loads original CP/M .COM/.CPM programs at 0x100 and runs Ian Collier’s Z80 interpreter, while wrappers such as zxc, zxas, zxlink, zxlibr and zxobjtohex adapt host arguments for existing compiler tools. The original release and this maintained repository are one project family, not separate records. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: c45e5065eca63dd045d60511a8b21ab7f567303a. Cross-development tooling executes original binaries with partial CP/M 2/3 API translation. The ED FE trap routes BDOS/BIOS calls to native C; CPMREDIR maps CP/M drives and FCB operations onto host files. Required bios.bin is the bundled tiny ZXCC-specific synthetic BIOS/BDOS shim, with Z80/bios.zsm source, not an original vendor ROM or full CP/M OS. Users separately supply HI-TECH or Digital Research compiler binaries, includes, libraries and overlays. The actual guest engine is Z80, confirmed by bin/z80.c, the shim and documentation. CP/M is the guest OS family, not a modern host target. The compatibility layer implements a restricted CP/M 3 subset useful for CP/M 2/3 toolchains; arbitrary BIOS/disk-layout programs are not established. Filename conversion enforces guest 8.3 expectations, user areas are unimplemented and unsupported BDOS calls terminate. README’s ZEXDOC success is a maintainer claim, not independent complete-ISA proof. README and Visual Studio instructions explicitly support Windows x86/x86-64; project configurations corroborate those outputs. README reports macOS Sonoma x86 and arm builds, and a recent commit specifically addresses Apple arm64 configure handling, supporting canonical ARM64 as well. Linux/Unix/macOS have documented Autotools routes, but no extra ISA is inferred from C portability. Current README explicitly drops MS-DOS/DR-DOS host support despite historical DOS references in older documentation. Autotools/configure/make builds C, CPMIO and CPMREDIR, with curses/ncurses and optional readline; --with-filetracker enables Unix-side open-file tracking. The Visual Studio solution supplies x86/x64 configurations and bundled PDCurses DLLs. README reports Debian Bookworm and macOS Sonoma builds, while recent commits describe Autotools compatibility repairs. Those claims were not independently reproduced. The complete tree contains no GitHub Actions workflow; no observed CI success is asserted. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. Documentation establishes installation/search requirements for bios.bin, BINDIR80, LIBDIR80, INCDIR80 and required guest libraries/overlays; Windows builds also depend on the matching PDCurses DLL. These are software dependencies, not quantified hardware or minimum-OS requirements. project.notes: Treeki/Ninji’s Rust runner loads original PowerPC PEF MPW executables and replaces imported Mac APIs with host callbacks through Unicorn. macOS is an implemented native-fork path, Windows is an incomplete MacBinary path, and Linux is a conditional user-reported path requiring a source workaround. src/main.rs reads the requested original tool through MacFile, parses its PEF data fork and resources, links it into emulated memory, forwards argv and returns the emulated exit status. README reports MWCPPC from CodeWarrior Pro 1 and DeRez results. These are upstream demonstrations, not independent compatibility tests; this record is the experimental runner rather than CodeWarrior/MPW itself. Root and record ID are absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior dedup index. Inspected main tip: a0d23d515987ae5b486da9430e0b78a02ac93b4f. Substantive emulator/development tooling: src/linker.rs builds transition-vector shims for imported symbols; src/emulator/mod.rs installs InterfaceLib/StdCLib and Toolbox/C-library callbacks and handles them through a PowerPC supervisor-call hook. Original PEF instructions run inside Unicorn without booting Classic Mac OS. Missing imports remain logged, the initialization vector is explicitly unimplemented, and the README lists missing PEF relocations and APIs. XCOFF support is not established. Unicorn is explicitly created with Arch::PPC and Mode::BIG_ENDIAN | Mode::PPC32. The original source platform is Classic Mac OS and source_cpu is PowerPC, specifically 32-bit big-endian PEF executables. This guest configuration says nothing about the native CPU used to run Rust/Unicorn. The inspected Cargo manifest, implementation and complete tree contain no explicit current native-output CPU matrix or host target triplet. The historical commit about Unicorn on M1 Macs is a dependency-workaround report, not a current minimum/support matrix, so target_cpu remains empty. Platform labels preserve implementation intent with important qualifications: native macOS xattrs, incomplete Windows MacBinary handling and Linux only after the manual xattr workaround described in merged PR #1. None is promoted to universal tested support. Cargo.toml selects Rust edition 2021, unicorn-engine dependency version range 2.0.1 and xattr 0.2.2 among the parser/runtime dependencies. No host build recipe matrix or CI exists in the complete tree. PR #1 reports Linux DeRez working only after manually commenting out the xattr::SUPPORTED_PLATFORM branch; that branch still exists at the reviewed tip and the same report reaches unimplemented fseek. Source availability and dependency declarations do not establish a clean build on all intended hosts. No explicit host OS version, CPU model or RAM minimum is documented, so runtime_profiles is empty. src/filesystem.rs uses com.apple.FinderInfo and com.apple.ResourceFork xattrs for the native path. Its MacBinary save branch calls unimplemented!(), after File::create has already opened/truncated the destination; Windows saving is therefore a material limitation, not just an absent test. project.status: Substantive source reviewed; experimental compatibility; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: TOSEMU is Johan Toverland Thelin’s hosted environment for original Atari TOS executables, not a decompilation of one guest application. The current PRG loader opens and maps the supplied file, checks magic 0x601A, constructs the guest environment and applies relocation entries. The tosemu executable runs a program directly; the separate tosaesd daemon supports shared GEM accessory sessions and is not a prerequisite for a single CLI invocation. README explicitly targets integration into Linux and excludes general games/demos. This repository is counted once; its hosted EmuTOS and Musashi components are dependencies, not additional runner discoveries. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot 443340b2dfcf9e691a080bc4e3722102bc9c2839, non-truncated tree with 274 entries. Tooling: original-binary CPU emulation plus TOS system-call reimplementation. src/musashi.c intercepts traps 1, 2, 13 and 14 for GEMDOS, GEM, BIOS and XBIOS, while src/gemdosfile.c maps guest file reads to host stdio and copies data into emulated memory. The guest instructions still execute in Musashi; native host API handling does not make the guest a source port or ahead-of-time translation. Hosted EmuTOS AES/VDI routines supply graphical APIs without booting an Atari ROM. Terminal usage, headless support and self-hosted retro development tests establish the requested runner category, without implying complete TOS or ST hardware compatibility. The guest ISA is Motorola 68000: tossystem.c selects M68K_CPU_TYPE_68000 and musashiconf.h disables later 68010/020/030/040 processors and the PMMU. Original .TTP/.TOS/.PRG guest binaries and TOS belong in source_platforms/source_cpu. The Musashi package’s broader M680x0 support is not TOSEMU support for those later guest CPUs. The FPU entry stubs abort and are not an emulated FPU. Neither the build’s __mcoldfire__ adaptation define nor EmuTOS source ancestry establishes a ColdFire host target. Linux is the explicit host target, but the inspected host Makefile and Ubuntu workflow do not establish a host ISA support matrix or minimum processor. target_cpu remains empty. GCC, C source, -no-pie, 32-bit GEM pointer fields and ubuntu-latest are not sufficient to label x86-64, ARM or another host architecture. The EmuTOS __mcoldfire__ define is a source-adaptation switch selecting portable C rather than a claim that the runnable host program targets ColdFire. README requires recursive Musashi and EmuTOS submodules and make; Makefile uses GCC, generates Musashi opcode tables and links hosted EmuTOS AES/VDI. NO_WAYLAND=1 removes the Wayland/xkbcommon headers, libraries and protocol-generation route; the Ubuntu workflow explicitly uses it for check and emuvdi-check. The GUI route needs Wayland tooling; optional detected integrations include D-Bus, libpng, FreeType/fontconfig and ALSA. The hosted EmuTOS build uses -fno-strict-aliasing and non-PIE flags because guest APIs contain 32-bit pointer fields. Devpac/Lattice tests are separate from building the host runner and require the original installations. Upstream describes excluding SoftFloat and dead-stripping unused later-CPU FPU/MMU code; this review did not inspect a resulting binary or certify link-time license composition. All four build flags remain null; inspected recipes and upstream reports are not local test results. A Linux terminal/headless host profile is documented: tosemu PROGRAM.TTP [arguments], TOSEMU_CONSOLE=terminal and TOSEMU_NO_WINDOW=1; make NO_WAYLAND=1 supports a host build without the graphical dependency. No desktop session or accessory daemon is needed for ordinary CLI execution. No verified CPU, OS-version, RAM or chipset minimum is stated, so none is populated. TOSEMU_MEMORY is guest memory configuration, not a host-RAM minimum. Windows and macOS are not asserted. Host filesystem access is direct: C: defaults to the host root, while TOS_BASE_PATH relocates it and rejects paths resolving outside that base; this is a path-mapping feature, not a demonstrated security sandbox. TOS basepage arguments have a 126-character limit, with the ARGV convention retained for cooperating programs. README explicitly acknowledges use of LLM technology. In the latest 30 default-branch commit messages, 27 contain explicit Claude co-author trailers: the tip names Claude Opus 5.5 and 26 others name Claude Opus 5. This is affirmative development-AI evidence, so ai.usage is true with canonical tool label Claude; model names remain in the evidence text. No AI use is inferred from docs/AGENTS.md, file names, provider addresses, gameplay logic or code style. This is a bounded recent-history review, not a claim about every contribution. README describes inspiration from 68kemu and Wine; neither is merged into this project identity. .gitmodules pins separate Musashi and EmuTOS dependencies; the inspected gitlinks are Musashi 313ebf1bd9f4d0d93341eb5ce21fd8a119e9dbdd and EmuTOS 978e37569bff95841e42675d11fcc6799aad8483. TOSEMU’s COPYING carries GPLv2 and source headers allow v2 or later; Musashi has its permissive MIT-like grant, and the hosted EmuTOS documentation records its GPL lineage. README/Makefile explicitly distinguish bundled later-CPU SoftFloat/MAME code from what upstream says is linked, so redistribution still needs the actual chosen build/dependency licenses checked. Original HiSoft Devpac 3.10 GEN.TTP and Lattice C 5.60 LC1.TTP, LC2.TTP, CLINK.TTP, LC.TTP and MAKE.TTP have documented upstream test recipes; those commercial installations must be obtained separately under their own rights. Their upstream self-hosting/byte-comparison claims are not independent verification by this audit. project.notes: Mark Ogden’s maintained Thames source explicitly derives from John Elliott’s Thames 0.1.1. Elliott’s official page identifies an ISIS-II runner for the tools used to build CP/M3, and the maintained loader/interpreter confirm direct original-binary execution. Count the original tarball and enhanced fork as one lineage under ogdenpm/thames-src. CP/M3 is the build product of example guest tools, not the OS API being emulated. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: dd545328888b6e989c5975053372d97a36dc336f. Modern tooling executes linked ISIS-II Intel OMF images, often without file extensions. isis_load accepts module/start/data/end records, loads bytes and rejects unresolved relocation/external/library records. main creates synthetic MDS BIOS/ISIS trap stubs in RAM, loads the argv-selected tool and enters the interpreter. ISIS OPEN/CLOSE/READ/WRITE/SEEK/LOAD translate to host files through device mapping; the path needs original tools/support files but no original boot ROM or booted ISIS OS. ISIS-II 8080/8085 binaries are the intended guest source. Ian Collier’s xz80 engine was reduced to 8080/8085 semantics by default; thames.h leaves Z80 disabled and documents an optional build switch. The VS Release|x64 project sets Z80 for thames.c only, not the z80.c interpreter unit; this is a configuration caveat, not evidence of universal Z80 compatibility. Source_cpu therefore records 8080 and 8085, preserving optional Z80 ancestry in notes. The Visual Studio project explicitly has Win32 and x64 configurations and MachineX86 for Win32, supporting host x86 and x86-64 labels. Windows/Linux device paths and Unix usage are explicit in documentation. The CMake route is portable C but provides no further CPU guarantee. macOS is not asserted merely from Unix/CMake portability; guest 8080/8085 and code emitted by ASM48/ASM51/PLM80 are not host architectures. CMake >=3.5 builds the C sources and runs Perl Scripts/getVersion.pl to generate version headers; a checked-in VS solution/project is the alternative. Unix line endings matter to the version generator’s dirty-tree detection. The complete tree contains no GitHub Actions workflow. Documentation’s successful guest-tool lists are maintainer reports, not current-host build proof, and the per-file VS Z80 define needs review if enabling the optional mode. No build or guest test was attempted. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. No numerical host RAM/CPU-generation floor or minimum OS release was established. The 64 KiB emulated address space and ISIS 6.3 filename limits are guest properties, while Windows SDK10/v143 are build settings rather than runtime minima. runtime_profiles remains empty. project.display_title: run68x — Human68k command-line executable runner
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: run68x is the maintained Human68k CUI emulator derived from run68. The README names rururutan/run68 and several run68mac forks as origins. The current C implementation has its own executable loader, 68000 interpreter, debugger and Human68k-compatible services. One family is counted; original run68 and the linked macOS variants are lineage references, not additional discoveries. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: fc28826dd795b1f0a3241f0b03fe2353e12e7233. Modern tooling executes original Human68k .X and raw .R programs from argv, using host files and the existing terminal. load.c reads the HU header, performs relocation and initializes BSS; run68.c builds a PSP and enters the interpreter. DOS calls, IOCS and FE floating-point helpers are implemented in host C. The initialized HUMAN.SYS name represents a synthetic PSP, not a required OS image. The inspected direct-run path needs no original ROM or booted Human68k. The guest is the Motorola 68000 instruction set, explicitly retained even when the -himem option expands addressability. The interpreter dispatches instructions by their upper nibble. High memory is a non-hardware-compatible extension and does not imply a 68020/68060 guest. The X-file loader rejects bound executables; partial DOS/IOCS and graphics-related stubs do not establish arbitrary X68000 application or hardware compatibility. The host executable has explicit Windows x64 evidence in README and the win-x64 release workflow, so target_cpu is x86-64. Windows and Ubuntu under WSL are maintainer-confirmed build environments. Linux and macOS also have configured CMake workflows with successful runs for this exact head. No host ISA is inferred from macos-latest, ubuntu-latest, C source, or the emulated 68000. NetBSD/MSYS/Emscripten conditionals are retained as portability hints, not verified runtime ports. CMake >=3.22 builds C11 source, with shlwapi on Windows and libm plus optional/default iconv on non-MSVC routes. README confirms Visual Studio 2022 x64 and WSL Ubuntu 24.04. At the pinned head GitHub reports successful Windows/Linux CMake, macOS CMake, win-x64 release and CodeQL runs. These are observed upstream results, not independent builds. CMake contains no registered tests; a successful ctest workflow step cannot prove guest compatibility. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. No explicit minimum host OS version, CPU generation, RAM or terminal requirement was established for the shipped outputs. VS2022 and Ubuntu 24.04 are build/test environments, and the 16–768 MiB -himem values describe emulated guest memory, not host minimum RAM. runtime_profiles remains empty. Experimental UTF-8 reading affects every read-only file including binaries, so enabling it can invalidate inputs; this option is not universal encoding compatibility. project.status: Substantive source reviewed; experimental compatibility; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: ParaTos is an experimental direct runner for original Atari TOS/MiNT command-line applications. README identifies Linux and explains the system-call translation approach. gemdos/loader.c reads and endian-converts the PRG header, builds the basepage/environment, copies text/data, applies relocation fixups and appends ARGV data. paratos.c loads the named executable and enters the CPU engine directly, without an ST machine boot. A 2023 upstream commit explicitly added OSX support, and current Apple-specific executable-path and byte-order code remains present; this refines the earlier discovery’s Linux-only evidence without asserting that a modern macOS build was tested. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot 9d43e70bce3ed4f82ee43e35375994332fc2ac4b, non-truncated tree with 106 entries. Tooling with CPU-emulator and GEMDOS/API-reimplementation capabilities. ParaTos invokes Musashi to execute original 68k instructions and dispatches guest trap calls to native host implementations; gemdos/path.c converts TOS/MiNT filenames to POSIX paths, with case-insensitive and 8.3-name lookup. It accepts U: and rejects other drive-letter mappings in this snapshot. This is not a compiler translating the guest to host source and not an ST hardware emulator. README restricts the intended programs to clean command-line tools avoiding direct hardware and OS trap-vector patching. The implementation is incomplete, and minimal BIOS/AES/VDI paths do not establish a desktop compatibility environment. The historical binaries are 68k TOS/MiNT programs. README calls the bundled engine m68000, while current paratos.c explicitly chooses M68K_CPU_TYPE_68020 for execution and disassembly. source_cpu records the documented 68000 family entry point and the concrete 68020 guest engine rather than silently retaining the discovery’s m68000-only description. paratos.c states that the FPU is not emulated. The test cross-toolchain prefix m68k-atari-mintelf- produces guest .tos binaries; it is not evidence for the CPU of the Linux/macOS host. memory.c contains an explicit __x86_64__ host branch that reserves the 68020’s four-gigabyte address space; this supports recording x86-64 as an implemented host target, not a tested runtime minimum. The alternative branch reserves 512 MiB and is not an identified support matrix for every 32-bit or ARM host; no additional CPU is inferred from that fallback, C11, Clang or macOS. memory.i explicitly assumes host unaligned loads/stores. Source-level Apple portability exists, but Apple Silicon support is not verified and is not implied by target_platforms including macOS. CMakeLists.txt declares CMake 3.10, C11, bundled mushashi and gemdos subdirectories and a paratos executable. Clang warning adjustments and the later explicit opcode-table definitions document maintenance of that route; they do not prove current build success. The original OSX-support commit adds Apple byte order and executable-path logic, with guarded host API differences, retained at the inspected tip. The guest test directory requires make plus a m68k-atari-mintelf- cross-toolchain and produces hello.tos, echo_args.tos, exit_code.tos and syscall proxies. The host virtual-memory and unaligned-access assumptions require validation on any selected platform. All four build flags remain null; inspected recipes and upstream reports are not local test results. Windows is unverified. Current memory.c reserves guest virtual address space and commits an initial region; these are implementation details, not host hardware requirements. The syscall-proxy suite shows intended testing scope, not successful commercial compiler execution. Trap #1 coverage remains incomplete, FPU operations are unsupported, and direct hardware/trap-vector dependencies remain outside the stated intended scope. project.notes: David Lee’s NT Virtual DOS Machine is an independent portable 8086/text-mode DOS runner, distinct from Microsoft’s system NTVDM component. ntvdm.cxx loads .COM and MZ/ZM .EXE files, applies relocations and runs i8086.cxx. README documents direct console/script use of MASM, Link, Microsoft C, Turbo Pascal/C, QuickBasic and other legacy tools. Original test software is included but does not become reconstructed source or separate runner records. Inspected default-branch head: 0649657d912f23e60b32971d1c45653d48b440e3. Tooling combines an 8086 interpreter with partial DOS 3.00-style APIs, BIOS/text-console and selected interrupt behavior. The loader creates PSP/environment and synthetic interrupt stubs; DOS file calls use native host fopen/fread/fwrite and -r maps a host directory to C:. Original executables run without a booted DOS OS or vendor ROM in the normal path. Optional boot-sector loading does not establish a complete PC hardware emulator. The guest CPU is explicitly Intel 8086 and source_platforms=DOS; a compiler producing other target code does not change the executed guest ISA. README excludes graphics, sound and mouse and cautions that CPU/cycle fidelity is incomplete. It documents application-specific limitations such as QuickC incremental linker access to missing memory control blocks and a COBOL linker requiring 286. The 8086 capability must not be expanded to general 286/protected-mode compatibility. README explicitly lists Windows x64/ARM64, Linux x64/x32/ARM32/ARM64/RISC-V, and macOS ARM64 M1/M3. It also reports big-endian builds for 68000 via m68 and SPARC v8 via sparcos, which are emulated-runtime outputs rather than independent tests on physical legacy machines. Canonical x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64, RISC-V and m68000 labels are retained. The pinned m68/ntvdm/mntvdm.sh recipe explicitly selects 68000 and builds ntvdm.elf using the newlib/BSP route; it assumes guest source files have been made available locally, and was not run. The SPARC-v8/Linux route through sparcos remains an explicit maintainer runtime claim in notes: no concrete ntvdm SPARC build/output recipe was identified, so SPARC is omitted from target_cpu. No cross-product guarantee across all hosts and CPUs is claimed. MSVC/g++ scripts build the C++ interpreter/runtime; Linux release links statically with OpenMP and macOS uses pthread/signed-char settings. mr.sh deliberately uses -O2 and documents a maintainer-observed g++11.4 -O3/-Ofast code-generation problem. The pinned-head Windows-2022 MSVC CI run succeeded and archived ntvdm.exe, but its workflow runs no guest regression suite. project.display_title: ntvcm — CP/M 8080/Z80 command-line runner
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: NT Virtual CP/M Machine is a standalone C++ command-line runner for CP/M .COM tools. ntvcm.cxx loads a selected host file at guest 0x100, creates CP/M entry hooks and enters x80.cxx. README documents asm/load, Turbo Pascal, Aztec C, WordStar and many other tools; they are compatibility examples, not separately reconstructed projects. The current head has removed the former GDB/MI debugger-host mode, so it is not advertised as a current capability. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: be598f65c1b649f5250dcd6d8fef266b1b86413e. An emulator with native CP/M BDOS/file and console translation, an 8080/Z80 trace disassembler and optional per-PC CSV profiling. It executes original instructions and synthesizes BDOS/BIOS hooks rather than booting a CP/M disk or requiring an original ROM. Host fopen/fread/fwrite implement FCB file operations. Original guest tools must be supplied with their own overlays/data; this record is the runner, not a full disk/hardware emulator or compiler reconstruction. x80.cxx and README explicitly implement Z80 with optional -8 8080 mode, making both guest source ISAs. CP/M 2.2 is the main guest API, supplemented by selected CP/M 3 and nonstandard services. README excludes BIOS disk-layout access, undocumented 8080 instructions and precise cycle accuracy. Recent commits distinguish optional Z80 R/MEMPTR accuracy and unattached I/O gaps; upstream validation reports do not establish universal instruction/hardware compatibility. msvcenv.bat explicitly selects Windows x86, x64 and ARM64 native toolchains. README documents a RISC-V Linux output runnable under RVOS and a real-mode DOS Watcom output; mwatcom.bat uses -0 with the DOS target, grounding 8086. Canonical target labels refer to these host executables, while source 8080/Z80 remains separate. RVOS’s AMD64/ARM32/etc host list does not automatically prove native ntvcm ports on every such system. Linux/macOS recipes do not establish an exhaustive ISA matrix. Native MSVC/g++ recipes and the Watcom real-mode DOS route are present. Unix release scripts default to RSS disabled; enabling RSS introduces cpp-httplib/OpenSSL dependencies, and README reports unresolved macOS RSS-enabled builds. Windows mr.bat enables RSS. A pinned-head Windows-2022 MSVC CI run succeeded and archived ntvcm.exe; the workflow contains no guest-test step. These observed upstream build results remain separate from maintainer CPU-test claims and this unrun review. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. The real-mode DOS output and explicit host toolchain choices are preserved in target fields, but no numeric RAM or supported minimum DOS/Windows/macOS/Linux version is established. Guest 64 KiB layout, 80x24 console mode and emulated MHz are not host memory/CPU minima. runtime_profiles stays empty. CR/LF inputs, uppercase/lowercase handling, terminal escape conversion and optional RSS dependencies materially affect actual workflows and need chosen-host testing. types: original DOS binary emulator with host DOS and BIOS API translation
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: Takeda Toshiya’s MS-DOS Player family, represented by cracyc’s maintained vt branch, runs original DOS command-line utilities directly against Windows files and console services. The official site and maintained fork are one counted project family. readme.txt explicitly targets 16-bit DOS command-line utilities and demonstrates msdos lcc sample.c followed by msdos sample.exe. msdos.cpp identifies Takeda as author, loads MZ/ZM EXEs with relocation and otherwise uses the COM entry at 0x100. The selected maintained source root is cracyc/msdos-player, default branch vt. Its README credits imported fixes from the cracyc fork; the official Takeda distribution is lineage/context, not a second project. Root and record ID are absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior dedup index. Inspected vt tip: b3ebaa8452be478afec604361db32e9451eb43e2. Emulator/development tooling with CPU execution plus DOS/BIOS service translation. The INT 21h dispatch sends 3Dh/3Fh/40h/4Bh to host-backed open/read/write/execute handling. The direct console workflow does not boot a DOS disk image, but this is not a CPU-only layer: text-mode hardware scaffolding, memory services and optional driver/VDD support exist. README excludes Win16, graphics/sound hardware and gaming as the project’s goal; protected-mode capabilities vary by CPU build. Original COM/MZ DOS binaries are x86 guests. README lists separate 8086, 80286, 80386, 80486, Pentium4, NEC V30 and IA32 emulation variants, including protected-mode capabilities and an optional V30 8080 mode. Canonical source_cpu=x86 describes the principal DOS guest ISA without mistaking the emulated model labels for host CPU requirements or claiming full PC compatibility. README explicitly distinguishes _x86 binaries for 32/64-bit Windows and _x64 binaries for 64-bit Windows; msdos.vcxproj independently contains Win32 and x64 output configurations. These support host target_cpu x86 and x86-64. The i86/i286/i386 suffixes and HAS_I286 macro select the emulated guest core, not the native output ISA. No native Linux or macOS support is established by these Windows/MinGW recipes. Source includes Visual C++ projects and build batch routes, plus MinGW Makefile.mingw. Current CI is configured on windows-latest for i86, V30, i286, i386 and i486 variants; it is configuration evidence rather than an observed successful run. The older simple Makefile selects an i586-mingw32msvc cross compiler and Windows libraries, so it does not establish a native Unix build. README’s packaged-binary count says 12 but lists 14 variants; record variant names rather than repeating that count. All four build flags remain null; no candidate compilation, guest execution, emulation, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. Two host-output profiles retain explicit _x86 versus _x64 Windows requirements from the README. No Windows version or numerical host RAM minimum is established from the reviewed pinned material. The emulated 1/16/32 MB memory configuration is guest memory, not host RAM. Direct commands use host paths; original COMMAND.COM is needed for batch execution. VDD support is limited to selected 32-bit process builds with companion ntvdm.exe and is not available in x64 process builds. One family combines Takeda’s MS-DOS Player and the cracyc maintained fork; GitHub fork=false is hosting metadata and does not negate the documented lineage. README licenses source under GPL v2 and credits MAME CPU cores, Neko Project 21/W, DOSBox/DOSBox-X, DOSVAXJ3 and ReactOS-derived portions; component notices need preservation. Guest DOS compilers, commands, libraries and COMMAND.COM retain separate rights and must be supplied lawfully. This is neither Microsoft’s original NTVDM nor davidly/ntvdm. project.display_title: m68 — CP/M-68K and 68000 executable runner
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
project.notes: m68 directly loads 68000 CP/M-68K .68K, Linux-style ELF and Motorola hex programs. The repository contains a substantial custom C++ 68000 interpreter, executable loaders and host OS-service implementations. README and cpm/m.sh show original Digital Research compiler/assembler/linker stages being invoked through m68; MT Pascal, CB68 BASIC, DDT, SVS tools and Forth examples are documented uses of this one runner. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: 45b0c7378c7adc4433141d33cf5dd119b9cca612. A tooling emulator and partial OS-API reimplementation, not recovered source for the guest compilers. load_cpm68k reads the 0x601a executable header, creates a basepage and relocates text/data/BSS; trap 2 implements BDOS and trap 3 BIOS, with host fopen/fread-backed files. Trap 0 handles supported Linux-style services and trap 15 Fondse-style calls. The direct-run path constructs runtime state without booting CP/M or loading a ROM. 68000 is explicit in README, m68000.cxx and the loaders. CP/M-68K is retained under canonical CP/M; Linux here means the supported m68k ELF/syscall convention, not every Linux executable. README requires its newlib startup/BSP stubs for sample applications, and source explicitly limits BDOS to calls used by tested compiler families. Addresses are not constrained to physical 68000 24-bit behavior. Nested 6502/Z80/x86 interpreters running as guests do not expand m68 itself into those guest ISAs. README explicitly reports host tests on AMD64 Windows/Ubuntu, ARM64 Raspberry Pi OS/Ubuntu/macOS, ARM32 Raspberry Pi 4 and RISC-V64 Debian. Canonical target labels preserve x86-64, ARM64, ARM and RISC-V. c_tests/mm68.sh also targets -mcpu=68000 with m68k-elf-gcc to run m68 recursively in an existing m68 instance; target_cpu=m68000 refers to that distinct emulated-runtime output, not an asserted physical CP/M host port or arbitrary Linux/m68k compatibility. MSVC and g++ release scripts compile the emulator; the Linux recipe links statically and the macOS recipe sets signed-char behavior. The nested 68000 build uses m68k-elf-gcc, explicit 68000 options and newlib BSP support. Guest cross-compiler construction is separate: README reports GCC 8.2 build difficulties on macOS/Pi 5 and a GCC13 guest-test issue. These are maintainer claims, not independent failures here. No .github/workflows entry exists in the complete tree; no CI result is asserted. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. The documented host test matrix and build toolchains do not specify a minimum supported CPU generation, RAM or OS version for a runnable m68 output. The default 40 MiB heap/mmap spaces and command-line size options describe guest address-space allocation, not minimum host RAM. The special Forth83 0x500 load address is a guest compatibility caveat. runtime_profiles remains empty rather than generalizing test machines or nested emulation into hardware minima. The selected primary documentation, implementation/build/licence sources and latest 30 default-branch commit metadata contain no explicit affirmative development-AI attribution. ai.usage remains null with no tool names; absence is not proof of non-use. This is a bounded latest-30 review, not full-history proof. Agent/config filenames, provider/bot email domains, implementation language, project age and gameplay AI are not authorship evidence. Root LICENSE dedicates the emulator work under CC0-1.0. Checked-in Digital Research, Manx/Aztec, SVS, Forth and other legacy tools/support files retain their own rights; CC0 does not relicense third-party binaries or libraries. The README explicitly says the DOS-hosted Aztec C68K distribution requires a DOS emulator such as davidly/ntvdm: that compiler is not itself a native m68 guest. ntvcm/ntvdm nested builds and RVOS/ARMOS are related independent runners, not aliases of m68. project.notes: Kelvin W. Sherlock’s mpw executes original 68K Macintosh Programmer’s Workshop commands directly from a macOS shell, combining the WinFellow-derived 680x0 CPU with a minimal Classic Mac OS Toolbox and MPW runtime. README identifies the mpw command, author, tool-search layout and native-shell invocation. toolbox/loader.cpp opens the original resource fork, loads CODE resource 0, constructs the A5/jump-table state and brings in additional CODE segments. This is a substantive original-tool runner, not a source-port compiler or a script around a fully booted Mac. Root and record ID are absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior dedup index. Inspected master tip: a6b58bf3828e78388ab70ce53bf7be7bbff19d18. Tooling with emulator and development-environment capabilities. The loader executes original guest instructions; toolbox/dispatch.cpp translates Classic Mac OS Open/Read/Write traps, and toolbox/os.cpp plus mpw/mpw_io.cpp route guest I/O into host-backed FDEntry operations. API reimplementation and embedded CPU emulation are distinct parts of the same runner. No full-Mac, arbitrary-tool or full-API compatibility is established. The original guest ISA is Motorola 680x0, grounded by the README’s WinFellow CPU attribution and loader/register conventions. Classic Mac OS belongs in source_platforms and m68k in source_cpu. A 68K MPW compiler producing PowerPC or Apple IIGS output would not establish that this runner executes PowerPC or 65816 guest instructions. types: PDP-11 Unix user-mode instruction simulator with native syscall translation
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; build and runtime independently untested
project.notes: Warren Toomey’s Apout loads original PDP-11 Unix a.out programs, interprets user-mode instructions and maps TRAP system calls to native Unix calls without booting a guest OS or disk filesystem. Current README 2.4 reports testing on 64-bit Debian Linux. The canonical DoctorWkt repository supplies the current Apout 2.4 source and identifies supported historical Unix binary families. main.c accepts an original pdp11_binary and arguments; aout.c identifies a.out magic/ABI, loads instructions and data and supports 2.11BSD overlays. Original commands and compiler binaries are guest inputs, not restored native-host sources. Root and record ID are absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior dedup index. Inspected master tip: bd9af21bd8bb2fa956dcda5db0b0aeec2cffc8f7. Emulator/development tooling: cpu.c fetches and dispatches original PDP-11 instructions, while v7trap.c directly implements guest read/write/open through native calls and bsdtrap.c provides a separate 2.11BSD ABI. APOUT_ROOT rewrites absolute guest paths; relative paths remain host-relative. This is not a full PDP-11 machine or guest OS boot. It provides host-file access, not containment; NATIVES is enabled by the Makefile and unrecognized binaries can be attempted with host execv. README explicitly names user-mode PDP-11 instructions and V1/V2/V5/V6/V7/2.9BSD/2.11BSD a.out guests; cpu.c supplies the PDP-11 register/instruction loop and aout.c selects the historical ABI. PDP-11 is a needed new canonical guest CPU label rather than x86, m68k or a host endian label. Source platform uses the existing Unix label, with guest versions retained in notes. README reports a 64-bit Debian Linux host and expects 32-bit little-endian Unix to compile, while excluding big-endian machines. Width and byte order do not identify an ISA, so target_cpu is empty: neither Debian nor 64-bit means x86-64. defines.h has Linux, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD and Apple portability branches and the latest history includes OpenBSD/musl fixes, but those do not establish a current complete host test matrix. The Makefile builds C sources with a C compiler, make and libm, with configurable emulation/debug options. Its current default APOUT_OPTIONS uses -DEMU211 -DEMUv1 -DNATIVES, but source checks the uppercase EMUV1; consequently the default spelling does not enable V1/V2. README likewise says V1 is disabled by default. README 2.4 is current but the Makefile’s distribution VERSION remains apout2.3beta1, so that old packaging string is not the current release claim. LIMITATIONS documents guest-specific compiler/archiver workarounds. All four build flags remain null; no candidate compilation, guest execution, emulation, gameplay or byte comparison was performed. README explicitly requires a little-endian host and Unix services; it reports testing on 64-bit Debian and expects 32-bit little-endian Unix portability. A host-environment profile records the endian/Unix requirement without inventing a CPU family, OS version or RAM floor. events.title: Use the two-half touch joystick in every layout; drop the two-finger turn
events.message:
Use the two-half touch joystick in every layout; drop the two-finger turn

Portrait touch fell through to the mouse gestures (tap to walk,
double-tap to leap, self-tap for the menu) because side touch was only
switched on by the fullscreen and landscape classes.  That was
accretion, not design: portrait was not a target when the joystick
went in.  Touch now always uses side touch; the mouse keeps its
gestures.  A tap on the status panel no longer opens the menu on
touch in portrait, matching landscape: the two-finger hold does.

Two fingers tapped together now trigger, like any other tap, instead
of turning the figure around.  Saul: "unnecessary and provisional
anyway".

What's left to teach a touch player is three things: hold or swipe to
move, tap a second finger to jump, hold two fingers for the menu.

Tests: the portrait browser check now walks with a held half and opens
the inventory with a two-finger hold (after the opening fall and
knockdown in B8, since airborne touches steer at once).  The browser
tests that drove the pointer gestures by touch now drive them by
mouse; the touch EAT block and the touch tap on the menu button are
gone, as touch can no longer reach those paths.

The spec, README and port Status describe one touch scheme.  The
spec's lone-tap row now says the game ignores the trigger with the
stick centred.

events.title: Click the power button on press, not release
events.message:
Click the power button on press, not release

The power button toggled on click, which waits for the mouse or finger
to come up, so the click sound trailed the press.  It now toggles on
pointerdown.  Keyboard and programmatic clicks (detail 0) still toggle
through onclick.  A pointer's own click only re-unlocks audio, since a
touch pointerdown is not a user activation and the context may only
start then.  mousedown's default is prevented so the button does not
take focus back from the screen.

The click files lose their 5 ms of leading silence as well.

events.title: fix(cd): serialize the HLE CD streaming state (#803)
events.message:
fix(cd): serialize the HLE CD streaming state (#803)

* fix(cd): serialize the HLE CD streaming state (#787)

The HLE BIOS streams CD_read data into RAM at drive rate from statics in
jagcd_hle.c (hleStream, the CD_read/CD_poll bookkeeping, the #766 align
phase) that were never in the state blob. Measured with
test_runahead_determinism: Hover Strike (HLE) failed all four checks at
warmup 200/400/700/1000; Myst (HLE) failed while its reads were in
flight (200/400) and passed after. Cart (yarc) and Hover Strike with the
real BIOS at 1000 pass, so the leak was the HLE path.

Append an HLE chunk strictly last, behind a magic word ("HLE1"),
extending v15 in place (v15 is still develop-only). Field by field, never
the raw struct (padding, sizeof(bool)). hle_active is boot-strategy
configuration and is not saved. A damaged bufOff/written drops the
transfer rather than reading past the sector buffer.

Backward compatibility, measured by saving at frame 400 (mid-stream) and
loading into this build:
- v14 states from v3.6.1 load and run byte-identically (per-frame hash
  CSV) to v3.6.1 loading its own state, for Hover Strike and Myst.
- v15 states written by develop before this change (zero-filled tail)
  load with the in-flight transfer dropped, as before.
- New states resume the transfer (Hover Strike: 200 distinct frames
  after load vs a frozen black screen without the chunk).
A pre-#787 state saved mid-read still cannot resume that read on any
build -- that data was never saved.

After: all eight runs above pass all four checks. make test gains a
ROM-gated Hover Strike HLE run-ahead check at warmup 400 (passes here,
exits 1 on the pre-#787 build).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(cd): validate a restored HLE stream; synthetic mid-stream round trip

Review on #803:
- Copilot: a damaged or crafted state could set dest near $FFFFFFFF,
  wrapping HLEStreamFinish's dest+total bound check into an out-of-bounds
  write, or point the GPU data base where CD_poll's +0/+8 reads land
  outside RAM. Load now requires dest/total/reqTotal/written and the
  CD_poll range to fit main RAM, and both data bases to be 0, main RAM or
  GPU local RAM; otherwise it drops the transfer and those pointers.
- Copilot: CI has no private discs, so nothing exercised an active
  stream through save/load. test_cd_synth_read gains
  inflight_stream_survives_savestate_round_trip on its synthetic disc:
  save mid-stream, finish, restore, and the same transfer must be in
  flight and complete byte-exact. Red with the chunk load disabled.
- Kimi: check room for the ~2.4 KB chunk before writing it, not after;
  JaguarCDHLEStateSize() is pinned to what Save writes by the same test.

events.title: Grip the shovel by each clip's share of the layered arm pose
events.message:
Grip the shovel by each clip's share of the layered arm pose

The grip slid between the carry's and the dig's by dig / (dig + carry), while
the bones layer the dig over the carry: at a full dig with the carry still
fading the arm was already in the dig pose but the shaft kept sliding through
the fist, pulling the other hand off its grip. The carry's share now counts
only what the dig leaves of it (and only as far as the clips own the arm). A
Vitest case checks the dig grip exactly while the carry still fades.

events.title: Ease each arm's clip ownership so a hand taken or given back blends
events.message:
Ease each arm's clip ownership so a hand taken or given back blends

When the code took the right arm (a gesture, a contact, a steadying hand) the
gait swing and the shovel carry dropped off it in one frame, snapping the arm
from the clip pose to the code pose (about 3 rad on a carrying walker). Each
arm now has a clip weight eased toward its free state over the transition
time, and the gait and carry layers blend by it. A Vitest case hands the
right arm (and briefly the left) to the code mid-walk and back.

events.title: Fade a lifted foot's hold correction over the gait cycle instead of dropping it
events.message:
Fade a lifted foot's hold correction over the gait cycle instead of dropping it

The held contacts' mean miss divided its own fading weight back out, so a lone
contact restored the full correction until it crossed the touch height, and
the foot jumped the whole miss after a turn or shove. The mean is now held
only as firmly as the firmest contact, and once no contact holds firm the
correction eases toward what is left over plantFadeCycle (calibratable, 0.15
of the cycle) of the phase walked, since the contacts lift within a frame or
two. A Vitest case shoves a walker sideways and bounds every later per-frame
foot step across the release.

- BankMirrors: "biased" identifying encoding (byte == bank + B on banks
  congruent to low mod 2^modBits, B == realized bank count, a power of two);
  tried only after every classic form fails. A biased byte is never a value
  source or RESTORED read-back -- its only consumer is the trampoline walk.

project.title: ACEBasicJS — browser compiler and Amiga-inspired runtime
project.display_title: ACEBasicJS — browser compiler and Amiga-inspired runtime
project.status: Substantive source reviewed; build, runtime and binary parity independently untested
project.notes: New recursive-descent ACE BASIC-to-JavaScript compiler with browser runtime for Amiga-inspired screens/windows, input, graphics, sound, menus and turtle commands. Compiler explicitly treats C ACE as a reference specification; it emits JavaScript and does not emulate Amiga hardware. Source and static-server instructions are present. Compatibility is incremental and tied to documented seed programs, not full ACE/AmigaOS equivalence. No standalone license file was found in this repository; original ACE licensing should not automatically be copied to the new implementation. The browser project treats native C ACE and its BASIC language/documentation as a reference specification; compiler.js explicitly says C ACE remains reference-only. No original binary is the input to this implementation, so source_cpu is not applicable; historical 68000 assembly output is lineage context. compiler.js is a new recursive-descent compiler emitting JavaScript; runtime.js supplies browser implementations of selected Amiga-style interfaces. It neither emits 68k binaries nor embeds Amiga CPU emulation, and browser JavaScript has no single verified host ISA. README gives static-server instructions and describes incrementally implemented control flow, graphics, sound, windows and seed examples. This is not evidence of complete ACE/AmigaOS compatibility, and this review did not compile or run any seed program. All build flags stay null. The runtime is browser-based; a static HTTP server is required for fetch-based example loading. No browser-version, CPU or memory minimum was established. Native ACE’s 512 KiB/Workbench requirements must not be copied to ACEBasicJS. Distinct new JavaScript compiler/runtime by original ACE author David Benn, not another archive of the already-tracked enhanced native ACE compiler. Original ACE and vidarh’s fork are parser/language references. No standalone repository license was found, so original ACE’s GPL terms cannot automatically be assigned to this new implementation. Original-author README attributes planning to Claude chat and implementation collaboration to Cursor; Cursor Agent commit co-authorship corroborates this. Original author explicitly attributes planning to Claude chat and implementation collaboration to Cursor; recent commit has Cursor Agent co-authorship. Review used cached primary repository metadata/tree, README when present, selected implementation/build/license files and available recent commit messages. No candidate was compiled, installed, executed, emulated or playtested here, and no original-binary comparison was performed. Repository creation and historical release years are not treated as the reverse-engineering start date. events.message:
Draw the 1702's own keys, LED and volume panel in the narrow layouts

The cropped phone layout and the caseless narrow layout fell back to
generic widgets: a grey icon button, a native range slider, and a power
switch with the LED inside it.  Every non-portable layout (new `keyed`
class) now uses the same art as the faceplate, redrawn in flat CSS with
colours taken from 1702.svg and 1702-dark.svg:

- fullscreen and power are the traced key (shadow plate, body, top band)
  with their Arial labels; on the faceplate the drawn art still shows
  through and the replicas stay hidden.
- the volume control is the traced panel: ticks, track, slot and label
  as an inline SVG under the faceplate-style thumb.  Its hit box is at
  least 32px tall everywhere.
- the power LED moved out of the button.  On the cabinet it sits in the
  badge as drawn; caseless puts it at the centre of the chin.

Cropped: fullscreen moves in to x 64mm, power to the gap between badge
and model plate (251mm), and the volume panel covers the cropped drawn
one from 256mm.  Caseless: one row (fullscreen, version key, centre LED,
volume, power).

events.title: Cut the first load from 2 MB to 0.56 MB and flatten its request chain
events.message:
Cut the first load from 2 MB to 0.56 MB and flatten its request chain

Measured on an emulated Pixel 7 at slow 4G (150 ms, 1.6 Mbps, 4x CPU)
over HTTP/2 + brotli: the title frame drops from 6.2 s to 2.9 s cold and
from 1.75 s to 0.91 s on a repeat visit.

- Desk tray images are 2x webp thumbnails (tools/thumbs.py, make thumbs)
  instead of the full scans: about 95 kB instead of 990 kB.
- The open box image is lazy, and a book fetches pages only while on
  screen; neighbouring spreads preload once the reader hovers, focuses,
  or turns.  The box still shows during loading, so its cover loads then.
- Dev notes are a separate dev-notes.html fetched on first open; the game
  pages shrink from 192 kB to 22 kB.
- Game pages carry modulepreload hints for main.js's whole import graph
  and fetch preloads for every data, charset and sprite file, and
  charsets/sprites no longer wait for rooms.json.
- _headers caches images, fonts and sounds for a day with a 30-day
  stale-while-revalidate; HTML, JS and data still revalidate because
  their names are not fingerprinted.  netlify dev overrides
  Cache-Control locally, so this only shows on a deploy.

The book browser test now opens the box before turning it, since a
hidden book no longer loads pages.

events.title: Stop the status panel flashing on touch; keep its taps off the menu button
events.message:
Stop the status panel flashing on touch; keep its taps off the menu button

Saul wants to play one-handed with two fingers on the status panel, and
the panel blinked on every touch.  The panel is covered by the
transparent #command-menu button, and Chrome flashes its default tap
highlight (18% black) over a tapped button.  #play now sets a
transparent tap highlight.

Touches on the panel already reached the side controls.  The button's
click skipped side-touch taps only when the click carried pointerType,
which Safari's does not, so there a panel tap could also open the menu.
The click now falls back to the pointerType of the press on the button;
keyboard activation (detail 0) still opens the menu.  Whether Saul's
phone hit this is unknown.

The landscape browser test now walks, leaps and opens and closes the
menu with two fingers on the panel alone.

project.status: source-reviewed; no independent build, runtime or byte-exact test
project.notes: Native PowerPC SANA-II virtio-net-pci driver implementing legacy PCI transport, virtqueues, packet paths and Roadshow integration for AmigaOS 4.1. Source virtio.c implements I/O register access and device/queue setup; Makefile builds device.c plus virtio.c with ppc-amigaos-gcc. Upstream reports end-to-end TCP on QEMU sam460ex, approximately 24–25 Mbit/s with zero retransmissions in measured runs. Legacy/transitional virtio device supported; modern-only 0x1041 is not yet supported. Introductory multi-gigabit claims are generic aspirations; actual documented measurements are much lower and slower than the e1000 comparison. License says same as sibling virte1000 without a license file in this repository; licensing remains unresolved. Only QEMU testing is established upstream. Upstream records end-to-end Roadshow TCP traffic and sustained ~24–25 Mbit/s on QEMU sam460ex, with code/build and supporting commits inspected. events.title: Rebuild landscape touch as a two-half joystick and trigger
events.message:
Rebuild landscape touch as a two-half joystick and trigger

Saul asked for a simpler model: the screen splits into left and right
halves, a hold or swipe on either is the joystick at that moment, a
tap is the trigger, and a hold plus a tap leaps.  The touch layer now
ignores game state except for a lone tap in the air, menus, and a tap
while pointing down; the C64 code already decides what a held
direction means (centring stops a walk and leaves a glide alone).

Gestures, as written into docs/spec/input.md:
- One finger held without a swipe points the stick at its half after
  120 ms, at once in the air.
- A swipe points it the swipe's way on either half; the vertical part
  outranks the sideways one, and back near the start centres it.
- A lone quick tap triggers on the ground and nudges in the air (Saul:
  every fall, not only the glide).
- A second-finger tap triggers on lift, and does nothing while the
  stick points down (the C64 maps fire+down to the menu).
- Two fingers held 200 ms without swiping open the command menu, or
  close it; this replaces the both-sides chord.
- Two quick taps landing together turn the figure around.  Saul wants
  to see whether he notices this one at all.  In menus they confirm.

Dropped: the top up zones, the dead middle and the picture-middle tap
rule, the glide's newest-finger steering, the airborne button role,
the two-holds brake from 02b48ed, and 46060f8's climb-on from a plain
hold mid-ladder (Saul chose to try the C64 rule; swipe to climb).

The second-finger leap now starts at its lift, about 100 ms later than
at its landing, because a held second finger means the menu.
