events.title: Blits: restores and keyed blits at the same phase in registers
events.message:
Blits: restores and keyed blits at the same phase in registers

Same-phase blits with no flags into an unmasked destination leave
STDL_BlitSurfaceEx for an out-of-line routine, in 68000 with C
twins:

- unkeyed (every restore at an x that is not a multiple of 16):
  edge groups merged a plane pair at a time as d ^= (s ^ d) & mask
  with the mask in both halves of a register, the groups between
  as move.l (a0)+,(a1)+. The per-word merge it replaces spilled to
  the stack at ~87 cycles a word.
- keyed (the SDL port's sprite at an aligned x): each group's mask
  word read first, nothing visible skips the group, everything
  visible copies it, the rest merge like the edges.

A single group rides the multi-group loop through two tests that
cost what the old bra into the dbf did. Moving the flag-free
instantiations out of STDL_BlitSurfaceEx, rather than adding a call
beside them, is what kept its entry path unchanged; the two ways of
adding a call cost every blit 1.2-5%.

Plain ST (Hatari --machine st, same-binary floor 0.2-0.3%):
  restores at x&15=5: 16x16 0.58, 32x32 0.46, 48x24 0.49;
  STDL_DirtyRestore of 16 16x16 rects 0.60;
  keyed aligned 16x16 0.80, 32x32 0.63;
  SPRCOST geometric mean 0.97 over 85 cases, PRIMCOST 0.97 over 21;
  entry, 16x1 and aligned restores within 0.3-0.6%.
BLITCOST on ste: the keyed (64 cells) and edge (16 cells) BLiTTER
thresholds still hold against the faster CPU paths; a Mega STE's
CPU would now keep more, and the constants stay the 8MHz numbers.
Pixel-path text 33748 -> 34696 bytes (budget 34700).

Tests: the partial-middle test runs from one group up at budgets 4
and 2, and a new keyed test paints groups all key, no key or mixed
so every branch runs; mutations in both twins fail them. The tile
test's model used the clip before the surface clamped it. PIXCHK
passes on st; BLITCHK identical at every budget on ste and megaste.

events.title: fix(fileops,gui): a FAT12 file whose cluster chain ends early is delivered as what was read — not padded with unread heap memory (MF-1600, P3-700)
events.message:
fix(fileops,gui): a FAT12 file whose cluster chain ends early is delivered as what was read — not padded with unread heap memory (MF-1600, P3-700)

fat12_extract_file() (reached from explorertab.cpp: readFileBytes,
onViewHex, onViewText) followed the cluster chain, stopped at an end
mark or at a cluster past the end of the image — and still returned
*size = f->size with rc 0. The buffer came from malloc(), so the rest was
never-read heap memory, handed out as file content.

Red proof first, in tests/test_fat_kopien_kette.c (builder from MF-874):
- directory promises 5 clusters, chain ends after 3: before, 5120 bytes
  delivered, 3072 read, rc 0;
- chain 2 -> 3 -> 200, image ends before cluster 200: before, 3072
  delivered, 2048 read, rc 0.
A first setup with a shorter image did not reach the path at all:
fat12_list_files() refuses anything under 163840 bytes.

Now *size = pos (what was read), and bit 1 of the return value says it
is less than the directory promises; bit 0 stays the FAT-copy
disagreement (MF-874). The GUI tests the bits one by one (fatRc == 1
meant "bit 0 only" before) and reports bit 1 with ONE text,
fat12KetteZuKurz(), at all three places. The buffer is at least one byte:
a file of size 0 is a file, and C11 lets malloc(0) return NULL.

After: 8 of 8, including the counter-check that a chain longer than the
file does not set bit 1. Mutations 2 of 3 red; the third (malloc(0)
again) is equivalent on MinGW, where malloc(0) returns a pointer — the
empty-file case was green before and stays as a guard.

GUI: compiled, test_explorer_tab_no_fiction green; NOT clicked through
by hand.

Named as open in P3-700: the other two FAT readers
(src/formats/uft_fat12_legacy.c, reached via uft_fat12_init(), and
src/fs/uft_fat12.c) are not measured for the same class;
fat12_extract_file() still substitutes defaults for a zero BPB field.

Numbering: MF-1515 and MF-1522 were claimed twice by two worktrees, and
checking before committing did not prevent it — both sides checked, the
race stayed. At the owner's request the two sessions now use disjoint
ranges: the session on main counts on from MF-1526, this worktree
(wt-dtc) takes MF-1600…1699 and P3-700…799. This fix was prepared as
MF-1526/P3-678 and moved before committing.

Kennzahl: none of the four.

events.message:
fix(formats): a sector greaseweazle could not read is not a read sector in ADF, ST, DO, PO, D64, D71 and D81 either (MF-1525, P3-677)

greaseweazle (@26690f8, Unlicense) builds every track with
'-=[BAD SECTOR]=-' in each sector and replaces only what it decodes:
codec/amiga/amigados.py:26 (ADF), codec/apple2/apple2_gcr.py:34 (DO,
PO), codec/commodore/c64_gcr.py:31 (D64, D71), codec/ibm/ibm.py:794
(IMG; '.st' maps to IMG in tools/util.py:311, D81 is an IMG subclass).
MF-1522 taught only the IMG reader.

Red proof first: tests/test_gw_fuellsektor_sektorabbilder.c overwrites
ONE sector of a free corpus file per reader in memory with the filler.
Before: 7 of 7 readers reported it with status 0x0 (read), 21 green /
7 red. After: 28 of 28 — per reader the filler sector is UNAVAILABLE
with its bytes kept, the next sector stays read, and the same sector
of the untouched file stays read.

The seven readers call uft_sector_is_gw_filler() (the one rule from
MF-1522) after adding the sector and mark it with
uft_format_mark_last_unavailable(), only when the add succeeded.

Mutation matrix 8 of 8 red: each of the seven sites switched off on its
own, and a helper that calls everything filler.

Also, in docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md P3-673, BERICHTIGT: the second index limit
128 was attributed to "the kfx plugin". Measured, the kfx plugin never
calls kf_stream_parse() (kfx_read_track passes the raw stream through)
and the function has no caller outside its own file; and uft_kfx.c:30-44
declares it against an invented struct layout — a trap for whoever
wires the call.

Named as open in P3-677: 19 image writers in greaseweazle's image/
build on IMG tracks; five are covered now (img, adf, apple2, d64, d81).
msa, acorn, mgt, dim, hdm, fdi, xdf, dsk, apridisk and others are not.

Eleven commits from the peer worktree, merged into the GCR register line.
Common ancestor 7031708c; 17 commits mine, 11 theirs.

Build and tests on the merged state: 0 errors, ctest **601/601** with the two
named skips. Gates on the merged state: constant families 56/97 unchanged,
CBM zones OK, name roll 0, Tor 72 self-test 18/18.

And the register survived the merge measured, not assumed: their commits add
six link targets (595 -> 601), and both blast-radius measurements still
report **0 unsupplied** — the one over `build.ninja` and the one over the
CMake text, because only the second can see an option-gated target.

THREE CONFLICTS, all in documentation, none resolved by dropping a side:

* `docs/ORACLES.md` — both branches appended an oracle row at the same
  place (`nibscan` mine, `a2tools` theirs). Both kept.
* `docs/OPEN_ITEMS.md` — thirteen register rows, merged in numeric order,
  664 through 676, every number distinct (checked before writing).
* `docs/STAND.md` — generated. Regenerated after the merge rather than
  patched by hand; the whole generator chain ran, `gen_stand.py` last.

THE SAME NUMBER COLLIDED TWICE, and this half is not repairable by me.
`e36346ce` (08:39:53) claims MF-1522 and P3-674; my `0a66fb21` (08:22:12)
claims both, seventeen minutes earlier.

* P3-674: mine moved to **P3-676** — pushed beats not-pushed. The row says
  so itself, because the message of `0a66fb21` still calls it P3-674, and a
  committed message does not get rewritten.
* MF-1522: **stays doubled**, like MF-1515 (87345aab / d39834ff). Both are
  written, one is pushed. That needs an owner decision, not a silent
  rewrite.

AND TOR 72 SHOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT. Measured just now: the hook is installed
(`.git/hooks/commit-msg`, 07:58:20, twenty-four minutes before e36346ce), it
contains the call, `core.hooksPath` points there in BOTH worktrees, their
reflog says `commit:` (no rebase or cherry-pick, where commit-msg would not
run), and fed their subject the hook refuses: "MF-1522 ist bereits
beansprucht von: e36346ce, 0a66fb21".

Why it passed anyway is **NOT MEASURED**, and this gap is not filled with a
plausible story — the same restraint MF-1171 shows for `repo_scope`
("observed once, not reproduced"). The consequence is recorded instead: a
self-test of 18/18 and a mutation matrix of 7/7 say something about the
CLASSIFIER, not about the HOOK. Tor 71 has the counterpart for that
(`--protokolle --seit <install time>`, which also reports how many calls it
saw); Tor 72 does not. Until that exists, Tor 72 counts as unproven IN
OPERATION, and the Fundus entry names the first step: the measurement, not
another gate.

A gate that is proven in its classifier and unproven in operation is not a
gate — it is a script with a hook in front of it.

AND THEN IT HAPPENED A THIRD TIME — on this commit, and the gate caught it.
The message above was written with MF-1524, measured free (`git log --all
--format=%s | grep -c "MF-1524"` gave 0). While the conflicts were resolved,
five generators ran, and a full build with 601 tests finished — close to an
hour — the peer committed `ea1f2436` claiming **MF-1524 and P3-676**. P3-676
was precisely the number my Brother-table entry had just moved to. Tor 72
refused this commit: "MF-1524 ist bereits beansprucht von: ea1f2436".

Resolved: the merge is MF-1526, the Brother entry P3-678. Measured free this
time over committed AND uncommitted numbers of both trees — MF-1525 and
P3-677 lie uncommitted in `wt-dtc`.

So the operational statement from further up gets sharper rather than
reversed: Tor 72 DOES fire, in this same hook, on this same day, at exactly
the class it was built for. What stays unproven is that it runs on EVERY
commit, and the operational probe that would answer it is still missing.

And the real lesson is not the gate but the SHELF LIFE of a number
measurement. Between "MF-1524 is free" and the commit lay conflict
resolution, five generators, a full build and 601 tests, and four foreign
commits came into being. The memory note already says "determine the number
directly before the commit"; measured, "directly" here means less than an
hour, and with a full build inside the hook that cannot be held. Which is
why the gate is the right place: it checks the number at the moment the
commit comes into being, not at the moment the message was written.

events.title: Lines, circles and spans: batched shapes, one register-only row routine
events.message:
Lines, circles and spans: batched shapes, one register-only row routine

STDL_Line and STDL_Circle drew through STDL_PutPixel and
STDL_FillCircle through STDL_HLine, paying a whole call's clip and
set-up per pixel or per row. They move to src/shapes.c and collect
into STDL_Points / STDL_HSpans batches, clipped before they go in;
the filled circle works out each row's half-width first and draws
every row once instead of up to four times.

Every CPU fill row now goes through span_row: edge groups merged a
plane pair at a time as XOR-AND-XOR, which stays in registers where
the per-plane form spilled, and a post-increment dbf middle in 68000
with its C twin. It serves STDL_HLine (which skips fill_rows' set-up
below the BLiTTER's size), each span of STDL_HSpans, and FillRect's
rows through an out-of-line fill_block, with one row inline.
fill_span_rows is gone. A memset per row lost to it at every screen
width, so 0/15 fills keep memset only for contiguous blocks and rows
of 32 groups or more. STDL_VLine and STDL_VSpans get the same merge
down a column.

Plain ST (Hatari --machine st, same-binary floor 0.2%):
  PRIMCOST geometric mean 0.83 over 21 cases: HLine 32 0.52, HLine
  300 0.56, VLine 0.66, Line 0.67, Circle 0.64, FillCircle 0.42,
  HSpans 0.84, VSpans 0.75; nothing else moved past 1%.
  SPRCOST geometric mean 0.94 over 85 cases: fills 16x16 0.55-0.85,
  64x32 0.56-0.75, 1x1 fixed cost 0.78; full-screen fills and every
  non-fill case unchanged within 1%.
Pixel-path text 34616 -> 33736 bytes.

A host test compares Line, Circle, FillCircle, HLine and VLine with
the algorithms they replaced, byte for byte including masks, at
budgets 4/2/3 with STDL_TRANSPARENT and random clips; mutations in
each new routine fail it. PIXCHK passes on st; BLITCHK is identical
at every budget on ste and megaste.

events.title: fix(scp): a single-sided image in consecutive table slots reads as its own cylinders — the plugin halved them and read the wrong track for the rest (MF-1524, P3-676)
events.message:
fix(scp): a single-sided image in consecutive table slots reads as its own cylinders — the plugin halved them and read the wrong track for the rest (MF-1524, P3-676)

Some tools wrote single-sided SCP images into CONSECUTIVE track-table
slots (0, 1, 2, ...) instead of cylinder * 2 + head. greaseweazle
recognises and fixes this (image/scp.py:246-254, @26690f8, Unlicense):
heads field 1 or 2 AND both even and odd slots occupied means slot n is
cylinder n of that one side. src/formats/scp/uft_scp_plugin.c used
cylinder * 2 + head unconditionally and (end + 2) / 2 cylinders.

Red proof first: tests/test_scp_einseitig_fortlaufend.c builds, in
memory, a legacy copy of tests/corpus_free/gw_fm_acorn_3trk.scp
(greaseweazle, modern single-sided, slots 0/2/4) with slots 0/1/2 and
compares the flux of every cylinder. Before: 2 green, 3 red (2 cylinders
instead of 3; cylinder 1 returned the flux of cylinder 2's slot, 28888
against 28886 cells; cylinder 2 not readable). After: 9 of 9, including
a heads=2 copy (side 1 only: head 1 carries the tracks, head 0 is
UNFORMATTED instead of someone else's track).

- include/uft/flux/uft_scp_ablage.h: the rule in ONE place,
  uft_scp_ablage_bestimmen() and uft_scp_ablage_platz().
- uft_scp_plugin.c: layout decided at open, geometry follows it,
  read_track takes the slot from the layout.

Mutation matrix 5 of 5 red (never consecutive, side always 0, head
ignored, geometry kept, no -1 guard). ctest -R scp: 23 of 23 green.

Named as open in P3-676: greaseweazle's second fix-up directly above it
(scp.py:239-244, C64 halftrack images from the Supercard Pro), and the
other SCP readers in the tree, which have their own slot arithmetic and

events.title: Text: one glyph-row routine in 68000, shared by DrawText and DrawChar
events.message:
Text: one glyph-row routine in 68000, shared by DrawText and DrawChar

Both drew a glyph row by shifting its bits twice into two words and
merging each into four planes a word at a time, and gcc 4.6 spilled
the row's masks to the stack doing it. stdl_glyph_rows replaces both
loops: the row goes into the top word of a long and one lsr.l places
it - the high word for the first group, the low word for the spill
into the second - and each group is updated as two plane pairs, a
long each, with old ^= (old ^ colour) & mask: the merge without an
inverted mask, the colour in two registers. Four variants (plane
budget 2 or 4, one- or two-byte glyph rows) with the C twin.

PRIMCOST on a plain ST (microseconds per call, mean of passes A/B):
  STDL_DrawText, 10 chars 8x8    7344 -> 4375   (-40%)
  STDL_DrawChar x10 8x8          8359 -> 5625   (-33%)
Nothing else moves beyond the floor. text.o +104 bytes, drawchar.o
892; both outside the pixel-path budget.

test_glyph compared the two calls with each other, which a shared
routine passes whatever it does, so test_pixel gains
test_text_model: fonts 5, 8, 11 and 16 wide and 6-13 high, every
phase, strings off the surface, random clips, colours above the
budget, budgets 4, 2 and 3, both calls, against a per-pixel model.
Shifting the spill half wrong makes it fail. PIXCHK (which runs
test_pixel on the machine) passes on st, so the asm meets the same
model.

events.title: Tiles: rows through the register-only copy, masks read first
events.message:
Tiles: rows through the register-only copy, masks read first

STDL_BlitTile stored every plane a word at a time and asked, for
every group of every row, whether the tile was masked (gcc 4.6 does
not unswitch). An unmasked tile is rows of whole groups, and now goes
through the row copy the background restore uses - moved from blit.c
to stdl_internal.h as stdl_copy_rows_groups, blit.o disassembling
identically - copying all four planes at any budget, since a plane
beyond it is zero in the tile and on the destination. A 68000 needs
only an even address for a long move, so the word-aligned tile data
malloc returns is fine; the C twin copies words. A masked tile reads
its mask first like a sprite: a transparent group is skipped, an
opaque one is stored without reading the destination.

PRIMCOST on a plain ST (microseconds, mean of passes A/B):
  tile 16x16               654 -> 372   (-43%)
  row of 20 16x16 tiles  12930 -> 7266  (-44%)
  tile 16x16 masked        796 -> 737   (-7%)
Nothing else moves beyond the floor. tileset.o is 1452 bytes, outside
the pixel-path budget.

test_pixel gains test_tiles_wide: four tile shapes, masked and plain,
random positions including negative and odd x, random clips with the
whole-group clipping modelled exactly, budgets 4, 2 and 3, against a
per-pixel model; storing a wrong plane or skipping the wrong number of
bytes between rows makes it fail.

events.title: fix(gate): Tor 72 crashed instead of judging — a missing or empty commit message file raised a traceback out of the commit-msg hook (MF-1523)
events.message:
fix(gate): Tor 72 crashed instead of judging — a missing or empty commit message file raised a traceback out of the commit-msg hook (MF-1523)

MF-1522 committed this gate one hour ago with a self-test of 14/14 and a
mutation matrix of 5/5. Both were true, and both only covered VALID input.

Measured: `Path(msg).read_text(...).splitlines()[0]` raises
`FileNotFoundError` for a missing file, `IndexError` for an empty one, and
an OSError for a directory. In a `commit-msg` hook that aborts the commit
with a traceback — for a reason that has nothing to do with the message. The
class is MF-1000 / Tor 64, "a crash is not a verdict", and `c_literal.py`
has made exactly this promise since MF-1171: return None for anything it
does not understand, and never throw.

How it surfaced is itself the point: the closing check after MF-1522 fed the
gate a path that did not exist, and `rc=1` LOOKED like a refusal. It was a
traceback. That is the confusion MF-1000 warns about, and it happened one
commit after building the gate.

Fix: `betreff_lesen()` returns None and never throws; the caller prints
"NICHTS geprueft" and passes, because an unreadable file says nothing about
the number. Refusing there would block commits for an unrelated reason.

Four cases added (missing, empty, a directory, first-line-not-second):
self-test 14 -> 18. Mutation matrix 5 -> 7, all seven red.

And the mutation probe found a SECOND half. With the exception handling
disarmed, the SELF-TEST itself died on the first missing file, so the
remaining cases never ran — a second defect would have hidden behind the
first. The four new cases now catch and report RED instead of aborting the
run; that is why two of the seven mutations report a clean 16/18 and 17/18
rather than no line at all.

Standing order extended by one line accordingly: a gate's cases are not only
the correct inputs — missing, empty, malformed, a directory instead of a
file. A self-test checks what it knows.

Verified on the real tree: a missing file exits 0 with the notice; reusing
MF-1522 exits 0 because HEAD claims it (the amend exemption); `(MF-1515)`
exits 1 and names BOTH claimants, 87345aab and d39834ff.

K3 unchanged at 97 — this commit moves no metric except K0's denominator,
and that is the honest direction: an error found is an error counted.

events.title: fix(img): a sector greaseweazle could not read is not a read sector — its "-=[BAD SECTOR]=-" filler reached the model as UFT_SECTOR_OK, 653 of 653 (P3-674, MF-1522)
events.message:
fix(img): a sector greaseweazle could not read is not a read sector — its "-=[BAD SECTOR]=-" filler reached the model as UFT_SECTOR_OK, 653 of 653 (P3-674, MF-1522)

greaseweazle (keirf/greaseweazle @ 26690f8, Unlicense) builds a formatted
track with every sector set to b'-=[BAD SECTOR]=-' * (size // 16)
(codec/ibm/ibm.py:794; the same text in codec/amiga/amigados.py:26 and
codec/apple2/apple2_gcr.py:34) and replaces only the sectors it decodes.
Every sector it could not read reaches the sector image as that filler.
src/formats/img/uft_img.c set UFT_SECTOR_OK for every sector
unconditionally. Measured in the uft-stack-code package review (neue-ideen,
t4): gw decoded a capture into an IMG with 653 filler sectors, the tree
reported 653 of 653 as read.

Now ONE rule, uft_sector_is_gw_filler() in include/uft/uft_format_common.h
— true only when the WHOLE sector is the 16-byte text repeated; a sector
that merely starts with it is ordinary data. uft_img.c marks such a sector
with uft_sector_mark_unavailable() and keeps its bytes (no bit lost; the
status says the medium was not read there).

Red proof first: tests/test_img_gw_fuellsektor.c, LBA 20 of
tests/corpus_free/fluxfox_sector_test_360k.img overwritten in memory:
  before: status 0x0 (OK)
  after:  UNAVAILABLE; controls green (bytes kept, a sector only starting
          with the text stays OK, the other 7 sectors of the track OK)
  mutation matrix 3 of 3 red (call removed; only the first 16 bytes
    compared; marked only as a CRC error)

Still open, named in P3-674: the same check belongs into the ADF, ST and
Apple sector readers (gw writes the filler there too) — each with its own
red proof, not in passing; whether the offered lossless path IMG->HFE
treats such a sector differently now is NOT measured.

events.title: Disassemble Fairlight from its protected tape, with how it works, the castle, its graphics, animations, the loading tune, bugs and pokes
events.message:
Disassemble Fairlight from its protected tape, with how it works, the castle, its graphics, animations, the loading tune, bugs and pokes

scripts/build_fairlight.py loads Release 2 of the tape -- the one Ville
Krumlinde's disassembly is of -- by running its Alkatraz loader, redoes the
loader's decryption on the tape's own bytes at every build, and stops at the
game's first instruction, $C47C. It maps the code by playing the game in
SkoolKit's simulator (every room, every door, carrying and using every
thing, game over and both endings) and lays out the rooms command by
command, the parts, the object table, templates, patches, font, textures,
sprites and strings from the game at build time. All 42240 bytes from $5B00
reassemble byte for byte and the snapshot rebuilt is the one loaded; 373
entries, every one titled, described and labelled, with the author's own
names where the assembler's symbol table and the source text he left in
memory give them; 3476 of 3545 instructions seen to run; no warnings.

Six page modules: how it works (the loader, a room's drawing program and
the textured fill, the four compositing pages, movement and collision,
things and creatures), the castle laid out by its doors with layers and
every room, textures, parts, object types, sprites, the panel, font and
title page, animations (each creature alone, as Nightshade's), the loading
tune -- Fairlight's only sound -- and four bugs, five tested pokes and eight
facts. notes/fairlight/ holds the working account, 36 files.

Krumlinde's disassembly has no licence: facts and names are taken from it
with credit, never its prose; where the running game disagrees with it the
notes say so. build_fairlight_krumlinde.py keeps assembling his source for
the emulator's Fairlight launch. No game bytes are committed.

events.title: refactor(gcr,core): the last GCR tables onto the register — 97 surplus copies, and the gate refused the move until it learned what a home site is (MF-1522, P3-666)
events.message:
refactor(gcr,core): the last GCR tables onto the register — 97 surplus copies, and the gate refused the move until it learned what a home site is (MF-1522, P3-666)

Measured, with the command in the tree
(`python scripts/audit_konstantenfamilien.py`):

  surplus constant copies   113 -> 97
  families in >1 file        58 -> 56   (one vanished entirely)
  CBM encode table       12 files -> 6
  CBM decode table       10 files -> 4

Rewired onto `uft_gcr_kodieren()`/`uft_gcr_dekodieren()`:
`src/formats/g64/uft_g64.c` (3 tables — the encode table stood TWICE, as
`gcr_enc` and `gcr_encode_table`), `src/formats/c64/uft_d64_g64.c` (2),
`src/flux/uft_flux_decoder.c` (1), `src/formats/c64/uft_gcr_ops.c` (3 —
its three public pointer functions now build their table lazily from the
predicate), and last `include/uft/uft_cbm_gcr.h` (2). That last one ends
the circle: the register holds the CBM assignment, the header calls the
register.

Why the header was last: until then the register READ the table from the
header. Moving it earlier would have meant the register owning a copy
while nine other copies still stood — which is what the gate caught at
MF-1509 (the register's first draft laid a thirteenth table).

FIVE PATTERN FAILURES led to a tool instead of more sed. Each assumed a
structure the tree only MOSTLY has: a `$` anchor (two CMake lines end in
`)`), a counter-check over `elseif` blocks (the collective library is
none), a table-block regex expecting `/* */` (the file uses `//`), a
nested-bracket regex that broke `gcr_encode_table[(data[0] >> 4) & 0x0F]`
into `(data[0) >> 4) & 0x0F]` at eight places, and a function-header regex
that cut `const` into `con` + `st`. `scripts/gcr_umhaengen.py` counts
brackets instead of matching patterns, runs its counter-checks BEFORE
writing (the earlier order reported a missing identifier after the file
was already broken), and has a self-test of 10/10.

THE TEST LOST ITS WITNESS, correctly. `test_gcr_praedikat_trifft_die_tafel`
compared the predicate against `cbm_gcr_encode_table` — once that table
moved into the register, the comparison would have been a self-check, and
the full build let the test fail. The table is now frozen as
`tests/oracles/gcr_cbm_tafel_87345aab.c`, carrying the commit hash of its
version in the name, and will never be brought into line with the
register (MF-644, two hands). That gave the test two assertions which were
impossible before — encode AND decode against an independent table,
including all 16 invalid quintets. 7 -> 9 assertions.

NINE LINK TARGETS called the register without getting it. Measured from
`build.ninja`, not from CMake structure — and the first version of that
measurement reported the wrong CLASS: it looked only for `uft_gcr.c.obj`
in the link block and missed that `libuft_core.a` supplies it too, so it
claimed 98 unsupplied when the linker found 1. Corrected, then 9 entered
in `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, then 0 unsupplied measured. Full build: 0
errors, ctest 595/595 with 2 named skips.

THE GATE REFUSED THIS COMMIT, and it was right to. Its ratchet only lets
the manifest get SHORTER — correct against a new copy, but a RELOCATION
looks the same: 5 gone, 1 added. The comment at `ZEUGENORTE` already
admits this gap ("cannot tell a relocation from an increase"); there the
answer was a place with a promise in its name, and here it is the same.
`REGISTERORTE` names the HOME SITE, held by three clamps, each with its
own case: the place is listed · the family stands there EXACTLY ONCE (a
register laying a second table falls — that happened at MF-1509) · the
family got SMALLER overall. A home site can therefore only arise as part
of a resolution, never beside growth. Self-test 14 -> 19.

And the clamps are proven one at a time, not as a group. A mutation probe
disarms each clamp separately; all three now drop the self-test to 18/19.
The first version had only two cases — with the LOCATION clamp disarmed it
stayed 18/18 green, so that clamp was decoration. Found by the mutation,
not by reading.

NEW: TOR 72 — an MF number belongs to exactly one commit
(`scripts/audit_mf_nummer.py`, wired into `commit-msg`). The occasion is
measured: MF-1515 sits on 87345aab (main) AND on d39834ff in the worktree
`wt-dtc`. Both sides had asked `git log`, just not the same one. Four more
numbers and two P3 numbers lay uncommitted in duplicate and could still be
moved (41 replacements, per line, never per file); the committed one
cannot, and needs an owner decision. The gate reads the LAST `MF-NNNN` of
the subject as the claimed one, because a subject may legitimately MENTION
a foreign number — 87345aab says "MF-1513 had broken 89 link targets" and
claims MF-1515. P3 numbers are not checked for uniqueness: an open item
spans several commits. Self-test 14/14, mutation matrix 5/5, and the fifth
mutation found a real gap — without the word boundary, `MF-15155` reads as
`MF-1515`, so a malformed number is now reported instead of silently
skipped. Red proof on the real tree: `(MF-1515, P3-666)` exits 1 and names
d39834ff, `(MF-1526)` passes.

Also measured, and it is a clean NEGATIVE: the constant gate only sees
`name[] = { … }`, so a mapping written as a `switch` or generated at
runtime would escape it. Searched for both across all versioned sources —
zero `case` labels on CBM or Apple quintets, zero runtime-built GCR
tables. The blind spot hides nothing here. (The first attempt at this
measurement did NOT carry and is not reported as a finding: an "8 of 16
literals" criterion flagged `crc.c` and `uft_adf.c` with 16 of 16, because
CRC tables contain every small byte value.)

STILL OPEN, and none of it is simply work: five sites remain in the encode
family — `src/dtc_components/src/encoding.c` (embedded foreign code,
untouchable), `tests/unit/test_flux_gcr_c64_sync.c` (test expectation),
and three orphans (`uft_d64_parser_v3.c`, `uft_g64_parser_v2.c`,
`uft_c64_protection_enhanced.c`). Rewiring those would lower K3 by 3
without any caller benefiting — "the number as a motive", the mirror error
of P3-338. It comes due when the orphans get a door. Four sites in the
decode family are the same case. Registered as Fundus: P3-674 (Brother
table without a source, no callers, comment says "5-to-8" but no value has
bit 7), P3-675 (`uft_vorpal_decode()` reads 4 of 8 quintets, zero
callers).

AND THE BLASTRADIUS MEASUREMENT HAD A SECOND BLIND SPOT, found while
waiting: `bench_decode_hotpath` links `uft_flux_decoder.c` but not the
register, and it hangs on `option(UFT_ENABLE_BENCHMARKS ... OFF)` — so it
was never in `build.ninja` and the link-block measurement could not see it.
A second measurement over the CMake TEXT found it: of 2 targets naming a
register caller, exactly that one was unsupplied, now 0. Red proof by hand:
without the register the link exits 1 with `undefined reference to
uft_gcr_dekodieren`, with it 0. A target nobody builds fails for whoever
switches it on first.

PERFORMANCE, measured instead of asserted. Table reads in an inline
function became calls into another translation unit. The existing benchmark
covers MFM PLL and sync search, not GCR, so the question was UNMEASURED.
Measured with a throwaway program against a local table in the same program
(an upper bound), three runs, MinGW gcc 13.1.0 -O3: **1.0–1.1 ns per
call**, which over the ~470 000 calls of a 1541 disk (42 tracks × ~1400
five-byte groups × 8 quintets) is **0.50–0.52 ms**. As a range, not a
factor. No GCR benchmark added: half a millisecond does not earn one.

K3: 113 -> 97 (56 families). The K0 figure is not written here — the balance
holds it and `commit_verified.py` appends it (MF-1507). Worth saying without
a number: most of this session's gate catches are the FULL BUILD, this
tree's most effective gate and its least frequently run, and the two errors
no gate caught were both blind spots of my own measurement.

And the gate from MF-1507 caught this very commit on its first attempt: the
message named a K0 figure that disagreed with the balance, because I had
written the number in three places and they drifted — the same error MF-1507
was built for, one day later, at the same metric. A gate does not replace
discipline, it outlives it.

events.title: grm-yjiq: bound jump tables read through an un-doubled index
events.message:
grm-yjiq: bound jump tables read through an un-doubled index

rcproam's MMC1 helper at ff89 was named caseD_1d because Ghidra over-read
the 9ad4 jump table and planted a case label there. The game keeps its
switch variable pre-doubled in RAM (LDX $0d / LDA $9aeb,X / LDA $9aec,X /
JMP ($001e)), so the decompiler walks the index at stride 1: every case
reads two bytes, consecutive cases overlap, and the extent collapses to a
single size-1 load table of caseCount+1 bytes. That does not divide by the
case count, so JumpTableBound declined it silently.

JumpTableBound now recognises that overlapping byte table and re-runs its
rules on the even cases, described as the 2-byte table they really are
(Result.stride/keep). rcproam's eleven handlers sit on both sides of the
table, so both extent rules still decline there; a new rule scoped to this
shape, boundByValidTargets, cuts at the first even entry whose target is
not in initialized memory (2120, the unmapped PPU mirror), confirmed by
the next entries. Hand-verified from the ROM: $0d is only ever stored with
values up to $14, i.e. 11 entries.

rcproam re-blessed: 9ad4 128 -> 11, ff89 is FUN_ff89 again, and the 9b05
handler gains its two bank comments. dodge's 8445 table (shift-scaled
index, Y = 0/2/4/6) is also bounded 8 -> 4, correctly, and left for the
grm-q1bi re-bless. ab-test vs HEAD: every other failing row is
byte-identical.

project.title: ghidra-retro-machines
project.display_title: Ghidra Retro Machines — bank-aware loaders and retro CPU languages
project.notes: Ghidra extension configures banked memory maps, ROMs, hardware registers and symbols for C64/C128/PET PRG and NES iNES analysis, and bundles explicit SPC700 and 65C816 language variants for SNES code. The SPC700 language is decode-capable with p-code still under rewrite; the 65C816 language is disassembly-oriented while its p-code is verified against exhaustive vectors. Current NES work resolves proven constant-pointer indirect jumps and bounds table-after-code jump tables by their switch window; Mega Man and Life Force rows were re-blessed, while Contra, Final Fantasy and TMNT changes remain held for owner review. Its exhaustive 65C816 vector baseline now reports 500 PASS, 8 N/A and 4 FAIL rows after isolating one named SBC (dp,X) test-vector oracle defect. The exception is guarded by tripwires that fail if the case starts passing or disappears, so it cannot mask wider regressions. Build and real-ROM gates therefore demonstrate bounded progress rather than universal correctness claims.

events.title: AGENTS.md and the skill: what this round of optimisation taught
events.message:
AGENTS.md and the skill: what this round of optimisation taught

AGENTS.md: the host BLiTTER model and the on-target probes (PIXCHK,
SPRCOST with sccmp.py, the five-kind BLITCOST); BLITCHK's forced
passes; the NFSR rule and the extra fetch FXSR costs; the ST-RAM
reach gate and why it is only asked on alt-RAM machines; that code
added inside STDL_BlitSurfaceEx moves its CPU paths through register
allocation, what arrangement survived and the ones that did not;
and that a threshold must be refit against every shape it chooses
between.

The skill: the reverse-link control stays, but on a plain ST the
library's own sweep times identically either way, so the per-scene
noise a game sees comes through what the link order moves along with
the code, not the code's address - and a change inside a big C
function is not a layout change.

events.title: Docs: three ways to lay out a hardware-scrolled play field
events.message:
Docs: three ways to lay out a hardware-scrolled play field

The skill gains the play-field patterns a mature STE engine is built
on, each expressed in STDL's existing calls: spreading a strip's
drawing over the frames that uncover it, instead of a spike at every
tile boundary; a horizontal "scan-walk", where the window's base
walks forward over a fixed-stride buffer and tile columns are drawn
at their unwrapped address (column c of tile row ty at group c % 21 of
surface row 16*ty + c/21 for a 168-byte stride) - unlimited travel
for about half a byte of padding per pixel, no copying; and a page
duplicated below itself for endless vertical scrolling. They are
labelled as patterns not measured in STDL. porting.md points to them.

examples/hwscroll.c's header described the old two-phase register
order; it now says what the library does.
events.author: neilrackett

Hardware scrolling: every request on screen at the next VBL

The Shifter latches the video base into its counter three lines
before the VBL, so a base written from the VBL is fetched a frame
later, while LINEWIDTH and HSCROLL written there apply at once. STDL
has always handled that by writing a request's base first and its
offsets at the VBL whose counter shows the base latched - correct,
but a request made more than 15ms into a frame, which is where a
game that draws first and scrolls after makes it, reached the screen
a frame late.

On an STE the video counter is writable, and until the fetch of the
first line begins it still holds the base it was reloaded from. The
VBL now checks exactly that - counter equal to the base registers -
and when it holds, writes the new base, the counter and both offsets
together: the request is on the frame just starting, as a matched
pair. A VBL that runs late into the picture falls back to the
two-phase path, so a late VBL can cost a frame but never tear one.

tests/hatari/hwlatch.c asks the hardware rather than
STDL_ScrollWindowPending: after each request it waits for the next
VBL, reads the video counter in the picture, and checks which of two
windows 200 rows apart the frame is fetched from. In Hatari:
  late requests on screen at the next VBL: before 0/100, after 100/100
  (ste; megaste 100/100); early requests 100/100 before and after.
HWSCROLL.TOS runs 32927 frames with nothing pending after one VBL.
Not yet run on a real STE: the thing to watch there is the fine
scroll crossing zero without a one-frame sideways jump.

Docs: stdl_hwscroll.h, the skill, porting.md and limits.md lose the
15ms rule.

events.title: Sprites on the BLiTTER: two passes a plane, shifted by the chip
events.message:
Sprites on the BLiTTER: two passes a plane, shifted by the chip

STDL_BlitSprite never used the BLiTTER. STDL's sprite layout is what
the chip wants already - per group [mask][p0][p1][p2][p3], planes
clear under the mask - so with a source x increment of 10 the mask
words are one plane of their own and each colour another: AND the
mask into each destination plane, switch the operation to OR (one
register write) and OR each colour plane in. An unshifted sprite at
an odd x is shifted by the chip exactly as a surface blit is (SKEW,
FXSR for a left shift, never NFSR); a pre-shifted variant needs no
shift. The clip is taken in pixels over the sprite's own width, so a
pre-shifted variant's pad group is never drawn. The source word a
skewed line reads past its span is inside the next group or the
sprite data's slack.

SPRCOST on an emulated STE, the library's choice, microseconds:
                               before    after
  16x16 unshifted, mean         2617     1074   (2.4x)
  32x32 unshifted, mean         6484     1846   (3.5x)
  64x32 unshifted, mean         7578     2637   (2.9x)
  32x32 pre-shifted, mean       3125     1855   (1.7x)
  16x16 phase 0                  940      884   (-6%)
85-case geometric mean 0.672. Pre-shifted and unshifted sprites now
cost the same on a BLiTTER machine, so there PRESHIFT's 16x RAM buys
nothing; the skill, porting.md, limits.md and the flag's own comment
say so, with the numbers. With a bottom border open an unshifted
32x32 still wins (3.7ms against 6.6), while a pre-shifted one lost
13% to the per-pass placement, so pre-shifted sprites stay on the CPU
while a border is open - refused before any clipping is worked out.

The path is spr_blitter in sprite.c, out of line: only programs that
draw sprites carry it, and the CPU loops are compiled as if it were
not there. The register block and the inline pass it shares with
blitter.c moved to stdl_internal.h. On a plain ST the CPU paths
measure unchanged within 1% (85-case mean 1.001; a few sprite cases
0.5-0.9% slower).

Size: sprite.o +828 bytes; pixel-path text 34616, and PIXEL_MAX
33740 -> 34700 with the argument above recorded beside it.

test_blitter draws sprites of widths 1-80, strips, unshifted and
pre-shifted, at random positions and clips, on the CPU and the
forced BLiTTER at budgets 4, 2 and 3, byte for byte under ASan;
turning the mask pass's AND into OR, or getting the source's y
increment wrong, fails it. BLITCHK gains the same: sprites of widths
5-80 and a strip, both kinds, all over the surface, and fails a
forced pass whose sprites never reached the BLiTTER. BLITCHK passes
on ste and megaste, PIXCHK on ste.

feat(ui): Cmd+O / Cmd+S host chords; Eject and DevTools in the pause hub; topbar Fullscreen/Screenshot (#60)

* feat(ui): Cmd+O / Cmd+S host chords; Eject and DevTools in the pause hub

Host chords (beads-idn): every action was an F-key — keys CPC software
also uses — and the only Command chord was Cmd+K. Cmd+O now opens Load
Disk A..., Cmd+S opens Save Snapshot... (Ctrl on Linux/Windows), and the
rule is explicit: a Cmd/Ctrl chord belongs to the host UI, an unmodified
key to the CPC. One resolver, host_chords.h, serves the SDL event loop
(which now dispatches the palette chord from it too — the palette's own
handle_key is gone), the ImGui Media menu's accelerator labels, the About
box, and the native macOS Media items, which get real key equivalents so
AppKit dispatches Cmd+O/Cmd+S itself as it already did Cmd+Q and Cmd+,.

Pause hub (beads-7sh): a paused user reaches for the debugger and for the
media they want out, and the hub offered neither. The Transport section
gains Eject A / Eject B / Eject Tape — enabled only while something is in
that drive or deck, raising the same confirmation the Media menu and the
status-bar LEDs use — and a DevTools button (the machine stays paused).
The enable logic is a pure helper, hub_media_buttons(). imgui_render_menu()
gets external linkage so the hub renders under the headless ImGui harness.

Tests: the chord resolver on both platforms (Cmd vs Ctrl, upper/lowercase,
non-chord letters, labels, key equivalents round-trip); the hub's enable
logic; the hub rendered headlessly (vertex count, and nothing fires
unclicked).

* feat(ui): Fullscreen and Screenshot buttons on the topbar

The two most frequent one-click actions had no fast path (beads-flt): the
topbar held only Pause and Layout. Both buttons dispatch the registry
actions the View menu uses — the deferred fullscreen request and the same
screenshot — so nothing new can drift.

* fix(review): SDL is the sole chord dispatcher; opt-out for the Ctrl chords; no dialog per key repeat

Review round on the UI batch (ce-code-review, seven reviewers).

- The native macOS Media items had been given real key equivalents for
  Cmd+O / Cmd+S while the SDL loop dispatched the same chords: both see
  the key, so the dialog opened twice — the F9 double-fire this codebase
  already fixed once (f85a8b69) and the reason the native bar registers
  no accelerators. The items show the chord as text ("  (Cmd+O)"), like
  the F-keys, and SDL is the only dispatcher on every platform.
- On Linux/Windows, Control is a real CPC key and CP/M software leans on
  exactly Ctrl+O/S/K (WordStar). `[input] host_chords=0` hands them back
  to the CPC; the default keeps them for the host, as Ctrl+K already was.
  host_chord_for() takes the flag so the rule is testable; documented in
  AGENTS.md's [input] block.
- A held Cmd/Ctrl+O opened a file dialog per auto-repeat; the chord branch
  ignores repeats, as the other key handlers do.
- The hub's Eject/DevTools row is its own imgui_render_hub_media_row()
  (external linkage), so a differential render test proves the row draws
  rather than a whole-hub vertex floor; the hub test keeps its save-state
  grid out of the working directory (a temp snap_path).
- The topbar's right cluster is clamped to the current cursor, so on a
  narrow window it no longer draws over Pause.
- HeadlessImGui moved to test/headless_imgui.h, shared by both render
  tests; the orphaned handle_key comment and the empty namespace the
  extraction left behind are gone.
- docs/ipc-protocol.md gains the `tape …` family and `devtools` — both
  implemented and in `help`, never written up; the hub now fronts them.

events.title: refactor(apple,core): Apple onto the codec register — four tables gone, the old ones frozen as oracles, and MF-1513 had broken 89 link targets (MF-1515, P3-666)
events.message:
refactor(apple,core): Apple onto the codec register — four tables gone, the old ones frozen as oracles, and MF-1513 had broken 89 link targets (MF-1515, P3-666)

Finishing the GCR line. Apple was IN the register since MF-1509 but the
Apple code did not use it: `src/formats/apple/uft_apple_gcr.c` carried four
tables — `A2_WRITE_TAB[64]`, `A2_TAB5[32]`, and two lazily built 256-byte
reverse tables. The last two are literally what `uft_gcr_dekodieren()` does,
built from the predicate instead of from a table.

## The file's own comment said it was impossible

    „welche weitere Bedingung die zehn ueberzaehligen ausschliesst, ist
     ohne die gedruckte Quelle nicht feststellbar, und sie zu erraten
     waere dieselbe Falschaussage in neuem Gewand."

The 74 were counted correctly. Two conditions were missing, and they were
not guessed: all combinations of seven condition building blocks were
computed against THIS table, and exactly one yields the 64 —

    bit 7 set · at MOST ONE pair of adjacent zeros ·
    a pair of ones in bits 6..0

"At most one zero pair" is stricter than "zero run <= 2": two SEPARATE
pairs also have run length 2, and those ten values (0x93, 0x99, 0x9C, 0xC9,
0xCA, 0xCC, 0xD2, 0xD4 …) are exactly the surplus. Corrected in place, not
deleted (MF-1077), with the ten named.

## The tables moved rather than vanished

`tests/oracles/gcr_apple_tafeln_f08d1a7a.c` — commit hash in the filename,
so which version is frozen is a fact and not prose. Their PROVENANCE moved
with them verbatim: 5&3 is a MEASUREMENT (MF-719) from a `to_woz2` WOZ
whose input held all 256 byte values, third-confirmed by `mamedev/mame`
`ap2_dsk.cpp`. A predicate cannot replace that; it can only agree, and it
does.

`tests/test_gcr_apple_gegen_tafel.c`, **8 assertions**, delivers what
`test_gcr_register_gegen_bestehende.c` said in its own header it could not:
the BIJECTIVE comparison. `A2_WRITE_TAB` was `static`, so only the count
could be proven. Now all 256 words are checked in both directions — that a
non-table word is invalid is the half that catches an over-wide rule.

Two hands per MF-644: producer is the predicate, checker is the table that
stood in production code. These oracles are never brought into line with
the register; if the predicate changes, the test falls. That is the point.

## And the gate had a gap this step exposed

`audit_konstantenfamilien.py` could not tell a MOVE from an ADDITION and
reported the frozen witnesses as new copies. It now knows `ZEUGENORTE`
(`tests/oracles/`, `tests/flux_gen/`) — on the same grounds as MF-644: a
table that is checked AGAINST must not come from the thing it checks.

Not an exclusion list in the MF-636 sense: two directories whose name is
the claim, and `tests/oracles/*` carries the frozen commit hash. Self-test
10 -> **14**, the four new cases in both directions — including "two
witnesses alone are not a family" and "the witness does not appear in the
findings list".

  surplus copies:  111 -> 107        families: 58 -> 57

## MF-1513 had broken 89 link targets, and the hook could not see it

The worst finding of this commit, and it is mine. `uft_g64_parser_v3.c`
started calling the register in MF-1513 — measured from
`build-tests-ci/build.ninja`, **99** link targets contain a register caller
(mostly via the collective library `uft_test_formatschicht`), and **89** of
them had no `uft_gcr.c`. They failed with `undefined reference`.

The pre-commit hook builds a CANARY target, not all of them, so MF-1513
passed green. Two attempts to fix it each missed part of the set, and both

src/formats/hfe/uft_hfe.c hfe_create(): `bitrate = (sectors > 10) ? 500 :
250`, while track length and rpm have come from the FDC profile since
MF-1242. A header whose bitrate does not fit its track length states a
rotation it does not have. The head comment said the rule "matches all
three HxC values (250/500/500)"; the third HxC file it names is
X68000_2HD_1232KB — the test had checked 1.2M instead.

Measured in the uft-medium-code package review (neue-ideen, t4), hxcfe
2.16.15.2 EXECUTED over all 84 layouts (-uselayout:<L> -conv:HXC_HFE): the
sector-count rule disagrees in 45; X68000_2HD_1232KB writes 500,
ACORN_ADFL_640K writes 250.

Now, with a profile, the bitrate comes from the same source as length and
rpm: new uft_fdc_rate_kbps() — the one mapping of the rate code to kbit/s,
next to the enum in include/uft/formats/uft_fdc_gaps.h (none existed).

Red proof first, in tests/test_hfe_create_zellen_statt_bytes.c (its
counter-check BERICHTIGT, not removed): X68000 500 and ADFS 250 as hxcfe
writes them, and the header satisfies track bytes = bitrate * 2 *
(60/rpm) / 8 — the equation HxC's own numbers satisfy — for 5 of 5
geometries.
  before: 3 of 27 red
  after:  27 of 27 green; the 20 HFE/FDC tests stay green
  mutation matrix 3 of 4 red (bitrate from sectors again; 500/250
    swapped; 250 read as 300). The fourth — 300 kbit/s mapped wrongly —
    cannot fail here: no profile carries 300 kbit/s since MF-1482.

stays (the header then says rpm 0 = unknown); FM — track_encoding is
fixed ISOIBM_MFM and the FM track is half as long as hxcfe's (Gazelle
SSSD: enc 2, track table 41712 against 20832). hxcfe stores FM at double
cell density; that is a question of the cell stream, not of a header
field, and is not decided in passing.

uft_disk_create_image() — the header is right in the writer, no product
path produces such a file today.

events.title: fix(ufi): a mounted USB floppy is refused before UFT writes to it — the Linux backend opened it O_RDWR with no mount or exclusivity check, on a write path wired into the product (P3-669, MF-1516)
events.message:
fix(ufi): a mounted USB floppy is refused before UFT writes to it — the Linux backend opened it O_RDWR with no mount or exclusivity check, on a write path wired into the product (P3-669, MF-1516)

src/hal/ufi_linux.c opened the device with open(path, O_RDWR | O_NONBLOCK)
and nothing else. The write path through that fd is wired
(hardwaretab.cpp:949 -> ufi_runners.cpp:257, WRITE(10) over SG_IO): a
floppy the desktop had auto-mounted was written to past its mounted file
system. Found by the review of the package UFT_LinuxSectorImager_v1
(neue-ideen, t4); nothing of the package is taken.

Two guards now:
1. The kernel's. open(2): "on Linux 2.6 and later, O_EXCL can be used
   without O_CREAT if path refers to a block device. If the block device
   is in use by the system (e.g., mounted), open() fails with the error
   EBUSY." The open now carries O_EXCL; EBUSY becomes UFT_ERR_BUSY with a
   plain message.
2. For a mounted PARTITION of the drive, which (1) is not documented to
   cover: the new src/hal/ufi_mountinfo.c reads /proc/self/mountinfo
   (proc_pid_mountinfo(5): field (3) "major:minor: the value of st_dev for
   files on this filesystem") and resolves partitions through sysfs. An
   unreadable mountinfo is a refusal, not a free device.

The check is a pure function over the TEXT of mountinfo, so it is tested
without hardware on every platform: tests/test_ufi_mountinfo.c — the
proc(5) example line, a mounted partition of an unmounted disk, "8:160" is
not "8:16", the raw mount point with its octal escape, a short buffer,
NULL and empty text, a last line without newline: 10 of 10 on Windows.
Mutation matrix 4 of 5 red (field 4 read instead of 3; partitions
ignored; major only; last line lost); the fifth (buffer bound written as
"< len" instead of "< len - 1") is equivalent — both give the same length
for every input.

Measured on a real Linux kernel (WSL2, 6.18): the device of "/" (8:48) is
found mounted through the real mountinfo — 11 of 11, also under
ASan/UBSan; ufi_linux.c compiles with -Wall -Wextra -Werror as gnu11 and
as c11 (no local Windows build compiles this Linux-only file; the
Linux CI does).

Not measured, and named in P3-669: the sysfs partition branch (in WSL "/"
is on no partition; the test runs it where it is, which the Linux CI
should show); O_EXCL/EBUSY on a real mounted device (no root, no
hardware, MF-310); an SG node (/dev/sg*) gets no mount check, its block
device would first have to be found through sysfs.

events.title: BLiTTER: unaligned blits shifted by the chip, and thresholds re-fitted
events.message:
BLiTTER: unaligned blits shifted by the chip, and thresholds re-fitted

Unaligned blits never used the BLiTTER: skew was always 0, and every
blit at differing phases went through the CPU shift chain. They now
use the chip's barrel shifter - SKEW for the shift, FXSR to prime a
left shift, never NFSR - with the destination's endmasks as before
and the source's y increment covering the one extra fetch a line
makes; a keyed blit is XOR-AND-XOR with the mask pass shifted the
same way. At equal phases it reduces to the old registers.

SPRCOST on an emulated STE, the library's choice, microseconds:
                          before    after
  blit 16x16 plain unal.    2153     1106
  blit 64x32 plain unal.    7383     1387   (5.3x)
  blit 64x32 keyed unal.   12383     3867   (3.2x)
  blit 160x64 plain unal.  27500     3730   (7.4x)
  restore 32x32 x&15=5      1387     1126   (-19%)
  dirty 16 x 16x16         17344    13477   (-22%)
  restore 32x32 aligned     1113     1008   (now CPU, -10%)
85-case geometric mean 0.786 against the previous commit (0.49
against the start of this work). One case is slower: a 16x1 blit the
CPU keeps pays ~40us for the size rules to refuse it (+9%).

How it is arranged is the result of measuring several arrangements
on a plain ST, which never takes any of it:
- The BLiTTER's work is stdl_blitter_blit in blitter.c, where each
  plane's pass is written inline (blit_pass) instead of a call to
  stdl_blitter_run that saved and restored eight registers - four
  passes to a copy, thirteen to a keyed blit. Every BLiTTER blit is
  cheaper for it, same-phase ones included.
- The size rules are stdl_blitter_wants, also out of line. Written
  inline in STDL_BlitSurfaceEx they made a plain ST's unaligned CPU
  blits 1-2% slower through register allocation alone; folding the
  work in there cost same-phase BLiTTER blits 8-11% on an STE.
- The short aligned row copy (tiles, restores) is now a small asm
  loop with a C twin. gcc had kept its strides and row count on the
  stack in some builds and in registers in others - the same C
  measured 7% apart - and written out it is also faster: aligned
  restores 15-25% on a plain ST.

The thresholds were stale: the CPU's inline row copy had made it
faster than the BLiTTER for copies the old constants still sent to
the chip (up to 40% slower there). Re-fitted from an extended
tests/hatari/blitcost.c, which now sweeps five kinds - aligned,
aligned keyed, unaligned, unaligned keyed, and same phase with
partial edge groups (every restore at an odd x, which the CPU merges
group by group and the BLiTTER wins from 26x8 up). Every blit the
BLiTTER takes is now at least as fast as the CPU would be.

Plain ST (SPRCOST, CPU): 85-case geometric mean 0.989; two cases are
0.7-0.9% slower (16x16 unaligned, plain). Size: pixel-path text 33724
of 33740.

test_blitter's randomised blits and BLITCHK's now run half at
independent phases, both shift directions, at budgets 4, 2 and 3,
forced and not: all pass on the host model under ASan and on ste and
megaste in Hatari; getting FXSR or the fetch count wrong fails the
host test. PIXCHK passes on st and ste. Docs: the skill, limits.md,
README.

events.title: grm-9nxj.20: classify E1.E's lone failure as a corpus defect
events.message:
grm-9nxj.20: classify E1.E's lone failure as a corpus defect

The one failing SBC (dp,X) emulation-mode case (e1 e 8669: D=$F400, LL+X=$FF)
is the corpus's fault, not the language's. RefDPIdxInd wraps the pointer high
byte fetch within the direct page (DH:$00), matching Bruce Clark's 65C816
tutorial section 5.11 and higan/bsnes. The corpus generator (TomHarte/CLK) wraps
the LL+X add but leaves the second fetch's increment mask at 0x00FFFF, which is
inconsistent with its own (d) mode.

Exclude it by name (W65816VectorHarnessSupport.CORPUS_DEFECT_CASES) with a new
(N corpus-defect) baseline token instead of leaving the row FAIL, because
OpcodeBaseline.compare only catches PASS->FAIL: a FAIL row can degrade silently.
The run fails if a listed case ever passes (verified by mutating RefDPIdxInd)
or is not found. E1.E: FAIL 9999/10000 -> PASS 9999/9999 (1 corpus-defect).

events.title: BLiTTER fills: one setup for all planes, one pass for 0 and 15
events.message:
BLiTTER fills: one setup for all planes, one pass for 0 and 15

A BLiTTER fill wrote the whole register set for every plane. The
setup is written once now and each plane changes only the logic
operation (STDL_BLIT_SET_OP). A fill of whole groups in colour 0, or
15 at four planes, is a single operation that walks all four plane
words of each group (x increment 2) - the BLiTTER's version of the
memset the CPU path uses for the same fills.

SPRCOST on an emulated STE, the library's own choice (microseconds,
mean of passes A/B), against the commit before the driver groundwork:
  fill 16x16 x&15=3 (any colour)   1250 ->  935   (-25%)
  fill 64x32 colour 0              1377 ->  793   (-42%)
  fill 64x32 colour 5              1377 -> 1062   (-23%)
  fill 320x200 colour 0            9297 -> 5723   (-38%)
Fills the CPU keeps are within the floor on STE and plain ST.

The groundwork's ST-RAM check was costing BLiTTER blits 3% on an
STE: four pointer compares, and what they did to register allocation
around the choice. STDL_Init now records whether the machine has any
alt-RAM (Mxalloc(-1, 1), TOS 1.04 on), and only then are surfaces
looked at - on the machines that exist, never. With that, BLiTTER
restores are 1.5-2.4% slower than before the groundwork, the rest of
its cost; the skewed paths that follow reshape that branch.

BLITCHK now runs each plane budget - 4, 2 and 3 - twice, once as the
library chooses and once with stdl_blit_force sending every eligible
operation to the BLiTTER, adds whole-group fills in 0 and 15, prints
how many blit rows the BLiTTER did, and fails a forced pass that
never reached it. All six comparisons pass on ste. Size +244.

events.title: BLiTTER driver: a skew argument, per-line advances, and ST-RAM reach
events.message:
BLiTTER driver: a skew argument, per-line advances, and ST-RAM reach

Groundwork for skewed BLiTTER passes, with every caller passing skew
0, so nothing it drives changes:

- stdl_blitter_setup and stdl_blitter_go take the SKEW register byte.
  NFSR is never set: on the real chip it does not behave as commonly
  described, and with one-word lines it gives wrong results; with
  FXSR alone a line reads at most one source word past its span.
- The split path around a border window advanced its addresses by
  (nwords-1) x steps and one y step per line, which is wrong once a
  line fetches an extra word under FXSR. The per-line advances are
  worked out in setup now, from the fetch count, and the split uses
  them: two 16-bit multiplies there rather than four in the loop.
- STDL_BLIT_SET_OP changes only the logic operation between runs
  that share every other register; STDL_BLIT_OP_OR and _ONES.
- The BLiTTER sees ST RAM only. The same-phase blit and the fill now
  ask whether the surfaces involved end below PHYSTOP (cached at
  STDL_Init) before choosing it, and take the CPU path if not. Until
  now a surface from plain malloc on an STE with alt-RAM would have
  been blitted as whatever ST RAM aliases it. Hatari cannot give an
  STE alt-RAM, so this is untested on the case it guards.
- Sprite data is allocated with one group of slack past the end, for
  the one source word a skewed pass reads beyond its span; noted in
  docs/format.md as an allocation fact, not a layout change.

Plain ST (SPRCOST): 85-case geometric mean 1.0003, floor 1.002; the
fill's reach test is written inline, because a call in that
condition made small CPU fills 1-2% slower where it is never reached.
BLITCHK passes on ste. Size +52.

events.title: STDL_Dirty: one restore list per page, so it works double-buffered
events.message:
STDL_Dirty: one restore list per page, so it works double-buffered

A double-buffered game draws frame N into one page and frame N+1 into
the other, so what a page needs erased is what was drawn into it two
frames ago. STDL_Dirty kept one list and replayed it onto whichever
page it was handed: with STDL_DOUBLEBUF it erased the other page's
sprites from this one and left this page's own behind, unless the
game pushed both frames' rectangles to paper over it. No port in use
calls it, which is probably why.

The lists are now keyed by the page's pixels, which STDL_Flip swaps
under stdl_screen - the per-buffer restore list a page-flipped engine
keeps. STDL_DirtyRestore(dst) replays that page's list and makes it
the one STDL_DirtyPush fills until the next restore; STDL_DirtyReset
forgets that list only. The API is unchanged, and a single-buffered
game, which only ever names one page, gets exactly the old behaviour:
test_dirty checks it byte for byte against a copy of the old
single-list code over 3000 random operations.

The second list is allocated when a second page appears. A third
page evicts the list of the page restored least recently, and that
page is restored whole when it next comes back (four such pages are
remembered - an occasional off-screen surface, or a border opening
with its own pair of pages); if there is no memory for a second
list, both pages share one and are restored whole. Restores call
STDL_BlitSurfaceEx directly. dirty.o: 508 -> 1036 bytes, outside the
pixel-path budget and linked only by programs that call it.

test_dirty: the one-page reference; two pages drawn alternately for
400 frames, clean after every restore, with overflowing frames and
an occasional third page. Collapsing to one list, or dropping the
owed whole restore, makes it fail. Docs: the header, porting.md, the
skill (which had no STDL_Dirty guidance at all), and design-
overview.md, whose signature for STDL_DirtyRestore was stale and
whose blit-path list claimed a movem copy the code never had.

events.title: Ask whether the BLiTTER is allowed without a call, where it pays
events.message:
Ask whether the BLiTTER is allowed without a call, where it pays

stdl_blitter_active() was a function in blitter.c, called by every
fill and every same-phase blit - on a plain ST too, where the answer
is always no - and fill_rows asked it only after a mulu.w for the
size threshold. It is now an inline test of two bytes (the user's
setting and has_blitter), and fill_rows asks it first.

STDL_BlitSurfaceEx keeps a call, now stdl_blitter_allowed(): inlined
there, the test measured faster on the paths that ask and about 1%
slower on unaligned blits that never do, through the way gcc then
allocated that function's registers.

SPRCOST on a plain ST (Hatari, microseconds, mean of passes A/B):
fills 1-4% faster (64x32 colour 5: 2949 -> 2832), no blit case moves
by more than the noise (<= 0.6%), 85-case geometric mean 0.997.
Size -40.

Also tried and reverted, recorded here because the reasoning was
plausible: moving every blit row loop out of line behind a job
struct, on the theory that the inlined loops' register pressure was
what made the blit's entry cost ~1700 cycles on a plain ST. The
entry cost did not move (216.6 -> 218.5us for a blit clipped to
nothing) and small blits got 5-25% slower for the extra call. The
fixed cost is the clip and set-up's own instruction count.
events.author: neilrackett

events.title: Fills: a whole block in any colour is one run of long-pair stores
events.message:
Fills: a whole block in any colour is one run of long-pair stores

A fill covering whole rows of a surface with no padding - the screen
cleared to a background colour - is one contiguous block. Colours 0
and 15 already got a single memset for it; every other colour went
row by row through the span loop, whose middle gcc 4.6 compiles to a
store at (a0), a store at 4(a0), an addq and a dbf: 46 cycles a
group. fill_longpairs (asm, with its C twin) stores the whole block
with post-increment long pairs, four groups to a pass.

SPRCOST on a plain ST (Hatari, microseconds, mean of passes A/B):
  fill 320x200 colour 5   35859 -> 14141   (-61%)
Every other fill case stays within the floor. It is out of line and
tested only once a fill is known to be whole groups in another
colour: inlined into the span loop, or tested first, it made small
fills 1.5-8% slower through register allocation - and on a plain ST
that is real, not layout: the same objects relinked in reverse order
time identically, to the tenth of a microsecond, on all 85 cases.

Size +120, pixel-path text 33020 of 33740.

test_pixel gains test_fill_blocks: whole-row fills in every colour
on 16-, 48- and 320-wide surfaces, bands of rows, and a masked
surface and a narrowing clip that must take the ordinary paths;
stopping the store run one group short makes it fail. PIXCHK passes
on st.

events.title: blit: unmasked unaligned blits store their middle groups outright
events.message:
blit: unmasked unaligned blits store their middle groups outright

An unaligned blit with no source mask and no composition flags now
has a shift loop of its own with the edge groups peeled: only the
first and last groups of a row can be partial, so every group
between them is opaque, and blit_store4 (asm, with its C twin)
writes the four shifted plane words without reading the destination
or masking - the CPU's version of the BLiTTER skipping the
destination read where its endmask is all ones. No mask window, no
per-group edge tests. Keyed and flagged blits keep the general loop,
unchanged: an opaque-group test inside it (tried first) caught few
groups there and cost keyed blits 2%.

SPRCOST on a plain ST (Hatari, microseconds, mean of passes A/B):
                           before    after
  16x16 plain, unaligned     2998     2148   -28%
  32x16 plain                3975     2793   -30%
  64x32 plain               11367     7383   -35%
  160x64 plain              45313    27500   -39%
  (left shifts the same within 2%)
Keyed unaligned blits are unchanged, 1.000-1.006 against a floor of
1.002. Over all 85 cases the geometric mean is 0.963.

Size: +1152 bytes, pixel-path text 32900 of 33740 - the loop is
instantiated for plane budgets 2 and 4, and a port at budget 2 gets
the same win.

directions, budgets 4, 2 and 3, with and without a destination mask,
against the model; clearing the wrong mask words makes it fail.

events.title: Sprites: split the row loop, peel its edges, one shift per word
events.message:
Sprites: split the row loop, peel its edges, one shift per word

STDL_BlitSprite drew every group of every row through one loop that
asked, per group, whether the sprite was being shifted (gcc 4.6 does
not unswitch a loop-invariant test), selected the clip cover with two
compares, loaded all five words before testing for transparency, and
for an unshifted sprite at an odd x built each word from two variable
shifts and four NULL tests.

Now the choice between the stored-groups loop (a pre-shifted variant,
or phase 0) and the runtime shift is made once, outside the loops.
Each peels its first and last groups, which carry the clip covers and
- for the shift - the transparent group past either end of the
sprite, so the middle runs with no edge tests. The mask is read
first and a transparent group's planes are never fetched; an opaque
group is plain stores with no read of the destination. The shift
builds each word from a 32-bit window, one shift instead of two, as
blit.c's shift chain already did. The frame's offset is one mulu.w
where it was six.

SPRCOST on a plain ST (Hatari, microseconds, mean of passes A/B):
                          before    after
  16x16 unshifted, mean     4922     2607   -47%
  32x32 unshifted, mean    14922     6465   -57%
  64x32 unshifted, mean    25000     7578   -70%
  16x16 phase 0             1357      938   -31%
  32x32 pre-shifted         5469     3125   -43%
  64x32 pre-shifted         7773     3672   -53%
All 36 unshifted and 6 pre-shifted cases improve (geometric means
0.425 and 0.551); no other case moves by 1%, against a same-binary
floor of 1.002.

Size: sprite.o 3040 -> 4268 (+1228), pixel-path text 31748 of 33740.
Two loops times two plane budgets, each with its edges inlined, is
what the speed is made of.

test_pixel gains test_sprites_wide: widths 1-80, multi-frame strips,
both loops at every phase, random clip rectangles, plane budgets 4, 2
and 3, each against the keyed blit of the same frame. Dropping the
last group's clip cover or corrupting the opaque store makes it fail.
PIXCHK passes on st.

A same-phase unmasked blit whose edges are partial groups - every

and word-aligned views, with and without a destination mask, against

events.message:
Tilesets and text leave sprite.o, and blitter.o joins the size check

STDL_TilesetFromSurface, STDL_FreeTileset and STDL_BlitTile move to
src/tileset.c, and STDL_DrawText and STDL_FreeFont to src/text.c,
unchanged. The linker's granularity on this toolchain is the object
file, so every program that drew a sprite carried the tile and text
code whether it called them or not. sprite.o goes from 5784 to 3040
bytes; tileset.o is 1372 and text.o 1392.

Measured on the examples, built at the previous commit and at this
one: the ten that link sprite.o without text or tiles are 2769 bytes
smaller each, and none grew. The ports were not rebuilt - each pins
its own STDL version.

blitter.o joins PIXEL_OBJS with the ceiling raised by exactly its
740 bytes, so moving logic into the driver cannot slip past the
check. With text and tiles now opt-in objects, like surfacefrom.o
and drawchar.o, the core pixel-path text is 30392 of 33740: room for
the sprite and blit work that follows, each step of which reports
its own delta.

events.title: Host tests: a software BLiTTER, so its paths run under ASan
events.message:
Host tests: a software BLiTTER, so its paths run under ASan

The BLiTTER paths were the one part of the pixel code tests/host
could not reach: stdl_blitter_active() was a constant 0 on the host
and the driver compiled to nothing. BLITCHK covers them on the
machine, but only by comparing results, so an overread the chip
silently fetches from a neighbour - exactly what a skewed source
does one word past its rectangle - passes there.

blitter.c now builds on the host, driving a register struct, and
starting an operation runs tests/host/blitmodel.c to completion: a
model written from the chip's documented behaviour (HOP, the 16
logic operations, endmasks, the 32-bit source buffer, SKEW and FXSR,
address stepping), modelling only what the library uses and
asserting on the rest - NFSR included. Host tests turn it on by
setting stdl.mach.has_blitter; everything else still takes the CPU
paths as before.

test_blitter pins the model to hand-worked operations, then runs
randomised fills and blits on the CPU and with the BLiTTER forced
(stdl_blit_force), comparing pixels and masks byte for byte at plane
budgets 4, 2 and 3, and through the overscan policy's split path
with a policy granting random line counts.

That split path was the first thing it caught: the address advance
cast a pointer through int32_t, which truncates a host pointer. It
is intptr_t now - the same type on the target, and the target's
blitter.o disassembles identically before and after.
events.author: neilrackett

events.title: PIXCHK: the host pixel tests, run on the machine
events.message:
PIXCHK: the host pixel tests, run on the machine

tests/host/test_pixel.c checks fills, blits, sprites and spans
against a per-pixel reference model, but natively, where every
pixel path is its C twin. Hand-written 68000 in a pixel path is
covered only by running the same checks on the target, and BLITCHK
cannot do it on a plain ST, where there is no second path to
compare against. PIXCHK includes the suite unchanged and runs it
with the BLiTTER refused and then allowed, so on a BLiTTER machine
the accelerated paths meet the reference model too.

Passes on st, and on ste with both settings.

events.title: Blit counters: count the shift chain, and let BLITCHK force the BLiTTER
events.message:
Blit counters: count the shift chain, and let BLITCHK force the BLiTTER

Under -DSTDL_BLIT_STATS the aligned per-group merge (masked blits,
partial edge groups, composition flags) counted itself as
stdl_blit_shift, and the real unaligned shift chain counted nothing,
not even stdl_blit_rows - so the one counter a port would read to ask
"is this the slow path" said the opposite of what happened. The merge
now has stdl_blit_merge, the shift chain counts its rows, and
stdl_blit_blitter counts rows as the public header always said.

STDL_BlitSprite gets stdl_spr_calls, stdl_spr_rows and stdl_spr_shift.

stdl_blit_force, stats builds only, sends every operation the BLiTTER
could do to it regardless of the size thresholds (never past the
correctness exclusions), so BLITCHK can reach the one-word rows and
clipped edges a threshold keeps on the CPU. BLITCHK now links the
counted build of blit.o, sprite.o and draw.o ahead of the archive.

A normal build is unchanged: pixel-path text 32396 bytes before and
after.

events.title: The brood's kill score and sprites (CS:0x89E6, SS:0x360A); every demo's score matches DOS
events.message:
The brood's kill score and sprites (CS:0x89E6, SS:0x360A); every demo's score matches DOS

A brood child's kill scores 1000 on the alive path right after the draw
(CS:0x89E6 -> 0x89F8) and restarts its frame; the alive frame cycles 0..3
(CS:0x8A00); SS:0x360A = 0217 0218 0219 0218, read live and in the static
image. Closes UNKNOWN_brood_score and UNKNOWN_brood_sprite_table.

score_cycle.py logs the score through a whole attract cycle; under the
Roland driver the running DOSBox uses, all six demos match per award
(score-compare.js) and the live brood dump matches 56 ticks (brood-compare.js).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

events.title: feat(app): surface rejected-trial counts in cleanup/repair/compact tidy frames (SQ-1637)
events.message:
feat(app): surface rejected-trial counts in cleanup/repair/compact tidy frames (SQ-1637)

Part 4: cleanup_overlaps_observed, repair_directional_hints_observed and
compact_empty_lines_observed each only emitted a frame when a trial was
COMMITTED — a rejected trial (scored, tried, discarded) left no trace at
all. That is exactly the shape at the heart of SQ-1636: a move that would
have genuinely improved the layout scored as a net loss under the (then-
buggy) reciprocity check and was silently thrown away with nothing to show
for it in the animation.

Scope decision (documented, per the quest's own allowance that this part
may end up smaller): each pass now tracks how many candidate moves it
actually evaluated ("tried") versus how many it committed, and emits ONE
trailing summary frame per call — "Overlap cleanup summary: N trials
tried, M committed, K rejected." (and the repair_hints / compact
equivalents) — rather than a frame per rejected trial, which the prior
SQ-1637 investigation measured at up to ~1,300 set_pos calls per pass and
flagged as too noisy to surface individually. Surfacing the single
best-scoring rejected trial (the more ambitious option the quest offered)
is NOT implemented — the simpler N/M/K summary was judged sufficient to
make a silent rejection visible without adding scoring-comparison logic to
three different trial loops for a debug-only feature.

compact_empty_lines_observed's "trial" is a different shape (an empty-line
collapse candidate, either committed or reverted because it would raise a
new overlap) but gets the same tried/committed/rejected treatment for
consistency.

Falsified: temporarily disabling the summary-frame emission and rerunning
cleanup_overlaps_summary_frame_surfaces_rejected_trials reproduces the
original symptom exactly — only the one committed-move frame appears, with
no trace of the 27 other candidates cleanup_overlaps evaluated and
discarded on the A129 fixture that test drives.

This closes out SQ-1637's four parts. Parts 1-3 are fully settled by tests
(a real gated-passage animated-vs-silent equivalence test, two contiguify
sub-step tests including a real A129-fixture case, and a normalization
consistency test — all four falsified by reverting their respective fixes).
Part 4 is deliberately smaller in scope than the quest's more ambitious
"best rejected trial" option, as explicitly allowed, and is itself
falsified above.
