Name The Hobbit's LOOK, DROP, TAKE and INVENTORY, and the gate every handler shares

FOR_REAL ($9D44) is the line through every action handler: the checks come
before it, and when the action is only being tested it answers "yes" and
leaves the handler. DO_LOOK, DO_DROP, DO_TAKE (TAKE and CARRY) and
DO_INVENTORY are named and commented, with their helpers MUST_CARRY,
CAN_LIFT, COUNT_HELD and PLACED_WORD. Things tied to the rope are taken and
dropped with it, and a liquid put down evaporates.

Object byte 4 is half decoded: its low bits say how things sit with the
object -- in, on, behind, under, tied to -- and its high bits group the
characters (the player's side, the goblins and Gollum, the elves), though
what reads those is not yet found.

feat(64-08): attach authenticated by its broker-minted handle alone, ahead of the token gate (G-64-1)

the per-boot control token, so every relay attach through the real
vice-proxy.ts failed with "missing or invalid control token" -- and owner

the listener binds on, closing a latent "relay always dials 19510" defect

stdio, against a real control listener and a real handleMonitorClaim()/
handleRelayAttach(), reading vice_ping's result instead of discarding it
-- the exact gap the pre-existing proxy test could not catch.

events.title: Name how The Hobbit narrates an action, and how it tests one before doing it
events.message:
Name how The Hobbit narrates an action, and how it tests one before doing it

NARRATE_ACTION ($712B) builds the sentence the player reads about anyone's
action from its ACTION_PATTERNS entry: who, "cannot" if refused, the verb or
GO and a direction -- GO SOMEWHERE in the dark -- then the objects, with
their particle and preposition. The top nibbles of a pattern's four word
references are flags (PATTERN_FLAGS): one of them marks LOOK and INVENTORY
as never narrated, and two say which objects the sentence has.

WOULD_WORK ($7AF5) runs the action through DO_ACTION with $B6FA clear, and
that flag turns out to mean "for real", not only "print": with it clear a
handler just reports through $B6FB whether it would work. ACTOR_TRIES asks
this first, the same test-then-do SCRIPT_DO uses for a script's routines.

Checked: rebuilds byte-for-byte; the words (CANNOT, SOMEWHERE) decoded from
the dictionary. Not yet worked out: $7A14, which answers for patterns with
objects to match, and a few calls marked so.

events.title: Βήμα 24: μουσική στην αναμονή — και ο συναγερμός που χτυπούσε σε κάθε νέο παιχνίδι
events.message:
Βήμα 24: μουσική στην αναμονή — και ο συναγερμός που χτυπούσε σε κάθε νέο παιχνίδι

Τα δεκατρεισήμισι δευτερόλεπτα της γέννησης έχουν σκοπό. Δύο κανάλια, λίστα
νότες το καθένα, 420 από τα 768 ελεύθερα bytes της γεννήτριας.

ΓΙΑΤΙ ΔΕΥΤΕΡΟΣ ΠΑΙΚΤΗΣ. Ο ήχος του παιχνιδιού ζει στην τράπεζα 2, που δεν
υπάρχει ακόμη όταν τρέχει η γεννήτρια: η PAGE2.BIN κάθεται σε πρόχειρο χώρο και
την κατεβάζει το επίμετρο (§13.1).

ΤΟ ΡΟΛΟΙ ΕΙΝΑΙ Ο ΙΔΙΟΣ Ο ΚΟΣΜΟΣ ΠΟΥ ΧΤΙΖΕΤΑΙ. Οι διακοπές είναι κλειστές, άρα
δεν υπάρχει frame interrupt: χτυπάει ο βρόχος των πλακιδίων, ανά 32 πλακίδια
(~17 ms). Ο ρυθμός ΚΟΥΝΙΕΤΑΙ και δεν είναι λίγο — μετρημένες νότες 22, 21, 30,
12, 74, 47, 56, 112 frames για παρτιτούρα που λέει 30, 30, 45, 15, 60, 30, 30,
60 χτύπους. Τα πλακίδια δεν κοστίζουν ίδια: η μουσική αργεί εκεί που ο κόσμος
γίνεται περίπλοκος. Ακούγεται σαν μουσικό κουτί που ξεκουρδίζεται, και γι'
αυτά τα δεκατρία δευτερόλεπτα δεν είναι το χειρότερο.

Η ΕΝΤΑΣΗ ΕΙΝΑΙ ΛΟΓΙΣΜΙΚΟ, ΟΧΙ ΦΑΚΕΛΟΣ ΥΛΙΚΟΥ. Ο φάκελος του AY θα κόστιζε δύο
εγγραφές τη νότα, αλλά τότε ο R8 λέει μόνο «χρησιμοποίησε φάκελο» και η
πραγματική ένταση ΔΕΝ ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ στους καταχωρητές — ούτε η δοκιμή ούτε το
tools/ayrender.py θα μπορούσαν να πουν τι ακούγεται. Κάθε δεύτερος χτύπος
κατεβάζει την ένταση κατά ένα: 13 ως το 0 σε μισό δευτερόλεπτο, και ό,τι
ακούγεται το λένε οι καταχωρητές. Είκοσι bytes για να μείνει δοκιμάσιμο.

ΚΑΙ ΜΙΑ ΑΛΗΘΙΝΗ ΒΛΑΒΗ, από τη δοκιμή που απαιτεί σιωπή όταν ξεκινά το παιχνίδι:
κάθε νέο παιχνίδι χτυπούσε συναγερμό στο πρώτο δευτερόλεπτο. Το ml_alert
χτυπάει στην ακμή «εντάξει -> όχι εντάξει», και η αρχική κατάσταση ξεκινά με το
POK να λέει «εντάξει» — γίνεται μηδέν μόλις η πρώτη περιστροφή του τροχού
υπολογίσει το ισοζύγιο ρεύματος. Δηλαδή σειρήνα για βλάβη που ήταν πάντα
αλήθεια. Τώρα ο συναγερμός περιμένει τρεις κλήσεις πριν αρχίσει να κοιτάζει.

Δοκιμές (test_disc): πέντε τουλάχιστον διαφορετικές νότες, δέκα τουλάχιστον
δείγματα με ένταση, και ΣΙΩΠΗ όταν ξεκινά το παιχνίδι. Αρνητικός έλεγχος:
χωρίς την κλήση wg_beat, μηδέν νότες σε 53 δείγματα.

Δύο δοκιμές που έπεφταν στα ίσα, διορθωμένες: το test_save διάβαζε τον πίνακα
πριν προλάβει το ρολόι του HUD (16 frames), και σύγκρινε δύο σωσμένα παιχνίδια
που διέφεραν όσο και η ανοχή του ελέγχου.

events.title: support: one rule for writing a file the user already has
events.message:
support: one rule for writing a file the user already has

Every path that replaces a file the user already had opened its destination
with Truncate and checked the byte count afterwards, which reports a failed
write honestly and still leaves the file empty: on a full disk or a quota,
the only copy of the source being edited, the sprite document, an export or a
floppy image is gone. The project file had moved to QSaveFile and was still
exposed, because Qt 6.8.1 - the Qt every release archive bundles - checks
only its own writeError before the rename, and a flush that fails inside
commit() never sets it, so the truncated temporary file goes over the
destination and commit() returns true. Qt 6.10 folds the device error in
first, which is why a development machine never saw it.

files::write() is that rule in one place: stage in the destination's own
directory, flush, check the device error, cancel the temporary when any of
them fails, and only then let it take the destination's place. The editor's
source save, ImageDocument (.pim), the ST image exports, the bitplane export,
the floppy extraction, FloppyImage::saveRaw and ProjectSettings::save all go
through it now. The files PiST generates for a session - the discovery file,
the debugger bootstrap script, the AUTO-folder image - are not user data and
keep their plain write.

Pinned by aFailedWriteKeepsThePreviousBytes, beside the project-level
saveFailureKeepsPreviousFile and sharing its RLIMIT_FSIZE fixture: with the
naive truncate-and-check body both fail on Qt 6.8.1, and both pass with the
rule. Full suite green on 6.8.1, the Qt the archives bundle.

events.title: Work out The Hobbit's RANDOM: 0 to A inclusive, and not evenly
events.message:
Work out The Hobbit's RANDOM: 0 to A inclusive, and not evenly

RANDOM ($9CA8) mixes its last result with bytes from a pointer that steps
through memory, halves the byte until it is no more than twice the limit,
and takes the limit off; RANDOM_POSITIVE drops the sign. So every value from
0 to A comes up: all five HIDDEN_ROADS can be shut, the first and last half as
often, and all four RIDDLES entries are chosen about equally.

Checked by calling RANDOM_POSITIVE 3000 times each for limits 3, 4 and 9 in
the simulator. Rebuilds byte-for-byte.

events.title: Βήμα 23: τα κείμενα στην τράπεζα 7 — και μια μέτρηση που ακύρωσε το σχέδιο
events.message:
Βήμα 23: τα κείμενα στην τράπεζα 7 — και μια μέτρηση που ακύρωσε το σχέδιο

Το βήμα 22 τελείωσε με 37 ελεύθερα bytes στην τράπεζα 0 και ένα σχέδιο: να πάνε
fdc+save+newgame (1.301 bytes κρύου κώδικα) στην τράπεζα 2, πληρώνοντας τον χώρο
από το GH_LOG — 1.600 bytes αρχείου αναίρεσης που ΕΜΟΙΑΖΑΝ γενναιόδωρα.

ΔΕΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ. Ενα φάντασμα DOME L γράφει 1.532 από τα 1.600. Μετρημένο διαβάζοντας
το gh_ptr όσο το φάντασμα είναι στην οθόνη:

  κέρσορας 124 · 2x2 348 · 3x3 592 · 4x4 776 · 6x6 1.204 · 8x8 1.532

Εξήντα οκτώ bytes περιθώριο. Το gh_run αρνείται να καταγράψει λωρίδα που δεν
μπορεί να πάρει πίσω — δεν τη ΖΩΓΡΑΦΙΖΕΙ — οπότε μικρότερο αρχείο δεν θα
χαλούσε τίποτα, θα έτρωγε αθόρυβα κομμάτια του μεγαλύτερου φαντάσματος.

(Η πρώτη εκδοχή της μέτρησης έλεγε 1.600 με σκέτο κέρσορα. Ηταν η ίδια η
μέτρηση που χαλούσε αυτό που μετρούσε: γεμίζοντας τον buffer με σημάδι σβήνεις
τις εγγραφές που το gh_undo πάει να ξετυλίξει, κι εκείνο μετά διαβάζει
σκουπίδια για κεφαλίδες και γράφει όπου να 'ναι.)

Ετσι ο χώρος ήρθε από αλλού — από εκεί που τον κρατούσε το §4.2 από την αρχή:
και τα 35 κείμενα του hud.asm και του ui.asm, 496 bytes, πήγαν στο δεσμευμένο
«text» της τράπεζας 7. Η τράπεζα 0 πήγε 37 -> 488.

Ο μηχανισμός είναι 14 bytes: το hud_text7 σελιδοποιεί την 7, καλεί το hud_text,
ξαναβάζει την 1. Το ui_msg κάνει το ίδιο γύρω από το τύπωμα ΚΑΙ το μέτρημα
μήκους, το sl_digit γύρω από τα τρία μπαλώματά του. Μόνο το bd_name μένει στο
hud_text: ζει στην τράπεζα 2.

Τρία που ισχύουν μόνο γι' αυτή την τράπεζα:
- Μόνο δεδομένα ανάγνωσης. Κώδικας εκεί θα έσβηνε τον εαυτό του μόλις
  σελιδοποιούσε την 4 ή την 6.
- Δύο διευθύνσεις: στο bankset 1 του rasm η τράπεζα 7 είναι στο #C000,
  σελιδοποιημένη στο #4000. Το uitext.asm γράφει στην πρώτη και ορίζει κάθε
  ετικέτα στη δεύτερη.
- Ενατο αρχείο στον δίσκο: το BANK7.BIN το φτιάχνει το pack.py, που δεν ξέρει
  τι λέει το παιχνίδι. Το TEXT.BIN πέφτει πάνω από το δεσμευμένο κενό, ΜΕΤΑ.

Και ένας assert: αν τα κείμενα ξεπεράσουν τα 1.024 bytes, ο assembler σταματά
αντί να γράψει πάνω στα επόμενα δεδομένα της τράπεζας 7.

Το test_disc δειγματίζει τη μπάρα «όσο φορτώνει» αντί για «ως το frame 1400» —
το σταθερό όριο έσπασε μόλις μπήκε το ένατο αρχείο.

events.title: Carry out file changes inside hard-drive partitions
events.message:
Carry out file changes inside hard-drive partitions

Deleting and renaming inside a partition of a hard drive failed whatever
the partition held: those changes were sent to the engine's command line,
which addresses a whole image, and a drive with a partition table has no
single volume there to act on. The same applied to replacing a file from
the editor, applying a patch and installing into a partition.

When a partition is selected, the remove, move and make-drawer commands
now run through that partition's own mount, so they work for FFS and SFS
partitions alike, and Validate checks the partition on screen rather than
every partition of the drive.

Opening one partition also no longer leaves a handle open on the whole
drive, which matters once the drive is a real device rather than a file.

events.title: Read and write Smart File System volumes
events.message:
Read and write Smart File System volumes

Amiga drives prepared for large partitions often use SFS rather than FFS,
and the workbench could list such a partition in the drive's Rigid Disk
Block but not open it. Amiganut now reads and writes SFS 1.x volumes,
whether bare or inside an RDB partition, and can format new ones.

Changes follow SFS's own crash protocol. File data goes only into blocks
free both on disk and in the pending change; changed metadata is logged
to free space, a TRFA marker points at the log, the blocks are written
in place and the marker returns to TROK, with a flush between stages.
Power lost at any point leaves the old volume or the new one, and a
volume SFS left mid-change is read as SFS would replay it.

Validate now checks what SFScheck checks, and runs in seconds on a
60 GB partition. The work was checked against real SFS 1.277 on an
emulated A1200: SFScheck accepted volumes built and changed here, and
every change real SFS then made read back intact.

Also fixes RDB partition placement when a partition groups several
sectors into one filesystem block, as SFS partitions often do: the
offset was scaled by SectorPerBlock a second time, putting such
partitions at twice their real position.

events.title: Name DO_ACTION, where every action in The Hobbit is carried out, and its checks
events.message:
Name DO_ACTION, where every action in The Hobbit is carried out, and its checks

DO_ACTION ($950F) is shared by the player and the characters. It refuses an
action that makes no sense (SENSIBLE: doing it to yourself, or to a thing with
itself), limits the dark to what the actor carries, and refuses the player an
object another character is carrying (CARRIED_BY_ANOTHER). Then the objects
get the first say through their own handlers -- the second object first for
the five container actions in SECOND_FIRST ($A20B) -- before ACTION_TABLE's
ordinary one; records keyed 0 after a handler run too, which is how drinking
the wine both drinks it and makes you drunk; and any character acted on
reacts.

itself. Not yet worked out: what sets $B6FE, $B6FF and $B711, and the message
printed for the player in the dark at $95A2.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's character scripts, the orders the player gives, and the win
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's character scripts, the orders the player gives, and the win

Every other character is driven by a script, walked each turn by
CHARACTERS_ACT ($980E) from a 7-byte slot in CHARACTERS ($CACB). A step is an
action tried exactly as the player's sentences are -- the action code and its
objects in $B6E7-$B6E9, carried out through ACTION_TABLE -- or a routine, a
pause, a jump, or a switch to another script from the character's own
FIND_RECORD table, at random or by key. The keys past the ordinary scripts are
reactions: REACT sends a character to the script it keeps for whatever the
player has just done to it. An order the player has given (ORDERS, $B738)
replaces the step unless the step is marked uninterruptible.

ACTION_PATTERNS ($AB53) is the key to all of it: 59 sentence patterns whose
place in the list is the action code, so every code in the scripts and in
ACTION_TABLE now has a name. CHECK_WON ($A9D6) is the ending: the treasure in
the wooden chest.

The routines the scripts call are reached only through JP (HL), so the build
walks the scripts the way the game does and seeds them: 6720 instruction
starts, from 6567.

Checked: rebuilds byte-for-byte; over twelve WAIT turns in the simulator, 166
of 168 script pointers landed on steps as decoded, and the two that did not
were the warg's, past a pause the test walker had wrongly taken for an end --
which is what the SCRIPT_BARE description now says. Not yet worked out: the
sentence printing in ACTOR_TRIES, byte 6 of a slot, and how RANDOM uses A.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's timers: the barrel, the bog, the magic door and the rest
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's timers: the barrel, the bog, the magic door and the rest

END_OF_TURN ($96B3) counts down ten 7-byte timers at $CA84 once a turn,
running each one's routine when it reaches zero and a warning routine in the
turns before, with at most one firing a turn. Those routines are reached only
through $9B80's JP (HL), so they are now code-map seeds (6567 instruction
starts, from 6440), and every one is named and commented: the barrel thrown
up on the long lake, the spider web, the goblins' door, the deep bog, the
magic door and the elf, the wine wearing off (which clears DRUNK, so
WINE_DRUNK's last step is starting timer 7), the eyes in the forest and the
hole in the mountain's side. Also START ($6C00), which saves the changeable
state aside and restores it on each new game, and the helpers the timers use:
RUN_ROUTINE, MOVE_CONTENTS, MOVE_HELD and EMPTY_OUT.

A misaligned annotation now stops the build instead of logging a line that
is easy to miss: one did exactly that here, and the only other symptom was a
40002-byte assembly.

Checked by rebuilding: 40000 bytes reassemble byte-for-byte. Timer 1's web
change, timer 6's ring check and $B6F3 are described as read, not seen in play.

Ο δίσκος είχε τρεις θέσεις από το βήμα 16. Το sv_save και το sv_load έπαιρναν

build: gate packaging on the test suite

The Release workflow published 0.8.2 from a tag whose CI run was still in
flight, and would have published it just the same had CI been red: the
two workflows share a trigger but nothing else, so the archives were
built, verified as bundles and attached to a release without a single
test having run. The project-save bug tst_settings catches on the
bundled Qt shipped in all seven assets.

Run ctest after the build and before anything is deployed or packaged.
Linux runs the full suite against the fork it is about to bundle, with
PIST_REQUIRE_EMULATOR so a missing prerequisite fails rather than skips;
macOS has no emulator in this job and Windows sessions never reach the
entry stop, so those legs run the unit suites - the same ground CI's
Windows leg covers. Everything the suite needs is already staged here:
the assembler and linker in bundle/bin, the ROM in bundle/share/emutos.

events.title: test: make the Windows leg's three checks honest
events.message:
test: make the Windows leg's three checks honest

All three were test defects, not product ones; the Windows leg had been
reporting them as failures since the review batch landed.

- gitDiscoveryFollowsTheOpenedProject: the cmd.exe fake recorded
  `<cwd> ^& <args>` while the checker it feeds splits on `|`, so field 0
  was the whole line, canonicalFilePath() of it was empty, and every
  invocation read as git running outside the project. Record `<cwd>^|<args>`
  with the redirection in front of echo, so no space can be echoed into
  either field. %CD% was already the scratch tree: GitService's working
  directory was right all along.
- settingErrorLinesRepaintsTheGutter: the error mark is a "!" glyph and
  the runner has no fonts at all (Qt ships none and the offscreen
  platform loads none), so drawText puts down no pixels and `marked`
  cannot differ from `plain`. Assert the breakpoint dot instead - drawn
  as geometry precisely so it does not depend on a font - keep every
  paint-count and clear-restores-plain check unconditional, and skip the
  glyph comparison last, naming the environment fact.
- floppyUpdateKeepsForeignNamesByteIdentical: the expected name was
  QStringLiteral("caf\xE9.txt"), and QStringLiteral pastes its narrow
  text after u"", which leaves the UTF-16 meaning of that byte to the
  compiler's mixed-literal interpretation - MSVC's is not U+00E9. Spell
  it QString::fromLatin1, the decode the product itself applies to the
  field, so the expectation is compiler-independent.
events.author: idontwantyourspamthanks

events.title: emu: widen the owed-prompt drain to a tail still on its way
events.message:
emu: widen the owed-prompt drain to a tail still on its way

drainStderr() waits 20 ms, which suits the completion path: Hatari
flushes a response before it prints the prompt that closes it, so the
bytes are in the pipe and the wait only collects them. The owed-prompt
path is different - the command was abandoned at its 10 s timeout with
the emulator still running it, so the rest of its output can be written
after the prompt we swallow for it. 20 ms lost that race on the macOS
runner, and the dead command's tail landed in the next command's
response (aTimedOutCommandsTailDoesNotContaminateTheNext, red in CI
while green on Linux).

Give that one path 200 ms and leave the completion path at 20: nothing
is waiting on an owed prompt, since its command was reported failed ten
seconds earlier. The fake's gap goes from 10 ms to 50 ms so the margin
is the assertion's, not the scheduler's - narrowing the window back now
fails deterministically, which is what the old 10 ms gap could not do.

events.title: settings: keep the project file when a save cannot reach the disk
events.message:
settings: keep the project file when a save cannot reach the disk

QSaveFile's atomicity depends on commit() noticing that the write failed,
and on Qt 6.8.1 - the Qt every release archive bundles - it does not: the
payload is buffered, so write() reports success and the failure surfaces
in the flush commit() performs internally, which sets the device error but
not the writeError commit() checks. It then renames the empty temporary
file over the project and returns true. Qt 6.10 checks the device error
there, so a development machine on a newer Qt is green either way - which
is how 0.8.2 shipped this.

Flush explicitly and check QFileDevice::error() before committing, and
cancelWriting() when either is wrong so the commit discards the temporary
file instead of renaming it. Reproduced on both versions side by side
under RLIMIT_FSIZE=0, and pinned by saveFailureKeepsPreviousFile, which
fails on 6.8.1 without the check and passes on both with it.

events.title: Read the tokeniser: abbreviations, and punctuation as words
events.message:
Read the tokeniser: abbreviations, and punctuation as words

TOKENISE is commented step by step, and reading it through shows two
things about what a player may type.

Words can be shortened, and within limits lengthened. A candidate is
taken when it and the typed word agree over the shorter of their lengths
(LETTERS_AGREE, $6FBA) and the typed word is the shorter; when the typed
word is the longer, only if the entry has at least four letters and the
next candidate does not agree as well. Tried through the game: EXAM gives
EXAMINE, INV gives INVENTORY, SWORDS gives SWORD, INT gives INTO because
IN is too short to stretch, and EXAMINING is unknown.

And punctuation is tokenised as words (PUNCTUATION_TOKEN, $6F30): a full
stop takes THEN's class and a comma AND's, so they parse exactly as the
words they stand for.

It also confirms the word classes at the code level: the class nibble is
built from bits 5-6 of an entry's first byte above bits 5-6 of its
second, the rule found earlier from captured tokens.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
events.author: jonsole

events.title: Read how the parser ends a command, handles AND, and dispatches special words
events.message:
Read how the parser ends a command, handles AND, and dispatches special words

PARSE_THEN is where a command is finished. It refuses one with no verb --
"what ?", outside a quotation -- sets the ALL bit when $B719 says ALL was
used, counts the frame, and carries on into the next frame when it was an
AND that ended this one. Then it shares words between frames: a frame with
no verb takes the one before's, so TAKE THE MAP AND THE KEY is two TAKEs,
and a frame with the same verb but no second phrase borrows the previous
frame's, so PUT THE MAP AND THE KEY IN THE CHEST puts both in the chest.
It also fits the words of a reply into a command left unfinished, filling
whichever of the old noun and adjectives are empty. More on the line is
left to the main loop, except inside a quotation, where orders to a
character are parsed in one go.

PARSE_AND saves the checkpoint a following verb goes back to, which is
what makes AND separate commands as well as join nouns.

PARSE_SPECIAL searches SPECIAL_WORDS ($8271) and jumps to a handler for
each: ALL, EXCEPT, IT and ONE, and the game's own commands -- SAVE, LOAD,
QUIT, PAUSE, HELP, SCORE, PRINT and NOPRINT. The handlers are seeds now,
since nothing branches to them and the playthrough never types SAVE or
LOAD; the code map gains 157 instruction starts, to 6440.

events.title: Read the parser's verb, noun and preposition handlers
events.message:
Read the parser's verb, noun and preposition handlers

A preposition gathers any more prepositions, lets one article through,
and hands on to the adjective or noun handler; a noun goes into PHRASE,
which FILE_PHRASE then copies into the frame's first empty noun phrase --
E's bits 6 and 7 say which are still empty -- and a third phrase is an
error. PHRASE's first byte, left open before, counts its prepositions.

A verb is stored at the head of the frame by STORE_VERB, which clears E
bit 1 so that a second verb, not joined by AND, gets "what ?". It first
looks ahead past any adverbs for a direction, so RUN QUICKLY WEST puts
WEST at offset 2. And straight after AND a verb ends the command at the
checkpoint PARSE_AND saved and begins another, so TAKE THE MAP AND DROP
IT is two commands.

That last point corrects this commit's first draft, which read E bit 3
the wrong way round: E starts as $FF, so the bit is set for an ordinary
command and PARSE_AND is what clears it.

events.title: Read the parser's loop and its small class handlers
events.message:
Read the parser's loop and its small class handlers

PARSE_COMMAND starts each command at the first frame and keeps in E a set
of flags for what may come next -- bit 1 a verb, bit 2 an adverb, bit 4 an
article -- fetching each token with NEXT_TOKEN and jumping to its class's
handler. A command left unfinished, as after "which key?", is entered in a
different state so the new words are fitted into the old frame.

The small handlers fall through into one another, and that is the
grammar: a direction where a verb could start is the verb, so NORTHEAST on
its own is a command, and anywhere else it takes the adverb's place, as
after GO; GO and RUN are verbs; IN is a preposition except straight after
AND at the start of a command, where it is a verb; an article is noted and
dropped; an adjective goes into the phrase being built, PHRASE ($757A),
which refuses a third. STORE_WORD writes words into the frame low byte
first, which is why frames and object names hold them little-endian while
tokens do not. A word in the wrong place goes to NOT_ALLOWED_HERE, which
says "what ?" -- printed through the game to check -- unless it is inside
a quotation, where orders to other characters are let off.

events.title: Βήμα 21: η οθόνη φόρτωσης — τριάντα ένα δευτερόλεπτα που δεν έλεγαν τίποτα
events.message:
Βήμα 21: η οθόνη φόρτωσης — τριάντα ένα δευτερόλεπτα που δεν έλεγαν τίποτα

Ο παίκτης έβλεπε «Ready», «run"habitat» και ένα περίγραμμα να αλλάζει χρώμα
εφτά φορές· μετά η αποικία εμφανιζόταν ΠΑΝΩ σε εκείνο το κείμενο και έμενε έτσι
ως την πρώτη πλήρη σχεδίαση. Καμία δοκιμή δεν είχε άποψη. Βρέθηκε με
screenshots της εκκίνησης από δισκέτα.

Τρεις αλλαγές, σε τρία προγράμματα, γιατί τα 31 δευτερόλεπτα ανήκουν σε τρία:

- Ο φορτωτής (firmware ζωντανό) καλεί SCR SET MODE 1 ως πρώτη εντολή — που
  ΣΒΗΝΕΙ την οθόνη — και γράφει τίτλο, υπότιτλο και «LOADING» με TXT OUTPUT.
  Κάθε ld_file τυπώνει μία τελεία: η σειρά των τελειών ΕΙΝΑΙ ο μετρητής
  αρχείων. MODE 1 και όχι 0, επειδή σαράντα στήλες χωρούν λέξεις.
- Η γεννήτρια γράφει μπάρα ΚΑΤΕΥΘΕΙΑΝ στη μνήμη οθόνης: 128 σειρές του
  wg_plane, 64 bytes μπάρα, ένα byte ανά δύο σειρές. Το wg_prog είναι 30 bytes,
  δεν χαλάει καταχωρητή, και το worldgen.asm δίνει κενή προεπιλογή ώστε το
  gentest — που δεν έχει οθόνη — να μην αλλάξει.
- Το παιχνίδι σβήνει την οθόνη πριν ζωγραφίσει (hw_clear, 16 KB ldir, 86 ms).

Δοκιμές, όλες από τον ΔΙΣΚΟ (το snapshot δεν περνά ποτέ από τον φορτωτή):
οι δύο πρώτες σειρές χαρακτήρων είναι άδειες στα 6 δευτερόλεπτα ενώ οι σειρές
του τίτλου όχι· η μπάρα δειγματίζεται κάθε 30 frames σε όλη τη γένεση και
πρέπει να ξεκινά στο μηδέν, να μη γυρίζει πίσω και να φτάνει και στα 64· το
hw_clear τρέχει πάνω σε οθόνη γεμάτη #AA. Αρνητικοί έλεγχοι: χωρίς το SCR SET
MODE μένουν 292 bytes κειμένου BASIC· χωρίς την κλήση ανά σειρά η μπάρα μένει
στο μηδέν και τα 13,5 δευτερόλεπτα.

Και ένας ακόμη έλεγχος στο mkdsk: η γεννήτρια δεν επιτρέπεται να φτάσει στη
στοίβα του BASIC (#8F00). Μένουν 768 bytes — αρκετά για τη μουσική, που είναι
το μόνο που λείπει πια από αυτή την αναμονή.

Comment the message printer, and find that words have more than one ending

RUN_MESSAGE, PRINT_WORD and PRINT_LITERAL are commented step by step.

The full reading of PRINT_WORD corrects an assumption: an inflected word
does not always take "s". Bits 5-7 of its third dictionary byte choose one
of eight four-character endings in ENDINGS ($B71F): "s" for fifty verbs,
"es" for GO, CROSS, PUSH, SLASH, SMASH and TORCH, "ies", "d", "ing" -- and
a backspace followed by "ies", which is how CARRY prints as CARRIES: the
backspace takes the Y back off. EMPTY is given plain "ies", which would
print EMPTYIES if it were ever inflected; that is noted, not checked.

PRINT_WORD also starts a new line when a word will not fit on the current
one, and puts a space before a word when one is wanted.

events.title: tools: jsbeeb 2.0 changed keyDown's type, and it fails silently
events.message:
tools: jsbeeb 2.0 changed keyDown's type, and it fails silently

verify_dynamic.mjs had been returning all zeros since jsbeeb-mcp 4.0.0
brought jsbeeb 2.3.0 into the npx cache - the resolver takes the highest
version it finds, so the harnesses moved to 2.x on their own.

MachineSession.keyDown took a numeric browser keyCode in 1.x (16 = SHIFT,
88 = X). In 2.x it takes a KeyboardEvent.code STRING naming the physical
key ("ShiftLeft", "KeyX"). Passing the old number matches nothing and DOES
NOT THROW: the key is simply never pressed. So SHIFT+BREAK stopped booting
the disc, every counter read its power-on value, and the harness printed

  {"fields":0,"frames":0,"scrollIdle":0,"scrollAfterX":0}

which is indistinguishable from a game that hangs. Nothing in the output
said the boot had not happened.

Found by reading &1900 after the boot instead of trusting the counters:
0d ff 00 00 under 2.3.0, where 1.25.0 had a2 ff 9a a9 - LDX #&FF : TXS,
the game's own entry. The disc had never been read.

jsbeeb_src.mjs now exports keys(), returning the right form for whichever
jsbeeb was resolved, and both harnesses say K.SHIFT / K.X. Adding a key
there rather than writing a literal at the call site is the point: the same
silent failure cannot come back through a new harness.

Measured after the fix, the documented result on both:

  jsbeeb 2.3.0   {"fields":100,"frames":50,"scrollIdle":0,"scrollAfterX":200}
  jsbeeb 1.25.0  {"fields":100,"frames":50,"scrollIdle":0,"scrollAfterX":200}

probe_shot.mjs boots and screenshots the panel and strip again too.

hardware-facts.md records it beside the MCP's own key-name change - same
rework, one layer down - with the rule that follows: an all-zero harness
result is a boot that did not happen, so check &1900 before believing it.

events.title: fix: a reset or power cycle no longer swallows the lazy disk write
events.message:
fix: a reset or power cycle no longer swallows the lazy disk write

The drive's reset sequence and power switch flushed the pending track into
disk.bytes and then re-attached the disk, which marked it synced: the flush
report the daemon's lazy host-file write arms on was consumed and lost, so a
write made just before a drive reset, a drive power cycle, a held reset, or a
C64 reset on the IEC reset line never reached the user's file on its own.
"Written into disk.bytes" and "reported" are now two facts: the drive keeps
an unreported-write flag that its reset and power paths set and carry with
the disk, and only flush_disk_writeback takes it. A C64 power cycle carries
the report through the session's media registry, and the lazy write no longer
disarms while the disk sits in that registry.

vic/inspect/origin searched drive 8's disk.bytes without a flush and missed
the latest writes; it now searches disk_as_written().

events.title: Stop reading past the end of a filename
events.message:
Stop reading past the end of a filename

put_name filled all 16 bytes of the directory's name field from the string it
was given, substituting the pad byte wherever it read a zero. For any name
shorter than the field that walks off the end of the literal and copies
whatever the linker put next, so every entry carried a few bytes of the
following name, or of the disk title.

It hid well. The byte the terminator becomes still ends the name, so anything
reading the disk gets the right one back and all ten files verified; only a
drive listing the directory shows the rest. And it read as deterministic on
this machine, because the two compilers here happened to lay the literals out
the same way. The release build did not: the .d64 it wrote differed from the
local one in 87 bytes, all of them in the directory.

The expected checksum moves with it, since the old one was taken from an image
with the stray bytes in it. Windows and Linux now write the same disk.

events.title: Lay out the object record's head: size, weight, description and flags
events.message:
Lay out the object record's head: size, weight, description and flags

Byte 2 of an object's head is its size and byte 3 its weight; for a
character, byte 3 is the most it can carry. Three routines say so in their
own failure messages, printed through RUN_MESSAGE: the one at $8CF1
compares a thing's weight and load with the actor's byte 3 and says it is
too heavy to lift, the one at $93AB says you are carrying too much, and the
one at $A596 compares the actor's size with the room at the thing's byte 2
and says you are too big. Doors, walls and fixtures are $FF in both.

Bytes 14 and 15, where not zero, point at the object's own description:
the map's is the one about symbols you cannot read, the river's describes
a fast black river. Both land on message starts.

Four flag bits are now described from the data and the code together: bit
7 there to be seen and reached, clear only on the secret side door and the
butler; bit 6 a character, set on all twelve and nothing else; bit 5 can be
seen into; bit 1 a liquid. Bytes 4-6 and flag bit 0 are left open.

events.title: Find what an object is held by, and what the player can reach
events.message:
Find what an object is held by, and what the player can reach

Byte 1 of an object's record is what holds it or has it inside, $FF for
nothing. The map's is $3E, Gandalf, on the tape and 0, the player, at the
first prompt -- the opening turn is the one where the game says Gandalf
gives you the map -- and the large key's is $47, the hideous troll, as the
trolls' clearing says. Every object's block now says what holds it when
the game starts.

IN_REACH ($9E34), which the matcher and the darkness test both use, is
built on it. Nothing is within reach whose flags have bit 7 clear.
Otherwise an object is within reach of a character inside it, or shut in
the same container, or -- when neither is shut in anything -- in the
character's location, checking every location the object is in, which is
how a door is reachable from either side. SHUT_IN ($9E7A) follows byte 1
upward through holders that can be seen into and stops at the first that
cannot; the player can be seen into, so carrying a thing does not shut it
away.

Called directly from Bag End with the player as actor, IN_REACH says yes
to the chest, the map in the player's hands, Gandalf, Thorin and the round
green door, and no to the troll's key, the heavy rock door and the short
strong sword -- which is lying in the trolls' cave, where Bilbo finds
Sting.

events.title: Find how the parser decides which object the player means
events.message:
Find how the parser decides which object the player means

A read watchpoint on the command frame's first noun stopped in
COPY_PHRASE ($7C91), which copies a noun and its two adjectives out of
the frame into one of two slots: TARGET_NAME ($7942) or INSTRUMENT_NAME
($7948). The code before it decides which phrase is which by whether the
second phrase's prepositions are the ones the command expects, so in
ATTACK THE TROLL WITH THE SWORD the troll is the target and the sword the
instrument. Those slots and their flags sit in 35 bytes the generated
listing called unused, because they are zeros on the tape; they are the
parser's working space, now described, with the parts still unexplained
said to be.

TRY_TARGETS ($7CFC) then asks FIND_NAMED_OBJECT ($9DD9) for the next
object fitting the target's name, makes it the target, tries the
command, and goes round again if that did not take. FIND_NAMED_OBJECT
walks the object index with the exits' iterator and passes over anything
whose name does not match, anything excluded by a mode on its flag byte,
and anything out of the actor's reach.

What counts as a match was settled by calling NAME_MATCHES ($71F3)
directly on the small curious key. The noun must match; the adjectives
may be left out and are accepted in either order; one that does not
belong rules the object out. So KEY, CURIOUS KEY and CURIOUS SMALL KEY
all match, and LARGE KEY and SMALL LARGE KEY do not. WORD_MATCHES
($722E) is why: an untyped word fits anything, and only the twelve-bit
offset is compared, never the flag nibble.

Also: check_annotations' preliminary pass now keeps sub-block directives
as well as block ones. Without them a data block's comments were checked
against the default eight-byte lines and all reported as misaligned,
though the build itself was right.

events.title: build: the second zx02 bug - v2 can emit a stream that is not the data
events.message:
build: the second zx02 bug - v2 can emit a stream that is not the data

No, we were not on the latest zx02: tools/zx02src/ is tag v2 of 2022-07-22
and main is 26 commits ahead. The output_size patch fixed one of v2's two
known compressor bugs. This is the other.

optimize.c uses `return 1024` as the bit cost of an invalid Elias code -
the optimiser's way of saying "never pick this". On a long enough input
1024 bits stops being prohibitive, the parse picks one anyway, and the
compressor emits a stream that is not the input. Measured: 19,200 bytes of
a repeated 2,560-byte pattern compressed to 99 bytes, and those 99 bytes
decode WITHOUT ERROR to 4,096 wrong bytes. A port could ship that and find
out on hardware.

That is upstream dmsc/zx02#8 (someone else, 2025), fixed on main in
5d2f2e3 by raising the sentinel to 1<<20. Cherry-picked here, two lines.
It is a COST-FUNCTION change, not a format change, so it cannot move a
stream that was already valid - verified over the same 31-file corpus, all
31 byte-identical. With it, that input gives 310 bytes which round-trip,
and which equal tools/zx02.py's own output exactly. The Python port agrees
with a fixed C compressor for the second time today.

I had this backwards twice and should say so plainly: I first called it a
decoder edge case, then corrected that to "v2's own decoders refuse the
stream". Neither. The stream is accepted and decodes to the wrong bytes,
which is the worse failure.

Not taking main wholesale: the rest is 6502 decoder work (the kit uses its
own transcription), tests and docs, and f4427e7 also changes the bit-size
ESTIMATE, which can move streams and so the disc. Two targeted patches keep
tools/zx02src/ diffable against v2 while fixing both known bugs. Take the
next tag whole when there is one - dmsc/zx02#11 asks for it.

game.ssd is sha256 adb8baba... at a pinned SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, unchanged;
78 python tests pass.

events.title: Carry the C64 zero-page move as a rule, not as bytes
events.message:
Carry the C64 zero-page move as a rule, not as bytes

The three images the C64 build changes turned out to differ by one mechanical
rewrite and nothing else: zero page $00/$01 becomes $28/$29, at 311 sites and
with no other kind of change anywhere. So the value tables held 311 bytes
between them to say "$28" and "$29", and those bytes came out of a game image,
which is the one thing the header is supposed never to carry.

They are offsets now, with the rule applied at build time and checked at every
site: a byte that is not $00 or $01 fails the build instead of producing a disk
nobody can account for. The generator asserts the same thing before it writes,
so the two cannot disagree.

Also report each image as a unit. The .dsk checksum was printing three images
late, under the .d64, and the ProDOS and C64 detail lines sat beneath the
previous image's "wrote" line as though they described it. And a failed write
of the .po or the .d64 left the exit status at zero, because the checksum is
taken from memory and still said the image was good.

events.title: Find the parser's dispatch and the command frame it fills
events.message:
Find the parser's dispatch and the command frame it fills

PARSE_COMMAND dispatches on each token's class: the class nibble shifted
right three places indexes PARSER_CLASSES ($75D2), thirteen handlers from
adverbs to the end of the line, reached through JP (HL). That is why the
table showed as anonymous data -- nothing branches to its entries -- so the
handlers are now named, one per class, and seeded into the code map;
twelve were reached in play, and the thirteenth, IN or INTO, is new. There
is no entry for an unknown word, which never gets this far.

What the parser builds is COMMAND_FRAME ($B9C8), 24 bytes just below the
room pointers, with further commands in a line built in the frames below
it. The v1.0 disassembly credited in the docstring gave the layout; v1.2's
was then confirmed by stopping at OBEY after real sentences. The verb is
at offset 0, with bit 7 of its second byte set by TAKE ALL; an adverb or
direction at 2; and two noun phrases at 4 and 14, each two prepositions, a
noun and two adjectives. Articles are dropped.

The words are stored little-endian, which is what made the first capture
look like nonsense when read as tokens -- and what makes the best finding
here. PUT THE SMALL CURIOUS KEY IN THE WOODEN CHEST leaves A5 03 E1 05 63
01 as its first noun phrase, which is byte for byte the name in the key's
own object record. A noun phrase is written in the same form objects are
named in, so finding what the player means is a straight comparison.

The corrected word classes also widened the verb drill to 59 verbs, so the
playthrough now types 126 commands.

events.title: Watch the tokeniser, and correct what the dictionary's class bits mean
events.message:
Watch the tokeniser, and correct what the dictionary's class bits mean

A word's class is four bits: bits 5-6 of its first dictionary byte and
bits 5-6 of its second, read together. That is what TOKENISE ($6E97) puts
in the top nibble of each two-byte token, and all eighteen tokens captured
from real sentences carry exactly the class this predicts. Bit 7 of the
second byte is not part of it -- it marks the 58 words PRINT_WORD may give
an -s, 53 of them verbs -- and folding it in, as the dictionary blocks did
until now, is what made the verbs look like a class of their own number.
The labels are corrected: twelve classes, from adverbs and directions
through verbs, nouns and adjectives to AND and THEN, with the game
commands SAVE, LOAD, SCORE and QUIT sitting among the quantifiers.

The captures also show the tokeniser at work: synonyms are resolved before
anything else sees them, so GET SWORD arrives as TAKE SWORD; and a closing
quote has a full stop token put in front of it, so what is said to a
character is a complete sentence. An unknown word never reaches the parser
at all.

GET_KEY ($7249) turns out to be where "time passes" comes from. It counts
down while it waits, and when the count runs out it types WAIT into the
line itself -- four letters from $7291 -- and returns ENTER. Which exposed
two bugs in hobbit_drive.py. ready() ran on when the game was already
waiting, so every command it sent was preceded by a WAIT nobody asked for
and the other characters had an extra turn each time; and because the key
scan reports only changes, stopping with ENTER held left the next ENTER
unheard. Both are fixed, and GET_KEY's annotation says why.

that print a pushed object or word, the actor's or target's name, HIS or

endings, a jump and a sub-message. Four codes share the do-nothing handler
at $738B, which is the XOR A; RET ending code $02's own.

Codes $02 and $0B take a byte after them -- a signed distance, for the jump
and for the sub-message -- and the decoder had been reading that byte as an
element in its own right. The pointer checks still passed, but one operand
had been taken for a terminator and split a message in two: there are 177,
not 178. It walks them correctly now.

Where the codes' meanings came from the v1.0 disassembly credited in the
docstring, four were then confirmed by running real messages through
RUN_MESSAGE and capturing every character at PRINT_CHAR ($858B).
Location 66's description prints the west bank of the black river and
skips the east, so $02 is the jump and the two banks are one message. And
one message's bytes print YOU ARE NOT CARRYING IT with the player as actor,
GANDALF IS and THORIN IS with them, which is $10; $0C gives YOUR or HIS,
with the verb taking its -s for a character; $06 gives the name.

That capture is now Hobbit.message() in hobbit_drive.py -- the game's own
rendering of any message, for any actor, rather than a decoder's guess.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's messages, and every way into them
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's messages, and every way into them

Nearly everything the game says is a message in a compact bytecode, run
by RUN_MESSAGE ($72D3): a byte with bit 7 set starts a two-byte word
reference whose flag nibble can end the message; $60-$7F is one of 32
common words from COMMON_WORDS ($AD3D); $20-$5F a literal character; and
below $20 a control code, dispatched through CONTROL_CODES ($7295) --
below $14 as a subroutine, from $14 up as the end.

It was checked against the screen rather than only read. Location 4's
description pointer decodes to exactly the words the game printed on
arriving there, and so does Bag End's. The v1.0 disassembly credited in
the docstring describes the same bytecode, and is what said where to look.

The messages are stored end to end from $AD7D, straight after the common
words, up to the last room description; zeros and then the variables
follow. 178 of them, walked one after another, and every one of the 92
pointers to messages -- room descriptions, and LD HL,msg before a call
into RUN_MESSAGE, found by decoding the code map's own instructions --
lands on a start or on a known way in. The build stops if one does not.

There are five known ways in. Four enter another message at an element
boundary and share its tail; the last of those is the black river, whose
two banks are one description entered at two places. The fifth begins on
the second byte of the word that ends the message before it and reads that
byte as a control code -- one byte doing two jobs, as the code does at
$8113.

The 23 control-code handlers are code seeds, since a dispatch is what
following branches cannot see through; fifteen were reached in play.

The local disassembly now shows each message's text beside its bytes.
That is gitignored with the rest of the build output, and the docstring
now says so rather than promising the prose never leaves the bytes.

events.title: Βήμα 20: ήχος — και ένας εξομοιωτής που μπορεί πια να τον ακούσει
events.message:
Βήμα 20: ήχος — και ένας εξομοιωτής που μπορεί πια να τον ακούσει

Οκτώ εφέ στον AY-3-8912: κέρσορας, κατάλογος, άρνηση, χτίσιμο, «τελείωσε»,
πλοίο, συναγερμός, θάνατος. Τρία κανάλια, ένα εφέ στο καθένα, και η
προτεραιότητα κρίνει ποιος μπαίνει — αλλιώς ο κέρσορας, δεκαπέντε φορές το
δευτερόλεπτο, θα έκοβε τον συναγερμό σε κομμάτια.

Ο AY δεν έχει δικές του θύρες: κρέμεται από τη θύρα Α του PPI, και το
ΠΛΗΚΤΡΟΛΟΓΙΟ κρέμεται από τη θύρα Α του ΙΔΙΟΥ AY. Μία εγγραφή καταχωρητή είναι
πέντε εγγραφές θύρας και, αν λείψει μία, δεν φτάνει τίποτα — αθόρυβα. Το bit 6
του R7 μένει για πάντα μηδέν: είναι η κατεύθυνση της θύρας Α, και αναμμένο κάνει
κάθε γραμμή πλήκτρων να διαβάζεται #FF, δηλαδή «όλα πατημένα».

Κόστος 100 us ανά frame στη σιωπή, 195 όσο παίζει κάτι — μισό τοις εκατό του
frame. Οι καταχωρητές γράφονται μόνο όταν αλλάζει ΒΗΜΑ, όχι κάθε frame.

ΟΙ ΔΟΚΙΜΕΣ ΔΙΑΒΑΖΟΥΝ ΤΟ ΤΣΙΠ. Ο headless εξομοιωτής δεν έδινε πρόσβαση στον
PSG (κι έτρεχε με volume 0), οπότε ο ήχος ήταν εξ ορισμού αόρατος σε κάθε
έλεγχο: προστέθηκαν cpcemu_psg_reg / cpcemu_psg_addr στο ~/cpcemu/cpcheadless.c
(προσθετικά, με το παλιό .so δίπλα). Τώρα το tests/test_sound.py:

- παίζει κάθε εφέ tick προς tick και συγκρίνει ΚΑΙ ΤΟΥΣ 14 καταχωρητές με
  αναφορά Python γραμμένη από την προδιαγραφή της μορφής,
- ελέγχει προτεραιότητα, σιωπή στο τέλος, και ελευθέρωση του καναλιού,
- σαρώνει πληκτρολόγιο ΚΑΙ ήχο εναλλάξ, επειδή μοιράζονται το PPI,
- και μέσα στο ΠΑΙΧΝΙΔΙ: πλήκτρο -> ήχος, άκυρη θέση -> άρνηση, και ο
  συναγερμός μόνο στην ακμή.

Τρεις αρνητικοί έλεγχοι πέφτουν όπως πρέπει: χωρίς το «γράψε» του PSG δεν
αλλάζει κανένας καταχωρητής· με βήμα ένα frame μακρύτερο η αναφορά αποκλίνει στο
tick 1· με το bit 6 αναμμένο το πληκτρολόγιο λέει ότι πατήθηκαν όλα.

Και επειδή ο ήχος δεν κοιτιέται, ΑΚΟΥΓΕΤΑΙ: το tools/ayrender.py φτιάχνει
build/sounds.wav από τους καταχωρητές που πήρε ο AY — τετραγωνικά κύματα, LFSR
17 bit, λογαριθμική ένταση. Εκεί φάνηκε και σφάλμα του ίδιου του renderer: ο
μετρητής τόνου τρέχει στο ρολόι/8, όχι /16, και όλα έβγαιναν μία οκτάβα χαμηλά.

Δύο ακόμη που βρέθηκαν στον δρόμο:
- Το tools/mkdsk.py έγραφε τη διεύθυνση φόρτωσης του GAME2.BIN με το χέρι
  (#B440) και το PAGE2_CODE είχε κουνηθεί στο βήμα 19. Τώρα βγαίνει από τον
  πίνακα συμβόλων, και υπάρχει έλεγχος ότι ο κώδικας της τράπεζας 2 δεν
  ξεπερνά το #C000 — έμειναν 69 bytes.
- Οι σταθερές του PPI ήταν δηλωμένες σε τέσσερα αρχεία. Μία φορά, στο const.asm.

events.title: Write the C64 + VERA .d64 as well
events.message:
Write the C64 + VERA .d64 as well

The port also runs on a C64 with a VERA card, and that disk had no build at
all: every copy of it so far was made by taking an existing image and running
c1541 to replace one file, so nothing regenerated the other nine.

It turns out to be the same game rather than a second one. The payload and the
APU divide LUT come out byte-identical to the Apple II ones, the VERA upload is
the same seven chunks written back to back instead of padded to sector
boundaries behind a header sector, and the game, resident and LC audio differ
by 311 bytes in total, so they are carried as deltas rather than as second
copies. Only the boot program and Krill's drive loader are genuinely C64.

This does not reproduce the shipped beta4 image byte for byte and does not try
to. That image's sectors record a dozen rounds of c1541 edits rather than any
layout rule, down to PAYLD starting at 10/19 and running backwards into track
9. The check that replaces it is the one a drive cares about: all ten files
read back off the generated image are byte-identical to the shipped disk's, and
the image boots to the title screen.

Krill's loader is BSD-3 and its notice is now in LICENSE.

events.title: fix: a checkpoint carries the disk as the drive has written it
events.message:
fix: a checkpoint carries the disk as the drive has written it

The medium a checkpoint embeds for each drive position is now the image a
persist would write at the capture: every written track folded in, the
pending dirty track included, in the mounted format. It is built on a copy by
the write-back's own encoder (Drive1541::disk_as_written ->
Rotation::writeback_image, sharing fold_dirty_track with
drive_gcr_data_writeback). Used for position B's driveB node, drive 8's ring
_ringDriveDiskBytes, the .c64re media payload (and its summary sha) and the
recorder's disk medium. Dumps no longer flush the live drive.

Before, the embed was DiskImage.bytes, which only a flush with a dirty track
pending brought up to date: a track written and then left by a head move sat
in the rotation's write-back image alone, and a restore mounted a disk without
it - lost from every later persist. flush_disk_writeback now also copies the
write-back image out when a head move has folded a track in since the last
copy (Rotation::writeback_gen).

drive_disk_checkpoint_gate: D64/G64 x position A/B(unit 9), SAVE mid-way,
capture, restore - red on all four before; plus the stale-flush case.

events.title: build: zx02 wrote uninitialised memory into the disc - found, fixed, guarded
events.message:
build: zx02 wrote uninitialised memory into the disc - found, fixed, guarded

puzzle-beeble's note (its BUGS.md #2, in docs/build-portability.md) said the
released zx02.exe's LAST TWO BYTES follow the environment. Chased it to the
line, and it is worse than the tail.

compress.c sets *output_size from optimal->bits - an ESTIMATE, so an
allocation BOUND - and zx02.c then writes exactly *output_size bytes to the
file, while the writer only filled output_index of them. The slack is
uninitialised malloc memory and it goes straight into the .zx02. On Windows
that is commonly the process environment block: instrumenting the two
counters, a 19,200-byte input predicted 224 bytes and emitted 99, so 125
bytes - more than half the file - were heap, and the tails read as ASCII
("ocal", "Modu"). One short extra environment variable is enough to move it.

Not rare: over 31 real data files from this kit and edge-beeb, 9 carried
surplus bytes, 1 to 8 each. A published image could carry fragments of
whoever's environment built it.

AND IT SETTLES AN OLD QUESTION THE OTHER WAY. VENDORED.md said zx02.py
"ended one byte shorter" than the reference on Edge's tiles.chr.bin, and
dfs.py called it a trailing pad. Neither: the exe was writing one byte of
uninitialised memory - 0x65 in one run, 0x3D in the next. With the fix the
exe and zx02.py agree on that file BYTE FOR BYTE. The Python port was right
all along, and the kit had been recording the bug as a property of its own
correct implementation.

Fixed three ways:

  - tools/zx02src/src/compress.c: one line, *output_size = output_index,
    recorded in VENDORED.md, which no longer claims "unmodified". Upstream
    main fixes it identically but there is no tag after v2, and main also
    changes the size ESTIMATE, which would move streams and so the disc.
    This patch moves NO emitted stream byte: verified over the same 31
    files, the 22 with no slack byte-identical, the 9 with slack the same
    bytes minus the surplus.
  - make_disc.py refuses any stream with bytes after its END marker,
    whatever compressor made it. NOTE: the obvious check - re-run the
    compressor under a changed environment and compare - DOES NOT WORK. I
    built it first and it passed a compressor I knew to be broken, because
    the leaked bytes often repeat. Testing the stream is deterministic:
    zx02.py stops at the END marker, so the shortest prefix that still
    decodes is the real length.
  - py/tests/test_zx02.py compares the STREAM, not the file, so its old
    `mine + b"\x00"` tolerance can no longer hide an uninitialised byte that
    happened to be zero.

local.ps1 (gitignored) pointed ZX02 at ..\..\Bin\zx02.exe calling it "the
same bytes as tools\zx02src". It was not. Now the project's own build.

Why the kit never saw this: the template's only compressed file is PANEL,
whose slack is 0. game.ssd is sha256 adb8baba... at a pinned
SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, unchanged by any of this, and 78 python tests pass.

events.title: Name every room and object from its own words, and find the only lamp
events.message:
Name every room and object from its own words, and find the only lamp

Rooms and objects are named the same way: three 12-bit word references,
the noun first and then up to two adjectives, which PRINT_WORD expands --
bytes 2-7 of a room's head and 8-13 of an object's. So every room and
object block is now titled from the game's own data: location 5 the
trolls clearing, object 5 the round green door, object $0E the short
strong sword, and all twelve characters from Gandalf to the six goblins.
The order they print in is the stored order of the adjectives followed by
the noun, checked against what the game says on screen.

That named object $0E, which is what made the rest make sense. Bit 7 of a
room's first byte is whether it is lit, and TOO_DARK ($95ED) is where it
is read: characters never need light, the player can see in a lit room or
from inside something, and otherwise only if the sword is with him and
its flag byte has bit 2 set, bit 3 clear and bit 4 set -- tested in one
go by XOR $F7, AND $1C. It starts as $94, so it glows from the first move:
the sword is the game's lamp, as Sting glows in the book. The 26 rooms
with bit 7 clear are exactly the places the story makes dark. In the dark
MOVE throws the direction away for a random one, and CLEAR_CANVAS blacks
the picture out.

The v1.0 disassembly credited in the docstring is what pointed at the
sword; the mechanism, the flag test and the starting value were then read
from v1.2's own code and data. A room's bytes 8-9 point at a longer
description where it has one, which the game prints in place of the name.
A room's byte 1 and most of an object's head are still open.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's rooms and every exit
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's rooms and every exit

Each location has a record, found by number through ROOM_POINTERS
($B9E0, two bytes per location, 0-79) by GET_ROOM ($9BB1). A record is a
10-byte head and then its exits, three bytes each -- direction, the object
the way goes through or zero, and the destination -- ending at $FF.

Found by asking the game rather than searching for it. A write watchpoint
on the player's location stopped in MOVE as EAST took Bag End to location
4; rewinding from there to where FIND_EXIT ($9F08) returned found IX on
$BAA1 and the record 03 05 04 -- east, through object 5, to 4 -- and one
step further back, the room lookup returning Bag End's record at $BA97.

The whole table then proves itself: 79 records end exactly where the next
begins, the last exactly where the object index starts, every exit's
direction is one of the ten, every destination a room, and every object an
exit goes through a real object. The build enforces all of that. Doors
agree from both sides: object 5 is listed in locations 1 and 4 and is the
way between them, object 1 in 7 and 6 and the way north from 6 to 7.

The direction codes are settled by what the game prints rather than by
pattern. Location 4's exits are 3, 1, 5 and it says "east north
northeast"; the trolls' clearing's are 8, 7, 1 and it says "southwest
southeast north". With 1-4, 9 and 10 already watched in MOVE, that leaves
6 as northwest -- which the map's round trips had suggested too, pairing
5 with 8 and 6 with 7. An attempt to read the codes by stopping in MOVE
mid-turn gave self-contradictory answers and was not used.

Location 0 is not a room: 13 bytes, an empty head and no real exits.
Three exits lead to location 0, which FIND_EXIT passes over -- ways that
exist but go nowhere until the game writes a destination in. Nothing
addresses those bytes directly, so what opens them is still to be found.

events.title: docs: 1942 is Master-only, so those rows are its target, not an excursion
events.message:
docs: 1942 is Master-only, so those rows are its target, not an excursion

Correcting the provenance I wrote in 2028b3d. I recorded the Master load
measurements as an aside - "nothing 1942 ships depends on them: its
stage-seam load rests on the masked row, which is the one the kit reached
independently on a B" - which reads as though a Master-only port's design
rested on a Model B measurement. It does not, and cannot.

1942-beeb is Master only (its decision 2, one disc). The masked row is a
MASTER measurement it made on its own target and relies on; the kit's B
run corroborates it rather than supplying it. The hangs are on the machine
1942 ships for, which makes them worth more, not less - what stands is
only that its stage seam rests on the masked row, not on any of them.

Two consequences now said out loud:

  - Which machine you ship for decides which rule you need. Master-only
    takes the Master rules; B-only has the looser result; a port targeting
    BOTH takes the Master's, being the stricter, and the B has never been
    shown to need the looser one for anything.
  - Re-running the hangs on B-DFS1.2 is THE KIT'S to do, not 1942's. A
    Master-only port has no reason to, and the kit is what tells a
    two-machine port which rule holds where.

Also lands the rule in target-portability.md, whose whole subject is which
machine you are building for - flagged as not a kit default, since it only
applies to a port that loads mid-game.

Docs only: game.ssd is sha256 adb8baba... at a pinned SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH,
unchanged.

events.title: Write the 800K ProDOS image as well as the .dsk
events.message:
Write the 800K ProDOS image as well as the .dsk

The port also runs from an 800K ProDOS-protocol disk, and until now the only
way to get one was the .po build in the a2vera tree, which needs an assembler
and a Python toolchain. Both images ship the same content, so the .po is laid
out from the 140K one rather than built a second time; building it separately
would only create a way for the two to drift, and that shows up as a wrong
track on a real drive instead of as a failed build.

What genuinely differs is the boot block and a resident built on rwts_po,
since ProDOS reads 512-byte blocks, plus the rwts entry the payload calls by
address. That last one is four bytes, patched on the way in rather than
carried as a second copy of the payload.

events.title: docs: the retracted DFS claim, and what a Master does instead (1942-beeb)
events.message:
docs: the retracted DFS claim, and what a Master does instead (1942-beeb)

From 1942-beeb's docs/note-to-kit.md, both items outstanding until now.

1. lib/irq.6502 still carried the claim hardware-facts.md retracted on
   2026-09-09 - "the DFS needs the MOS's interrupt ... a load after
   install hangs". loader.6502 was corrected that day; the IRQ header was
   not, and every fork of it carries the header. It propagated into
   1942-beeb's main.6502 and CLAUDE.md and was load-bearing in a plan for
   mid-game loading before anyone noticed. The kit is upstream, so the fix
   belongs here. Replaced with the reasons that do hold: DFS pages its ROM
   over &8000, its workspace is live until the last call returns, and a
   load costs whole frames.

2. The retraction was a Model B with an 8271. On a Master 128 / MOS 3.20 /
   1770 DFS the same shape does NOT survive, and the kit was recommending
   the thing that broke:

     SEI ... CLI around the call            byte-identical
     IRQ1V on a null handler                HUNG, MOS spinning at $EE72
     IRQ1V chaining, JMP (old vector)       byte-identical
       + System VIA T1's latch changed      HUNG
       + T1's interrupt disabled            HUNG, in the DFS ROM at $8673

   So the rule is narrower than "interrupts are not needed": EITHER MASK,
   OR CHAIN AND CHANGE NOTHING. A rupture's own T1 cadence therefore
   cannot run across a filing-system call, and a chaining handler hands
   back the tick that writes &0800-&08FF. Chunking is no escape - a call
   costs ~15 centiseconds plus ~4 a sector, so even a one-sector load
   blocks for nine fields.

Recorded in hardware-facts.md with 1942's provenance and its caveat: the
three hangs are jsbeeb, not hardware, and want a b2 or real-Master run
before anything is designed against them. Nothing 1942 ships rests on
them - its stage seam rests on the masked row, which the kit reached
independently on a B. NOT re-measured here.

Also in PORTING.md 5.3, which stated the B result without the caveat, and
in lib/README.md's one-line summary of the irq.6502 header.

Comments only: game.ssd is sha256 adb8baba... at a pinned
SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, byte-identical to the build before these edits, and
both trees assemble clean at --warn 2.

fix: a restored drive runs on cycle for cycle with the one captured

Measured first divergence, not the assumed one. The DRIVECPU module now
carries VICE's interrupt status (DRIVECPU 1.4, appended at the end so older
readers skip it; the reader checks the version and refuses an unknown
major by name; 1.3 restores with the status reset). But no capture instant
tried needs that block; what parted the machines was:

- restore_int was a no-op: the VIAs' IRQ levels never reached the drive's
  interrupt status on restore (VICE interrupt_restore_irq). Ported.
- the head was placed after the VIA2 undump, throwing away the rotation
  that undump does while keeping its clock. Placed before, as VICE reads it.
- GCRIMAGE restore forced the GCR circuit engine on (VICE: "TODO verify"),
  so a D64 drive that never wrote switched engines. GCRIMAGE 3.2 carries
  complicated_image_loaded at the end; 3.1 keeps VICE's 1.
- the lazy rotation lag was rotated at undump in the restoring machine's
  read/write mode. The capture now catches the rotation up first (on B's
  copy, and B's overlay is taken from that copy).

events.title: feat(64-05): two reap passes in broker-kill.mts, opposite lifetime rules (XFER-07, D-07/D-08)
events.message:
feat(64-05): two reap passes in broker-kill.mts, opposite lifetime rules (XFER-07, D-07/D-08)

Task 2: reapOrphanedConfigScratch() and sweepOrphanedStaging(), a second
and third pass in the module that already owns identity-verified,
only-when-actually-gone cleanup -- not a new seam.

reapOrphanedConfigScratch() is the LIVE-PID-GUARDED pass: a config-scratch
directory whose recorded pid is alive and whose recorded binary identity
matches is left completely untouched; alive-but-mismatched (a reused pid)
is treated as stale and removed; no readable record is logged by name and
left alone -- removing on a guess is the exact failure D-08 forbids. It
reuses this module's own defaultIsAlive/defaultReadProcessArgs rather than
writing a second liveness check.

sweepOrphanedStaging() is the pass with NO pid check, deliberately: a
staging directory is not itself a process, and its real teardown trigger
is its own session's connection closing (already wired, SESS-03/SESS-04).
Every session directory still present at broker STARTUP is by definition
residue a crashed broker left, and is removed unconditionally.

Both pass their result-shaped {found, removed} summary through a single
log line including the zero case, and neither throws past a single
directory's own failure. Every enumeration/read/liveness/removal seam is
injectable; no test signals a real process.

events.title: Find where objects are, and drive the game by handing it whole commands
events.message:
Find where objects are, and drive the game by handing it whole commands

The list after an object record's 16-byte head is where the object is, and
byte 0 of the head says how many places. Watched rather than inferred: over
several turns the one byte that changes in any character's record is the
first of its locations, as it wanders; and walking the player east out of
Bag End and back moved object 0's location 1, 4, 1, matching at every step
the location whose picture DRAW_LOCATION_PICTURE looked up. Object 0 is the
player, which fits $B6EA being zero for sentences about you. Things in
several places are fixtures: object 5 is in locations 1 and 4, exactly the
two rooms that walk went between, so it is the round green door. Its record
does not change when it is opened and closed, so that state is kept
somewhere else -- most likely on the room's exit -- and is left open.

The walk was worth more than its result, because it kept failing. Typed
commands arrived mangled -- OPEN THE DOOR as R -- and the fixed waits that
were supposed to prevent it were guesses. hobbit_drive.py does what the
game does for its own opening LOOK: it puts the command in INPUT_LINE
($6FF9). READ_LINE keeps its cursor only in HL and B, so the driver stops
at $6DF3 just after they are set, writes the text, moves them past it and
presses ENTER; readiness is a breakpoint, not a sleep.

That also corrects an earlier explanation. The first command after the
opening picture was not lost because the drawing ignores the keyboard, or
not only: the game then waits in WAIT_FOR_ANY_KEY, and the first key is
taken as carry-on rather than as a letter. The settle comment says so now.

events.title: Decode The Hobbit's object records, each with its own action handlers
events.message:
Decode The Hobbit's object records, each with its own action handlers

An object record is a 16-byte head, a list whose length is byte 0 of the
head, and then a FIND_RECORD table of [action, handler] triples ending at
$FF -- the object's own handlers for particular actions. The game states
the grammar itself: FIND_OBJECT_HANDLER ($9B81) adds byte 0 and 16 to IX
and calls FIND_RECORD, and it is what runs straight after the action
dispatch, asking whether this object handles this action itself before the
ordinary handler gets it.

The proof is in the fit rather than in any one record. Parsed this way,
all 61 records end exactly where the next begins, the first starts exactly
where OBJECT_INDEX ends, and the last ends exactly where ACTION_TABLE
starts. The build now enforces that and stops if it ever fails.

The handlers are code on the same argument as the dispatch table's: the
same format, reached through a lookup rather than a branch, and 78 of the
143 reached by the playthrough. The other 33 distinct addresses are now
seeds, and they passed the check that no executed address lands inside a
decoded instruction -- which is the evidence that they begin real
instructions rather than just sitting near them. The code map goes from
5832 to 6263 instruction starts. One handler value is $0000, which is not
an address in the game: it is left out as a seed and described as the
object doing nothing special for that action.

The 16-byte head and the list are described by extent only. What their
bytes mean has not been worked out and is not asserted.

events.title: Identify the object index, and credit a third reference
events.message:
Identify the object index, and credit a third reference

$C063 is a FIND_RECORD table of 61 objects. Its keys come in two runs,
$00-$2B and then $3C-$4C, and the upper run is the characters: every one of
the nine seen wandering during a single turn has its number there, and
$B6EA, which says who a sentence is about, holds numbers from that same
run. A character is an object with a number in the upper block rather than
a separate kind of thing, which also explains why the narration's subject
ids looked like object ids.

The records are variable length and what the code does with them is only
partly worked out, so that is where this stops. $95DF tests bit 6 and bit 3
of (IX+$07), consistent with a flags byte at offset 7 of a record from this
table, but the path from one to the other has not been traced and the
annotation says so.

A third reference is credited in the docstring: a complete annotated
SkoolKit disassembly of the v1.0 tape, author unnamed and with no licence
for its annotations. Same treatment as the other two and as the Knight Lore
map -- used to know what exists and where to look, never as text to copy.
It documents v1.0, 37,888 bytes against this one's 40,000, so its addresses
do not transfer and the two disagree about where almost everything lives;
it says the action table is an 8-byte indexed array, where v1.2's dispatch
at $C730 is a keyed table, so they are not even the same structure. The
object index above was settled from the character ids already observed
moving, not from its say-so.

X is what 3.4.0 reported on 2026-09-07, so ONLY THE NAMES MOVED - every
internal and INKEY number in section 7 stands, and so does everything
measured through them.

What a caller has to change: digits are K0-K9, CAPS_LOCK is CAPSLOCK, and
BACKSPACE, QUOTE and EQUALS are gone. Everything the kit's own skills press
- Z, X, R, CTRL, SHIFT, ESCAPE, the cursor keys, F0-F9 - is unaffected.

read the table, so do not guess one.

0.3.0 era could not do. The shared ..\..\Bin\ copy stays on 0.3.0.

Nothing moved. Both template images, both raw images, the symbol dump and
the listing are byte-identical across the two binaries; test_lib comes out
identical at RELEASE=0 and =1; vscroll likewise; make still matches
build.ps1 (sha256 adb8baba..., SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH pinned), and game.ssd
boots in jsbeeb to the panel and the scrolling strip.

Two of the kit's issues closed:

  #2  a store aiming a literal address into the ZA_POOL went unwarned -
      the one failure the allocator exists to prevent. Answered twice
      over, by the --warn 2 audit that was asked for and by ZA_WIPE for
      the deliberate boot-time sweep. The builds now pass --warn 2, and
      the template is silent at that level.
  #7  a string carrying a NUL byte cut the -v listing short, which this
      kit reads mechanically.

#3 stays open, but the finding on it is worth having: the -D quoting
defect is PowerShell 5.1's, fixed in 7.3+ (re-measured on 7.6.6). The
generated build_time.6502 stays regardless - it is what makes a rebuild
byte-identical, and it is the same path under make.

What a port needs to know, both in docs/toolchain-baron.md: the
unchecked-indexed-access warning is on by DEFAULT now, answered with
ZA_INDEXEDBY placed AFTER the access; and a ZA_AUTO read only through
var,Y used to be invisible to the allocator and could be reused while
live - a silent wrong answer, fixed here.

--warn is a hard floor: 0.3.0 and 7213c8b both exit 1 on it rather than
ignoring it, so the build scripts say 0.4.0 or newer.

events.title: video: setting the resolution did nothing at all
events.message:
video: setting the resolution did nothing at all

Setscreen read its rez argument off the stack, printed it in the trace and
threw it away, and a program writing the mode register itself got a value
that read back and changed nothing. Getrez went on answering for the screen
the machine was built with either way, so a program that switched to low
resolution and drew carried on painting four planes into whatever shape the
machine really had.

The register was half wired up already: video.c read it to decide the shape
of the picture, but only once the video base had been pointed away from the
screen the machine came with. That covered a debugger showing a screen of
its own and missed the ordinary case, because a program that means to draw
on the screen TOS handed it, in a resolution of its own choosing, never
moves the base anywhere - and with the base at home it was indistinguishable
from a program that had done nothing.

Nobody had noticed because the two populations barely meet. GEM applications
never touch the mode, and the programs that do have taken the machine over
and are not asking the AES anything; the tests covered the base moving,
which is the route a debugger takes, and nothing asked what the rez argument
was for.

So Setscreen writes the mode now, and taking the video hardware over means
the base having moved or the mode having been set - one question, in
hardware_taken_over, because the shape of the picture, whether there is a
picture and whether the screen counts as handed back all turn on it.

Which splits the two screens apart, and that is the point rather than a
side effect. The video hardware's screen is emulated memory read at the
shape the register says. GEM's screen is a surface of the host's, made once
when GEM starts and never reshaped. A resolution moves the first and leaves
the second where it was, so Getrez still answers for GEM's screen however
the mode is set - an application told it had shrunk to 320x200 would lay
its dialogs out for a screen it is not drawing on, and be centred off the
edge with nothing to say why. On a real ST Getrez is a read of that
register, so this is a departure on purpose; the note at the top of
xbiosscreen.c and the new section in docs/DETAILS.md say so plainly.

Two things fall out and are written down where they will be found. Setting
the mode cannot be given back the way moving the base can - on a TT screen
the register already says 2, so a program asking for ST high could not be
told from one undoing itself - so a program that has set it keeps the
picture for the rest of the run. And every ST mode reads 32000 bytes, which
is more than a single-plane screen the size of a modern display has, so
that combination now says which mode wanted how much rather than leaving a
picture that silently stopped changing.

tests/c-rez.c checks it on each of the ST's three screens: that the picture
follows through both routes, and that Getrez, the AES desktop and a VDI
workstation do not.

events.title: Print the messages the flight loop prints
events.message:
Print the messages the flight loop prints

Four of the original's in-flight messages were missing, and two of them were
values the simulation computes and nothing reads.

A ship firing a missile at us prints "INCOMING MISSILE" - recursive token 120 -
and makes the launch sound, which is the same table entry as our own missile.
MissileFiredAtUsThisFrame has been set for months with no consumer, so missiles
arrived in silence. Scooping prints the item's name, "token 48 + Y ... in the
range 48 (FOOD) to 64 (ALIEN ITEMS)", and ScoopedThisFrame was unread too. A
kill that pays prints the cash - control code 0, right-aligned then " CR" - and
a ship with no bounty prints nothing, because the original skips the block when
the blueprint's bounty is zero. And every 256th kill earns "RIGHT ON
COMMANDER!", which is EXNO2 incrementing the tally's high byte: laser kills
count there too, because part 11 calls EXNO2 when a shot kills the ship in the
crosshairs.

A missile destroyed beside us does 80 damage, and the test for "beside us" is
TA35's own: the OR of the three low bytes of its position must be zero. A
missile therefore has to sit exactly on a 256-unit lattice point for the damage
to land - one position in sixteen million - which is a faithful quirk recorded
in DIVERGENCES.md with a test that pins it.

Ship.Create now sets a ship's energy and maximum energy from its blueprint as
well as its speed. A Core-only simulation had a maximum of zero and the missile
rule asks whether a ship is down to half its energy, so no ship in it ever
fired a missile.

401 tests pass.

events.message:
feat(871): drive position B — a second 1541 on the one IEC bus

Machine gains drive_b beside drive8 (position A; the name stays). B is
built off with its jumpers at 9, so a one-drive machine is the machine it
was: not clocked, not folded, no driveB checkpoint node.

- IecCore carries a slot per position; the device map is what
  iecbus_status_set builds for the true drives present (Conf3 for two).
- At every sync point both drives are fed the bus as it stands, both are
  caught up, then both are written back — the advance order cannot change
  what the bus reads. Each drive's v_iecbus now carries the other devices'
  pulls, as VICE's one global iecbus does.
- ATN edges go to the drive at each unit; the C64's RESET reaches both.
- set_drive_power / set_drive_unit refuse two powered drives at one unit,
  naming the other position. drive()/drive_mut()/position_at_unit()/
  position_for_media().
- Checkpoints carry B (part, core blob, its disk, GCR overlay) as driveB;
  a checkpoint without it restores B off.
- A drive restored from a checkpoint no longer has a pending hardware
  reset: a never-run drive (B while off, or any drive in a freshly booted
  machine) ran its reset sequence over the restored CPU on the first
  catch-up.

events.title: Take the wrecks away, and let the bomb leave clouds
events.message:
Take the wrecks away, and let the bomb leave clouds

A destroyed ship stayed in the sky for ever: the exploding flag was set
and the cloud counter in byte #34 - which the port had a constant for and
nothing else - was never started, so a wreck sat motionless, because MVEIT
skips an exploding ship, and permanently on fire until it happened to drift
out of range.

The original runs the cloud through its drawing code. LL9 part 1 sees a ship
that is killed but not yet exploding and starts it: bit 5 on, the acceleration
and pitch counter zeroed so it stops flying, and the cloud counter set to 18.
DOEXP adds 4 to that counter every time it draws the cloud, and when the
addition overflows it sets the exploding and killed bits together, which is
what pays the bounty and removes the ship. So a wreck is a cloud for about
sixty iterations, and it grows as it ages, because the cloud's size is worked
out from the same counter.

The energy bomb's victims are part of the same rule: the bomb sets the killed
bit rather than removing anything, and "ships can't explode more than once" is
why it skips ships already exploding. Its victims used to vanish with no cloud
at all.

398 tests pass.
