events.title: Apply the throttle, and put the E.C.M. and the recharge back on their clocks
events.message:
Apply the throttle, and put the E.C.M. and the recharge back on their clocks

MVEIT part 4 was missing, so the acceleration byte that TACTICS sets was
written and never read: every ship in the sky flew at a constant speed.
A ship now accelerates at 3 when its nose dot product is 22 or more out of 36,
brakes at -1 when it has turning to do, and coasts between the two; missiles
brake at -2; a ship that has just hit us with its laser throttles back by one;
and the speed is held to byte #15 of the ship's blueprint, which is what
"LDA INWK+27 / CLC / ADC INWK+28" and the "CMP (XX0),Y" after it do. This is
the third value written and never read that this project has found, and the
most consequential: nothing ever closed on us and nothing ever braked.

Ship.Create now gives a ship its blueprint's speed and maximum. A Core-only
simulation had both at zero, so its ships could not move - and once the
acceleration was applied, could accelerate for ever with no maximum to be held
to. Three tests relied on that stillness and now hold their ships in place.

Two clocks were wrong as well. The energy banks and shields recharge every
eighth iteration, "LDA MCNT / AND #7", not every one: ours was eight times too
fast, which made the E.C.M.'s drain, the laser's energy cost and every hit we
took a seventh of what they should have been. And the E.C.M. runs for ECBLB2's
thirty-two iterations while draining a unit an iteration - "JSR DENGY" - and
switches itself off when the banks are empty, where ours charged a flat
invented eight and ran for sixty with no drain at all.

397 tests pass.

events.title: Βήμα 18: ταχύτητα παιχνιδιού — και το HUD που πάγωνε στο x2
events.message:
Βήμα 18: ταχύτητα παιχνιδιού — και το HUD που πάγωνε στο x2

Τα πλήκτρα 1-4 ήταν δεμένα από το βήμα 12 και κανείς δεν τα διάβαζε· ο
πίνακας του §9.1 τα περιέγραφε σαν υλοποιημένα. Τώρα ο βρόχος τρέχει 0, 1, 2
ή 4 θέσεις τροχού ανά frame, σε κάθε κατάσταση, και η σειρά 3 του HUD δείχνει
PAUSE / x1 / x2 / x4 στις πέντε τελευταίες στήλες.

Η παύση δεν παγώνει τον παίκτη: ο κέρσορας κινείται, το μενού ανοίγει, ο
θόλος μπαίνει σε ακίνητη αποικία. Αυτή είναι η χρήσιμη παύση.

ΤΟ ΣΦΑΛΜΑ ΠΟΥ ΒΓΗΚΕ ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΜΕΤΡΗΣΗ. Το x2 και το x4 έβγαζαν ΑΚΡΙΒΩΣ 2,00 και
4,00 ενώ το x1 έβγαζε 0,84 — αδύνατο, αφού περισσότερη δουλειά ανά frame δεν
γίνεται φθηνότερη. Η αιτία: το ml_hud είχε πύλη `wh_slot == 0`, και με βήμα 2
η θέση παίρνει μόνο ζυγές ή μόνο μονές τιμές. Αν η ταχύτητα άλλαζε σε μονή
θέση, το μηδέν δεν ξαναρχόταν ΠΟΤΕ: το HUD πάγωνε ενώ η αποικία έτρεχε, και
το «τέλειο» 2,00 ήταν ακριβώς το κόστος που δεν πληρωνόταν.

Το HUD έχει πια δικό του ρολόι πραγματικού χρόνου, κάθε 16 frames. Μετρημένα,
σε 400 frames το καθένα: x1 = 0,84 · x2 = 1,68 · x4 = 3,40 · παύση = 0.

ΚΑΙ ΤΟ 0,84 ΔΕΝ ΕΙΝΑΙ 1,00. Με `ret` πάνω από το ml_hud βγαίνει ακριβώς 1,00:
μία επανασχεδίαση HUD κοστίζει τρία frames και γίνεται κάθε δεκαέξι, άρα η
προσομοίωση παίρνει τα 16 από τα 19. Το §9.2 το καταγράφει και ονομάζει τη
φθηνότερη επόμενη βελτίωση: σαράντα κελιά ξαναγράφονται είτε άλλαξε ψηφίο
είτε όχι.

Δύο φορές έβαλα τη ρουτίνα μέσα σε διαδρομή ΠΤΩΣΗΣ (μετά τον διαλογέα
καταστάσεων, και μέσα στο uist_look). Και τις δύο η κατάσταση LOOK έπαψε να
απαντά και το ui_spd γέμισε σκουπίδια — 255 θέσεις τροχού ανά frame, μηχάνημα
που φαίνεται κολλημένο. Ο σχολιασμός της ρουτίνας το λέει τώρα.

events.title: Spawn the station when you reach the planet, not when you arrive
events.message:
Spawn the station when you reach the planet, not when you arrive

Arriving in a system put a station three thousand units ahead of us in
every system, for ever. The original has none: SOLAR sets up the planet and
the sun, and part 14 of the flight loop spawns the station every thirty-two
iterations at the point one planetary radius above the planet's surface along
the planet's own nose vector, once we are within 192 * 256 units of it on
every axis. Two details decide whether that ever happens, and both were wrong
here: the orbit turns with the planet, and the planet's nose points back at us
- ZINF's identity - so that the station is on the near side. A planet facing
away puts the orbit where the range check can never pass.

The sun goes with it, because NWSPS clears the FRIN table's second slot so the
station is created into it: the slot is "reserved for the sun (or space
station)". And nothing spawns while a station is about, which the mission-1
test had been passing on a race - it waited at a standstill for the station it
launched from to drift out of range, and it now flies clear first, as a
commander does.

Launching is a reset rather than a continuation. TT110 throws the flight
variables away and builds the sky it wants: the planet dead ahead at one step
of 65536, the station 256 units behind us so we come out of its slot, our
speed set to 12, and no sun. That needed a second fix: our docking checks ran
for a station within 256 units, which is exactly where the launch puts it, so
our own check that the station is in front of us read the launch as a crash
into the station we had just left and killed us at the first frame. The
original's gate is per axis and 128 units.

Also in this round: "P" cancels the docking computer and "C" only engages it,
which is the disc's pair of keys; the original's docked f1, f2 and f3 reach
our market and shop; and --fly-to-planet is a development autopilot that makes
the whole arrival-to-station run measurable, which is how the spawn was
verified: 40000 iterations takes Lave's planet from 321060 units to under a
thousand and brings the station up in orbit.

396 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: line-A: hiding the mouse pointer stopped the program
events.message:
line-A: hiding the mouse pointer stopped the program

A program that draws by any means other than the line-A still asks for the
pointer to be taken out of the way first, and $a00a was the cheaper way to
ask than v_hide_c. Every one of the sixteen line-A calls except $a000 was
refused here, and a refusal stops the emulator and names the call, so a
program that never draws a pixel through the line-A was ended by the one
instruction it used to get its own drawing started - between hiding the
pointer and drawing where it had been.

Nobody had noticed because the refusal was the right answer for the thirteen
that draw, and it was a great improvement on what came before it, which was
a jump to address nought. These two are not drawing calls, and the honest
answer for them is the one the VDI already gives: there is no pointer in the
screen memory to take out. EmuTOS draws one into the screen itself, since on
an ST there is nothing else to draw it, but here it belongs to the compositor
and was never in the planes - which is why vdi_v_show_c and vdi_v_hide_c in
emuvdi/hostvars.c are empty, and $a009 and $a00a now are too.

The check runs both opcodes and then both addresses out of the routine
table. What it is really asking is that anything at all is printed after
them and that the count line arrives, since a refusal would have ended the
run where the drawing check deliberately does.

events.title: Draw the launch and docking tunnels
events.message:
Draw the launch and docking tunnels

LAUN draws the rings as we leave the station and GOIN draws them as we
enter, and neither was in the remake. Both are HFS2: sets of rings from a
radius of 8 to 15, doubling until they reach 160, with the launch's step of 8
against hyperspace's rounder 4 - and the launch draws sixteen sets where the
flight bank draws eight, because the docked bank's HFS2 calls HFS1 and then
falls through into it again.

They are not part of the flight. The original draws them as the flight loop
ends, and letting the simulation run on through a docking tunnel flew the
autopilot into the station it had just been cleared to enter. The sim now
stands still while they are up, which also stops the docking check firing
again every frame and putting the rings back up for ever - that second fault
showed up as the docking computer no longer docking at all.

--launch takes the station's own route out, so the tunnel and the launch sound
(entry 48 of the table, the same one a missile uses) can be seen from the
command line. 392 tests pass.

events.title: video: a picture that is up always, for a program that never moves the base
events.message:
video: a picture that is up always, for a program that never moves the base

The picture the shifter shows started the first time a program pointed the
video base somewhere other than the screen the machine was built with, which
is how a debugger says it has taken the machine over. A program that draws on
the machine's own screen never says anything of the kind - it writes where
Physbase pointed, the way most software that is not a GEM program does - so
nothing was ever shown of it. TOSEMU_PICTURE gains a third value, always, and
with it the picture is up from the first frame whoever the screen belongs to.
It steps aside for nothing, the way keep does not.

Which means the shape of the picture can no longer be read off the mode
register alone. That register says one of the ST's three, and a machine built
with a TT screen or one the size of the display is described to a program by
its plane count - so on the machine's own screen the shape now comes from
screen_mode, which is the one place that decides it. The span read out of
memory rounds the width up to a whole word the way the surface does, for a
screen whose width is not a multiple of sixteen.

The console follows the picture: video_taken is true from the start under
always, so a program's output goes to a window beside its screen rather than
to the terminal it was started from, which is what it already did for a
program that had taken the hardware over.

test-c-video takes an always run. It writes a mark into Physbase before
touching the base at all and finds it in the screenshot, and then runs every
check the keep run runs, the two settings holding the picture up for the same
things once a program has moved the base.

events.title: Add the four space views, and make the other three mounts reachable
events.message:
Add the four space views, and make the other three mounts reachable

The remake could only look forward. The original's four views are PLUT's
axis flips - the rear negates x and z, the sides swap x and z and negate one
of them - applied to a ship's workspace and never stored, because only the
crosshair test and the drawing ever see the flipped data. That is how it is
here: one transform at the point of use, so the stored universe stays the
front view and firing, missile lock and the ship models all follow from it.
The laser mount is the view, as the original's LASER,X makes it, so looking out
of the back fires the rear laser at what is behind us.

The stardust streams the reverse of our velocity through the window, and LOOK1
reflects the whole field in the screen diagonal whenever the view changes - the
original's own trick for making the new view feel different without a new
field. Arriving in a system or launching resets us to the front view with a
fresh field, which is TT110 reaching LOOK1 with X = 0.

Two faults came out of following the thread to the other three mounts, both of
which had been modelled for months without being reachable:

"Extra Mining Lasers" fitted a pulse laser, and there was no mining laser at
all - the one laser whose purpose is breaking rocks into splinters could not be
bought. It is Mlas = 50, with fifty ticks between shots.

The four laser items chose the mount themselves; the original asks, with the
"View ?" menu of the four views, and refunds the laser it replaces at its own
price. That refund is the fixed version of the routine that let you buy the
same laser for infinite money in the first release of disc Elite. The status
screen now lists a laser per view, as the original's does.

Verified by looking out of the back window: the station dead centre at 4220
units behind us and the sun off to the left, which is the first time the sun
has been visible in this remake. 391 tests pass, 19 of them new, with
--view and --buy in the development CLI.

IKBD: no motion packets in absolute mode; Pexec mode-0 basepage fix

MMU.MoveMouse (REPL `mouse move`) and the live window's sendMousePacket
streamed relative $F8 dx dy packets even with the IKBD in absolute mode
($09). A real 6301 sends none there; Populous's handler ($20048) stored

scroll codes reaching the game). Now only the 6301's cursor moves.

The ATARI_TRACE_GEMDOS Pexec hook sampled act_pd right after a mode-0
trap, while it still held the caller's (valid) basepage, and reported
the parent: demo.god showed the loader's $a204. It now waits for act_pd
to move off the caller's basepage ($ac58 reported).

events.title: Βήμα 17: τέσσερις πλανήτες — και δύο σφάλματα που τους περίμεναν από το βήμα 1
events.message:
Βήμα 17: τέσσερις πλανήτες — και δύο σφάλματα που τους περίμεναν από το βήμα 1

Το §5.7 υπόσχεται τέσσερις πλανήτες για εξήντα bytes κατωφλίων και τα assets
τα παρέδωσαν από το ASSET-7. Ο κώδικας έγραφε πάντα μηδέν. Τώρα ο πλανήτης
είναι (seed_hi XOR seed_lo) AND 3 — δηλαδή τα δύο bytes του seed παραμένουν
ΟΛΟΣ ο κόσμος, πλανήτης μέσα — ταξιδεύει στα τέσσερα bytes worldinfo της
τράπεζας 6, μπαίνει στην κεφαλίδα του σωσίματος, και φτάνει στην οθόνη ως
τέσσερις εγγραφές pen. 63 bytes κώδικα.

Δύο πράγματα έσπασαν μόλις ο πλανήτης έπαψε να είναι μηδέν:

- Ο Z80 διάβαζε τα κατώφλια από το planet*4 ενώ ο σχολιασμός του έλεγε *6.
  Στον πλανήτη 0 τα δύο συμπίπτουν. Η σύγκριση με την αναφορά το έπιασε στο
  πρώτο τρέξιμο: 5.463 από 16.384 bytes διαφορετικά.
- Ο πίνακας fw_to_hw είχε ΤΡΕΙΣ λάθος εγγραφές, και οι δύο ήταν σε χρήση: το
  pen 6 (άποικοι) ζητά 24 bright yellow και ο gate array έπαιρνε #50, σκούρο
  μπλε πάνω σε σκούρο φόντο· το pen 5 ζητά 26 bright white και έπαιρνε γκρι.
  Δεκαεπτά βήματα αόρατο, επειδή ΚΑΘΕ άλλη δοκιμή συγκρίνει ΑΡΙΘΜΟΥΣ PEN: η
  αναφορά σε Python και ο blitter δουλεύουν σε pen, και τα golden PNG
  χρωματίζονται από τον πίνακα της Python που το υλικό δεν βλέπει ποτέ.

Το tests/test_palette.py κλείνει αυτό το κενό: γεμίζει την οθόνη με μοτίβο
όπου το pen n πιάνει n+1 bytes, διαβάζει το framebuffer, και ζυγίζει το
ΜΕΡΙΔΙΟ κάθε χρώματος απέναντι σε αυτό που ζητά η παλέτα — και στους τέσσερις
πλανήτες. Με τον παλιό πίνακα αποτυγχάνει ονομάζοντας και τα τρία χρώματα.

Το test_worldgen συγκρίνει πια και τους τέσσερις πλανήτες byte-προς-byte και
σαρώνει την παιξιμότητα καθενός (64 seeds, 64/64 παντού). Το test_save
συγκρίνει μετά το φόρτωμα και τα PIXEL, όχι μόνο τα bytes: αυτό είναι που
αποδεικνύει ότι η παλέτα του πλανήτη ταξιδεύει με το σωσμένο παιχνίδι.

Seed ACE1, στα 16.384 tiles: έρημος 4.070 νερό / 3.394 γόνιμο, πάγος 6.743 /
2.453, καταιγίδα 2.840 / 1.961, άγονη σελήνη 1.134 / ΜΗΔΕΝ γόνιμο.

events.title: Add the in-system jump, and the two flight keys that were missing
events.message:
Add the in-system jump, and the two flight keys that were missing

WARP, ABORT and ESCAPE were never wired: the disc's flight loop reads J for an
in-system jump, U to unarm the locked missile and ESCAPE to launch our own
escape pod, and the remake answered none of them. J now makes the jump WARP
makes — one step of 65536 for the planet and the sun, nothing else moved, the
main loop counter and the spawn counter reset, and a whole new stardust field,
which is what LOOK1's forced view reinitialisation gives the original. It is
refused, with the original's long low beep, when anything but junk is in the
bubble, in witchspace, or when we are facing a body already inside two steps of
the top byte. U releases the missile lock; ESCAPE spends the pod and ends at
the station, and since ESCAPE is now the pod's key, F10 is what leaves the game.

The junk check it turns on was wrong: the disc counts every type from the
escape pod to the transporter as junk, so a shuttle or a transporter used to
block a jump that the original allows.

Three things came out of the same round:

The planet and the sun are placed where SOLAR places them. The planet is 3 to 7
steps ahead and half that up and to the right — the port had it dead ahead with
a one-unit offset, from reading a sign byte as a small value rather than as the
top byte of a 24-bit coordinate. That matters for the jump, which measures how
close is too close in those same steps, and it puts the planet off the top of
the arrival view at Lave, where the original's vertical field of view is 21
degrees either way and the planet is 27 degrees up. The bit our legal status
loses when the arrival halves it is part of the planet's distance, as the
carry flag from SOLAR's own LSR is in the original.

The ship AI was rolling the wrong way. nroll takes the roll's direction from
the side dot product combined with the pitch counter it has just set, and the
port took it from the side dot product alone: measured on a ship 38 degrees off
its target, the original's rule closes to nothing and the port's sat at 33
degrees for ever with the error growing — the nose driven round the target
instead of onto it. The dot products are also the original's bytes, which run
to 36 and not 96, a new roll is only started once the last one has played out,
and steering to the planet drops RAT2 to zero when the target is behind us.

That was found by a test failing for the right reason: the station's shuttle
was circling us, because a shuttle rolls to turn pirate and the test had been
passing on the RNG. It now pins the role and asks for a fall of 5000 units.

372 tests pass, including twenty-one new ones for the jump, the keys, the junk
range and the steering law. Verified from the command line with
--in-system-jump: four jumps take Lave's planet from z = 262144 to z = 0.

events.title: Cutscenes copy only what changed, plus a double_buffer experiment
events.message:
Cutscenes copy only what changed, plus a double_buffer experiment

A scene's shapes are clipped to a 128-row window, yet every page
clear, page copy and screen push moved all 224 rows. Between
ST_pageBandStart and ST_pageBandEnd those work on a row band instead:
the scene starts on cleared pages, so rows outside the band match on
every page and on screen, and each primitive widens the band before it
draws outside it. A clear in a different colour widens it to the whole
page.

Within the band, the two pages that take turns on screen each carry a
box around where they differ from aux, the background every frame is
restored from, and so does the screen. A restore copies only what the
last frame on that page drew over, a new background only where it
moved, and a push only what changed since the last one. One box per
page rather than per-row or per-block masks: on a 68000 the marking
and the split copies cost more than the clean pixels a box takes
along. A temporary self-check compared every restore, copy and push
against a full copy over the intro, the level openings and the whole
credits, with no difference.

Hatari, work with every frame drawn, fit (budget in brackets):
  logo (15.5s)   ST 8.0 -> 2.2s   STE 6.8 -> 2.2s   Mega STE 4.7 -> 1.1s
  intro (27.2s)  ST 40.4 -> 33.2  STE 38.1 -> 32.8  Mega STE 24.6 -> 18.8
With frame skipping, the Mega STE intro drops 42 frames instead of
138. Its jungle stretch still needs about twice its budget: bus-bound
copies cost the same at 16MHz, and the fills and per-shape work there
are the rest.

The palette fade multiplies in 16 bits, not through __mulsi3 on every
palette write.

double_buffer=true (off by default, undocumented) draws on a hidden
page and flips at the VBL, copying what was drawn onto the other page
afterwards. Benchmarked and not worth it: every frame lands on a whole
VBL, so ST and STE fall from about 40ms to 60ms a frame and a Mega STE
from 25ms to 40ms, overscan or not.

events.title: Turn the stardust with the ship
events.message:
Turn the stardust with the ship

The starfield only drifted in z, so rolling swung the ships, the station and
the planet round the view while the dust hung still -- removing the one cue the
eye uses to tell that the ship is turning.

The original applies our pitch and roll to every particle: "so the stardust
moves correctly when we steer our ship". Ours now puts the dust through the same
arithmetic the simulation applies to a ship's location, in the same order, with
the simulation's own signed angles, so the dust and the ships turn together.

Measured: at full roll deflection a particle at (100, 0, 1000) moves to
(99, -12, 1000) in an iteration, the 31/256 of a radian the angle asks for.

The density stays a departure and is now recorded as one: the original shows
eighteen particles in normal space and three in witchspace, ours many more,
because eighteen dots look empty on a widescreen view. The starfield's comment
used to claim it reproduced the original while doing neither.

events.title: Send the police after a commander carrying contraband
events.message:
Send the police after a commander carrying contraband

The original's main game loop, before it considers pirates, works out how bad we
look and rolls against it. That branch was missing, so smuggling had no
consequences: a hold full of slaves and narcotics brought nothing.

BAD is four times the slaves and narcotics plus twice the firearms, and -- only
if police are already in the local bubble -- that is or'd with our legal status.
The result is the chance in 256 of a police pack, and the pack takes the place of
the pirates, since the routine ends by stopping spawning once a cop is about.

The guard on ORA FIST is the part worth reading twice: a wanted commander with no
police about is not hunted by this rule, which is the bounty hunters' business and
already implemented through a Viper's E% flags.

Measured: no police at all for a clean commander over 200,000 iterations, 43
packs for five tonnes of slaves and 111 for a full hold.

events.title: Soak the simulation, and record where the fifty-hertz clock reaches
events.message:
Soak the simulation, and record where the fifty-hertz clock reaches

Reading IRQ1's line-scan entry point settles what else the fifty-hertz interrupt
drives: DL, which only WSCAN waits on, SVN, which is a save flag, and LASCT, the
laser's pulse counter. LASCT was the only one that touches the game, so the
dashboard is main-loop driven and the port now models both clocks.

Adds a soak test: four and a half hours of game time with spawning on, the
commander manoeuvring and firing throughout and jumping systems every fifty
thousand iterations, checking on every iteration that the bubble stays within
its twelve slots, that the energy, laser and cabin temperatures stay inside a
byte, and that every ship's coordinates stay inside the 24-bit range -- which is
where a sign-magnitude slip would eventually show as a wrapped coordinate.

Twenty-one command-line combinations also swept clean, including every screen,
the viewer, hyperspace, the autopilot and both simulation rates.

events.title: Spend the laser's pulse counter on the fifty-hertz clock
events.message:
Spend the laser's pulse counter on the fifty-hertz clock

LASCT is not a main loop counter. The original spends it in LINSCN on the
vertical sync -- "50 times a second" -- so a pulse laser fires every 10/50 of a
second, five times a second, whatever the flight loop is doing. Spending it one
per iteration, as the port did, gave a shot every 10 iterations: 1.25 a second.

The Electron version makes the same adaptation in its own source, decrementing
the counter by 4 per main loop iteration because its loop runs at a quarter of
the sync rate. Ours does too, so it is now spent four ticks at a time, and the
counter is allowed to go negative so the leftover ticks carry: ten ticks is two
and a half iterations, and clamping the overshoot away rounds every gap up to
four iterations.

Verified by counting shots: forty iterations of held fire give a shot on
iterations 0, 3, 5, 8, 10, 13, 15, 18 -- five a second -- against a beam laser
firing every iteration. Heat of 8, cooling of 1 an iteration and the 242-degree
cut-off already matched the original and decide the sustained rate.

events.title: Spawn on the original's cadence, not every frame
events.message:
Spawn on the original's cadence, not every frame

The original only reaches its spawning code when its main loop counter comes
round to zero -- once every 256 iterations -- and its extra-vessels counter
counts those boundaries, with a pirate pack storing its own size in it. The port
decided every iteration, gated only by a counter of iterations, so a roll that
said "nothing spawns" was retried immediately rather than 256 iterations later.

Measured over 200,000 iterations: 136 decisions where there used to be 2,344,
seventeen times the original's traffic. Each of the three rolls was right on its
own, which is why no test caught it; the cadence was missing. A test now asserts
decisions land on 256-iteration boundaries and are rare.

Also collapses three rules that existed twice, as a tested helper and as a
hand-written copy: the Constrictor's conditions (the tests were exercising the
copy the game never called), spending hyperspace fuel, and marks Mvt6 as
superseded -- it is a faithful port of the location rotation that the 24-bit
integer path replaced, and nothing calls it, which corrects an earlier note in
the roadmap that credited it with fixing the station's wobble.

events.title: Switch the docking computer on
events.message:
Switch the docking computer on

Nothing in the game called DockingComputer.Fly. It was written, tuned and
unit-tested, and the flight scene never invoked it: a commander could buy a
docking computer, see it listed as fitted on the status screen, and press every
key there was without it doing anything.

It is now engaged with C, as the original's DOKEY does, when one is fitted and a
station is in range -- and it refuses a station that has turned against us,
which on this build is the station's NEWB flag rather than the top bit of its AI
flag. That rule lives in DockingComputer.CanEngage so it can be tested, and the
key is rebindable with the rest.

The autopilot writes rotation counters rather than pressing keys, so the scene
drives it inside the fixed-step loop.

Two tests now fly it rather than calling it: from 6000 units out it must reach a
docking, once with the station rolling the original's way and once rolling each
of three other ways. Verified in the game too: --autopilot ends the run on the
market screen at Lave, having flown there.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Give MVS4 the sign of the roll angle, so rolling counters the station
events.message:
Give MVS4 the sign of the roll angle, so rolling counters the station

Docking means matching the station's roll, and it was impossible: rolling with
the station and rolling against it produced the same rotation. Measured, the
station's apparent spin was -10.47 degrees an iteration with the key held either
way, against -3.58 while coasting, so both directions made it worse.

MVEIT turns a ship's orientation vectors through MVS4 with two angle bytes that
the original builds as ALP1 ORA ALP2 and BET1 ORA BET2 -- "so ALPHA has a
different sign to the actual roll rate". We passed the bare magnitudes and left
the signs in their separate bytes, and MVS4 reads its angle as signed, so a
magnitude with no sign was a rotation with no direction.

The world's positions rotated correctly throughout, because the location
rotation does apply the sign, which is why the view felt responsive and only the
orientation of the thing being lined up with was wrong.

After the fix rolling right gives +3.32 against the station's -3.58, and the
residual crosses zero between coasting and a hard roll -- that crossing is the
roll to dock with. Two tests fail if the signs go missing again.

events.title: Plot the charts in the galaxy's own coordinates, and give stations their tactics
events.message:
Plot the charts in the galaxy's own coordinates, and give stations their tactics

The long-range chart plotted every system relative to the current system, so
sitting at Lave (x = 20) pushed the whole left of the galaxy off the chart and
left that half of the box empty. The original plots it absolutely: TT22 takes
the x coordinate as the pixel column and halves the y, because the galaxy is
twice as wide as it is high.

That exposed two more: both charts stretch x twice as much as y -- the short
chart draws four chart pixels across and two down -- and the short-range chart
shows systems within 20 across and 38 down, not the symmetric 26 we used. The
box is 2:1 for the same reason.

The stations had no AI flag, so they never thought, and the station's own
tactics are where most of Elite's traffic comes from: it launches shuttles and
transporters to trade with the planet and the police after a commander who has
annoyed it. TACTICS also sends peaceful ships to the planet (GOPL) rather than
merely away from us, which is why our traders used to flee in straight lines.

Hostility moved to the NEWB flags where this build keeps it: asking bit 7 of the
station's AI flag was the cassette rule, and would have refused docking at every
station once the station carried the AI flag NWSPS gives it.

SpawnFromParent gave its children no blueprint figures, so anything launched
arrived with no speed.

events.title: Run the simulation at the original's rate, not the BBC's refresh
events.message:
Run the simulation at the original's rate, not the BBC's refresh

The simulation has stepped at a fixed 50 Hz since the first milestone on the
reasoning that the BBC screen refreshes 50 times a second. It does, but the
original's main loop is not locked to it: Elite iterates as fast as the 6502 can
manage and everything in the game happens once per iteration.

The original's own source distinguishes the two clocks -- on the BBC the laser's
pulse counter is decremented every vertical sync, on the Electron by 4 on each
iteration around the main loop -- and Mark Moxon timed the disc version in an
emulator at 11.5 to 13 iterations a second in ordinary flight, 4 to 5 with a
crowded sky, and up to 36 with nothing to draw.

So one iteration is worth what it always was and we were running four times too
many of them: ships closed four times as fast and the station span four times as
fast, which is what made it look absurd. A station revolution took two seconds
where the original took eight.

Two station faults sat underneath that. The port gave the station a random roll
counter and renewed it every frame; NWSPS gives it 255, whose low seven bits are
all set and which MVEIT therefore never damps, and the renewal also reversed the
direction of the roll.

Smoothness is bought back by interpolating each ship between the last two
iterations when drawing, so the game advances in the original's steps while the
display stays smooth. --sim-rate overrides the rate.

Also counts damage that the shields absorb, which was previously only recorded
when a hit was fatal: the game made no sound when we were hit.

events.title: Read the ship NEWB flags from where the game reads them
events.message:
Read the ship NEWB flags from where the game reads them

The default NEWB flags were read from a byte pattern found in the docked code
rather than from the E% table inside the ship blueprint files. The pattern had
been taken from the bytes it found, so the reader could not have failed, and the
table it produced had zeroes for every pirate in the game: nothing hostile could
spawn and the sky was almost entirely peaceful. Only the Krait and the
Constrictor could ever attack.

The loader gives the address itself -- XX21 = &5600 and E% = &563E, both inside
the loaded blueprint file -- so E% is at offset 62 and type t at 62 + t - 1,
which is what NWSHP's LDA E%-1,Y reads. The reader now takes each type from the
blueprint files that define it and checks that all sixteen agree.

NWSHP or's the table into the ship's existing flags with bits 4 and 7 cleared,
so ApplyBlueprint does the same rather than assigning, and the spawner no longer
forces every spawn hostile: that is the NES behaviour, and on the disc the E%
byte decides, so a Fer-de-lance arrives as a bounty hunter that ignores a clean
commander.

Measured after: sitting still among pirates takes the energy banks from 255 to 1.

events.title: c64: NTSC — the C64 runs the standard System Mode asks for (S25)
events.message:
c64: NTSC — the C64 runs the standard System Mode asks for (S25)

The firmware writes C64_VIDEOFORMAT at boot and on every settings change, and
its default System Mode is NTSC (0x2b). The bridge only printed "the C64 core
is PAL-only" and every C64 ran PAL. TRX64 has had the rows and the switch
(`switch_model`) since Spec 863; the bridge now asks for them.

- The cycles-per-line field picks the row: 63 is c64-pal, 65 c64-ntsc. The
  colour encoding changes only the analogue carrier, so PAL-60 is NTSC timing
  and NTSC-50 PAL timing (confirmed by TRX64).
- The switch waits for a frame boundary: advance_to stops the slice two cycles
  past the frame end (TRX64 reports line 0 from the cycle after it) and calls
  switch_model there; a VIC not in line 0 leaves it pending.
- The emulator clock -> C64 cycle ratio and reSID's clock follow the row's
  cpu_hz; the clock is re-anchored at the switch cycle.

Measured, $02A6 after a reset, three resets each at 1-48 MHz: 00 under NTSC
and PAL-60, 01 under PAL and NTSC-50. The SID tone smoke plays 1038.1 Hz under
NTSC (the same register on a 3.8 % faster clock). Cart smoke 27 PASS, UCI,
ready, prg, type and freeze smokes pass.

A flash that never changed System Mode now boots an NTSC C64, as the device
does.

The game now opens on a title screen: the name, our ship turning in front of

settings and the music. The disc has no music at all -- one sound chip, used for

The notes come from a published score rather than from memory, reduced to one

That also turned up a rendering bug: the sprite batch's linear filtering sampled

can show it, and CTRL-S to save works again: the bare S that moved the cursor

events.title: Port the sun's cabin temperature and scooping; stop peaceful ships firing
events.message:
Port the sun's cabin temperature and scooping; stop peaceful ships firing

The dashboard's CT and FU bars were constants that had never been wired to
anything. Cabin temperature is now the original's sun check on iteration 20 of
32: the sun heats the cabin, a sum of squares below 30 is fatal, and at 224 or
more the scoops add speed/8, capped at a full tank.

Both that check and the planet's shared a sign-extension bug: shifting a signed
coordinate right by 16 made a nearby body on the negative side of an axis read
as 127, the furthest it is possible to be, so flying into the planet from that
side was never fatal.

TACTICS steers peaceful ships with a flipped vector to us, and the laser check
was made on that same flipped vector, so every ship flying away from us scored a
perfect hit and fired: launching and sitting still drained 150 energy to 5 in
twenty frames and lit ENERGY LOW with no hostile ship in the sky.

Also collapses the duplicate commander reference onto one property, removes the
wrong and unused ShipTypes.Planet, makes ENERGY LOW's threshold inclusive as the
original's BCC makes it, and prints the scene's final state on exit, since the
status line is otherwise printed at frame 2 before anything has happened.

Το AMSDOS δεν υπάρχει την ώρα που τρέχει το παιχνίδι: ο χώρος εργασίας του

  εκκίνηση. Ενα μπαγιάτικο next-hop δεν είναι σκουπίδι — είναι έγκυρος
  γείτονας ΑΛΛΟΥ κόσμου, και ο πράκτορας φεύγει προς τα εκεί.
- S σώζει, L φορτώνει, μόνο από το LOOK. Τα πλήκτρα επαληθεύονται στη μήτρα
  (το L δεν ήταν εκεί που το υπολόγισα· η δοκιμή το έπιασε).
- Η γεννήτρια αφήνει πια το seed της σε τέσσερα bytes της τράπεζας 6: είναι
  ξεχωριστό φόρτωμα και σβήνεται, και χωρίς αυτά το παιχνίδι δεν ξέρει από
  ποιο seed βγήκε ο κόσμος του.

Δύο δοκιμές. Το test_fdc διαβάζει τον ΚΑΤΑΛΟΓΟ του δίσκου και τον συγκρίνει
byte-προς-byte με την εικόνα .dsk στον host — ένας οδηγός που δεν μιλά στον

Fly mission 2 end to end, completing the mission chain's tests

The companion to the mission 1 test, and it passes on the first flight:

events.title: Keep the simulation in step with the universe on every system change
events.message:
Keep the simulation in step with the universe on every system change

Last round gave the simulation the missions and the galaxy. Auditing the same
class of fault across all of FlightSim's state found the third gap, and it is the
one that would have kept mission 1 broken after that fix.

Flight.System was set in exactly one place - Load, when a commander is read from
a save. After a hyperspace jump the simulation still believed it was in the
system we had left, and the mission rules read it to decide whether to put the
Constrictor in the sky, so a commander who flew to Orarra rather than loading a
save there would find nothing. Which is exactly what the mission test does - it
loads, so it passed.

One method now keeps them in step, called from the constructor, Load, a completed
hyperspace jump and a galactic jump, instead of three hand-written lines in one
of four places. Three of the four exits from a system changed it; the fourth was
the one that had been written.

The test walks all four and reverting the jump sync fails it. One test needed the
spawner turning off, which is itself a sign the wiring is real: with the
simulation knowing its system, AReleasedWormJoinsTheBubble began filling the sky
with traffic before the Anaconda could release anything.

Six of the seven faults in this family have been state one part of the port set
and another never received. 293 tests pass.

events.title: Give the simulation the missions and the galaxy, without which mission 1 was impossible
events.message:
Give the simulation the missions and the galaxy, without which mission 1 was impossible

Flying the mission chain rather than calling the mission rules found that
mission 1 was impossible in the game. FlightSim holds two pieces of state the
mission rules live on - the missions themselves and which galaxy we are in - and
neither was ever assigned anywhere. The simulation always saw Missions == null
and GalaxyNumber == 0, while the Constrictor is in galaxy 2, so SpawnMissionShip
returned at its first guard and the Constrictor could never appear.

Every mission test passed throughout. They call Missions.* directly and all of
those were correct; what none could see is that the object they were calling was
not the object the simulation had.

Three gaps filled: Flight.GalaxyNumber and GalaxySeeds, Flight.Missions, and
Flight.System - the last because the spawner checks it first and it was null for
the same reason.

The test flies mission 1 end to end, and reverting the Load wiring fails it. It
is the same shape as the live combat checks: mission tests that construct their
own Missions cannot find a fault in which Missions the game is holding. Sixth
fault of this family and the first in the mission system, which had been the most
heavily tested area. A test that calls a rule's methods directly proves the rule
and proves nothing about whether the game calls them. 292 tests pass.

events.title: fix(851): the Ultimate holds its C64 at 1 MHz for 2.06 s after a reset
events.message:
fix(851): the Ultimate holds its C64 at 1 MHz for 2.06 s after a reset

v0.8.6 fixed BUG-061 on an assumption: that the firmware applies the turbo after the C64
has booted. It does not. With the real firmware 3.15 the speed strobe arrives 445 cycles
after reset release (`C64::reset()` -> `effectuate_settings()` -> `setCpuSpeed`), so the
applied-flag was cleared by the reset and set again half a millisecond later, and the
KERNAL still booted under turbo. On the emulator driven by the real firmware nothing
changed.

The real mechanism is in the hardware, measured on the owner's device, reset-anchored:
the C64 runs at 1 MHz for 2.06 s after a reset, at 16 MHz and at 64 MHz alike, stable over
three runs each; a strobe inside that window has no effect and the last strobed speed
applies when it ends; a change without a reset applies at once. The KERNAL's PAL/NTSC race
at $FF5E runs ~1.5 s after reset, inside the hold — which is why the device detects PAL at
every speed.

`vic.u64_reset_hold`: armed by every reset on the U64 profile with 2.06 s of PHI2 taken
from the model's clock, counted down once per VIC cycle. `u64_speed_applied` is removed.
Unmeasured and modelled conservatively: whether a program's own $D031 write inside the
hold is honoured — here it is not.

Gate `u64_boot_speed_gate.rs` rewritten to drive the firmware's order (reset, strobe 445
cycles later): 5 tests, the two that matter red without the hold at 16 MHz. The CIA gate's
`booted@64` re-recorded, and it alone — the only workload that resets; every other digest
bit-identical. 350 lib, 92 across seven gates.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UsAKqeRcLNVeoQDfVY6QWa

events.title: Fly the whole loop again after the motion fix, and the fight that depends on it
events.message:
Fly the whole loop again after the motion fix, and the fight that depends on it

Changing the rotation touches every ship on every frame, so the loop was flown
again rather than assumed. Eleven checks, all passing: docked at Lave with its
seventeen items, bought and sold cargo, tanked up, launched, accelerated under
thrust to the ship's maximum, survived six hundred frames of hard manoeuvring,
jumped to Diso, arrived, docked there, and found its own market.

And the thing that depends most on bodies moving correctly - ships crossing the
gap to fight. In a busy system over twenty thousand frames: twelve ships in the
bubble, a hostile closed to zero distance, 7233 points of damage taken. The
spawner's ships still fly to us and still engage, which is the behaviour earlier
rounds had to fix twice and could easily have broken again.

One number there is not a fault: "closest a hostile got: 0" reads like a
collision or a teleport and is neither. TA4/TA5 send a ship that is right on top
of us away and the collision path removes it, so a hostile at close range is one
about to break off or already gone. It was left in the output because a bound
that reads as alarming and is explained is worth more than one chosen to look
tidy. 291 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Test and reject the update-order hypothesis for the rotation's drift
events.message:
Test and reject the update-order hypothesis for the rotation's drift

The planet's combined roll-and-pitch drift was traced to the routine updating
each component from the already-updated values of the others. That reads like
the obvious cause and the obvious fix is to compute all three from the inputs.

It was tested and it is much worse: computing all three from the original
values took the drift from 4.60% to 62.49%, a factor of thirteen in the wrong
direction.

Why the reading was wrong, and the reason is in the routine: k2 is a derived
quantity, y - x*alpha/256, and both z and y are computed from it, then x from
the new y. The chain is not an accident of ordering that a tidy-up would fix -
it is three successive applications of the rotation, and computing x from the
old y breaks the chain that makes the small-rotation approximation work. The
original's order is load-bearing.

Two hypotheses tested and rejected in two rounds, both recorded so they are not
tried again, and both rejected by a measurement that took a minute rather than
a round of reasoning. The rotation is approximately rigid, worse when both axes
turn at once, with the original's ordering load-bearing rather than incidental.
291 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Measure what the planet's drift actually depends on: combining roll and pitch
events.message:
Measure what the planet's drift actually depends on: combining roll and pitch

The question flagged two rounds ago was whether the drift depends on the
number of steps or on the magnitude of the coordinates. The answer is neither -
it depends on combining the two axes, which was not among the candidates.

Roll alone: 0.00%. Pitch alone: 0.79%. Both together over 1200 frames: 4.60%.
One step of 12 instead of 12 steps of 1: 0.00%. Radius 2000 against radius
262144: 0.00% both.

Roll alone cannot move a body on the z axis, so its distance cannot change -
that is geometry rather than precision, and it is why the first line is a clean
zero. Step count and magnitude make no difference, ruling out both candidates
from the previous round. What does matter is applying roll and pitch in the same
step: the routine updates each component from the already-updated values of the
others, so the composition is not exactly a rotation.

The drift is directional - 262144 down to 252166 over twelve hundred frames,
about four percent - small enough to be invisible in play, since the planet's
apparent size varies by the same amount, but a genuine accumulation rather than
the bounded oscillation measured for a station.

The counters driven here are the maximum the ship has, held for twenty-four
seconds; in play they are transient and the planet is a fixed backdrop, so the
practical effect is nil. The honest state is that the rotation is approximately
rigid, worse when both axes turn at once. 291 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Test and reject the truncation-bias hypothesis for the planet's drift
events.message:
Test and reject the truncation-bias hypothesis for the planet's drift

The planet's 4.6% wander looked like it should come from the rotation
dividing by 256 with truncation - C#'s / rounds toward zero where the
original's shift rounds toward minus infinity for a negative product, and that
asymmetry could bias every step one way.

It was tested and it is not the cause. Replacing the four divisions with a
rounded divide, symmetric so there is no bias either way, moved the wander from
4.60% to 4.61%. Unchanged.

A useful negative result for two reasons: it rules out the most obvious
explanation, and it does so in one run rather than in a round of reasoning about
which way a shift rounds. The remaining candidates are the structure of the
rotation itself - the three component updates use already-updated values, so the
composition is not exactly a rotation of the original vector - which is
consistent with a station drifting a third of a percent and a planet nearly
five.

The change is reverted, the test bound stays where the measurement put it, and
the hypothesis is recorded as rejected so it is not tried again. What is still
worth trying: whether the drift depends on the number of steps or on the
magnitude of the coordinates, which rotating a planet by half the step for twice
the frames would separate. 291 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record the planet's measured distance bound rather than a wished-for one
events.message:
Record the planet's measured distance bound rather than a wished-for one

Adding a test for the case most exposed to the arithmetic - a body hundreds
of thousands of units out, using the top of the 23-bit range - produced a
number worth keeping: a planet at 262144 units wanders 4.60% over twelve
hundred frames, some twelve thousand units.

That is the honest bound for a body that far out, and it is not nothing: it
shows as a body that swells and shrinks slightly over a long turn. It is
bounded, it returns, and it is three orders of magnitude better than the spiral
it replaced - but the first version of the test asserted one percent, which the
code does not meet, and the fix was to record what the code does rather than to
weaken the test until it passed quietly.

The cause: the rigid path divides by 256 with integer arithmetic every step, so
each step truncates toward zero. For a station's coordinates the errors cancel
within a third of a percent over five thousand turns; for a planet's the same
relative truncation is a much larger absolute step and the cancellation is less
complete.

Two harness errors on the way, both the same shape as before: I compared a
planet's radius against a starting radius of 1, reading (1,0,262144) as having a
radius of 1 from its x coordinate, and the 100% error that produced looked like
a planet collapsing to the origin. The rule this keeps earning: when a
measurement says something alarming, suspect the measurement first. 291 tests
pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Measure whether the rotation's rounding compounds, and pin it as a test
events.message:
Measure whether the rotation's rounding compounds, and pin it as a test

The open question from last round was whether the rigid path's rounding
accumulates or cancels. It was one script, and the answer is unambiguous: over
five thousand full turns the distance from the origin oscillates between about
0.35% below and 0.06% above where it started, and returns. It does not walk in
one direction.

Five thousand turns is over an hour of continuous rolling at the fastest rate
the ship has, and the worst excursion is a third of a percent. That is what
bounded rounding on a rotation looks like - each step truncates toward zero and
the truncations are as likely to go either way, so they cancel.

TheRoundingDoesNotCompoundOverManyTurns now runs the five thousand turns and
requires the distance to stay within one part in a hundred, which is a bound
compounding would have broken long before.

Where the rotation question stands: the rigid path is kept as a departure with
its reason in the code, its precision is bounded and measured, and the
original's method is recorded as drifting without the two possible causes being
separated - which waits for a reason to care rather than a free round. 290 tests
pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Update README.md rgx website
events.message: Update README.md rgx website

events.title: Restore the original's two-byte rotation, measure it, and keep the departure
events.message:
Restore the original's two-byte rotation, measure it, and keep the departure

With Mvt6 fixed the obvious next question was whether the departure was still
needed: if the spiral was Mvt6's truncation, the original's own two-byte routine
should now be rigid and the faithful method could come back.

It was restored, and it is not rigid. One full turn of pitch with the ship's
coordinates at (700,-400,1800) left the distance at 1829 where it started at
1900, a wander of just under four percent, against within 2.3% for the
full-precision path. So the original's method, or our port of it, drifts, and
fixing Mvt6 removed one cause without removing the symptom. The two
possibilities have not been told apart.

The departure therefore stays, with the reason set out where the code is: a
wireframe hides a few percent of positional error, a solid body visibly does not
stay where it should. That is the same argument that justified the rigid render
basis, and it is the only argument this renderer has for departing anywhere.

The test that compared the two paths exactly was wrong - it asserted they agree
to the byte, which was true while both used one arithmetic. It now requires that
both preserve distance and stay within a few percent of each other. 289 tests
pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix MVT6 discarding the coordinate's high bits, which was the wobble's root cause
events.message:
Fix MVT6 discarding the coordinate's high bits, which was the wobble's root cause

Two rounds of reading the listing produced two opposite answers and neither was
worth anything. One measurement of the primitive settled it.

Mvt6 adds a 16-bit value to a 23-bit coordinate and must use all 23 bits. It
took the coordinate's low 16 bits as a single value and added the delta to that:
70000 + 1000 gave 5464, 200000 + 5000 gave 8392. Exact below 65536 and wrong at
and above it, because the carry out of bit 16 had nowhere to go and the sign byte
was left alone. A body at 500 units off to one side has coordinates that exceed
65535 as soon as the roll carries them round, which is why the spiral appeared
when turning and not in a straight line.

The magnitudes now add or subtract in full and the third byte is written back
with the result's high bits.

Correcting two things from the last round: I said Mltu2 and Mvt6 "are already
covered by their own tests" - Mvt6 had no test at all, which is why the fault
survived a round that claimed to fix it by other means and a round that read the
listing twice. And I said the two readings of the original pointed opposite ways;
the truth is that our primitive was wrong and the original was never the problem.

Mvt6Tests now covers twelve combinations spanning the 16-bit boundary, and
reverting the fix fails exactly the six at or above it while the six below pass.
289 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record the open question about the original's rotation, and why two readings disagree
events.message:
Record the open question about the original's rotation, and why two readings disagree

Whether the original's own two-byte rotation is rigid or drifts is still not
settled, and the attempts to settle it disagree.

The first reading, from MVT6's listing, suggests the sum takes its low bits from
a 16-bit window while the sign comes from the 24-bit product, which would lose
the product's top byte and drift by the amount observed - supporting "the
original drifts too".

The second, as an implementation, transcribed MVEIT part 5 and MVT6 directly and
ran them on the same input. It produced x=4942, y=33098, z=8128 from a start of
(500,0,1500): a radius that explodes to six times its value rather than
spiralling. That is not the original's behaviour either, so the transcription is
wrong, most likely in MLTU2's complemented-P conventions.

So the two attempts point opposite ways and both are suspect. Neither is
evidence, and the honest state is that our port of the routine was wrong, which
is measured, and whether the original shares the fault is unproven.

What would settle it: not a third reading but driving the arithmetic primitives
with inputs whose product exceeds 16 bits and comparing against the listing's
stated intent. This project's readings have a much worse record than its
measurements. The practical position is unchanged - the rotation is rigid, the
wobble is gone, and the departure is documented as one. 277 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Verify the rotation fix over a long flight and record what is still open
events.message:
Verify the rotation fix over a long flight and record what is still open

The rigidity test measures a full turn at one offset; the fix was then measured
the way a player would use it - two thousand frames of continuous rolling with a
station off to one side at (1200,600,2400). The worst distance error is 1.45%
where the old path collapsed to 18.8% within one turn, the largest one-frame
movement is 171.9 units so the motion is smooth, and the z coordinate holds
exactly at 2400, which is what a pure roll about z requires.

The z holding exactly is the clearest statement that this is now a rotation: a
roll about z cannot change z. The old path happened to preserve it too, which is
part of why the fault looked like a shape problem rather than a position one.
What was wrong was x and y, whose combined radius wandered.

The pitch case is covered by the same test, which walks bet1 rather than alp1 and
requires both paths to agree exactly.

Left open precisely: the original works on two bytes here and this port now does
not. That is deliberate and recorded, but what the original's own routine does at
these magnitudes has not been measured - either the shipped game drifted the same
way invisibly in a wireframe, or our port of it was wrong. Reading MVEIT part 5's
MVT6 usage with that question in mind is the next piece of work. 277 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix the wobble: the ships' location rotation was a spiral, not a rotation
events.message:
Fix the wobble: the ships' location rotation was a spiral, not a rotation

The measurement that identified the fault was to compare the two rotation
paths on the same input, and they disagreed by a factor of five. From (500,0,1500)
the ships' path left the xy-radius at 94, 18.8% of where it started, while the
bodies' path left it at 511.7, 102.3%. One path rotates and the other spirals,
and which is which was never in doubt: preserving distance is the definition of a
rotation.

The fix is for the ships' path to use the bodies' arithmetic. That is a departure
in method and is recorded as one - the original works on two bytes here and this
port now does not. The reason is that the disc's coordinates are 24 bits and a
spiral is not a thing the original does, but the honest statement is that what
the original's two-byte routine does at these magnitudes has not been measured,
and it may be that the shipped game drifted the same way invisibly in a
wireframe.

Measured after: both paths preserve distance to within 2.3% and agree exactly
with each other. LocationRotationTests now rolls and pitches a body through a
full turn at the fastest rate and requires the distance to hold at five offsets;
reverting the fix fails it.

One test's premise had to change and the change is evidence:
ACommanderCanFightBackAndBePaid stopped passing because its target had been
spiralling out of the crosshairs on its own and the test relied on that. The
target is now held still, which is what the test was always about.

Thirty rounds, and the reason: the wobble was reported as a rendering problem and
I probed the renderer four times, every probe clean, because the renderer was
never wrong - it was drawing a spiral faithfully. 277 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Reproduce the reported wobble: the location rotation is a spiral, not a rotation
events.message:
Reproduce the reported wobble: the location rotation is a spiral, not a rotation

Thirty rounds after it was first reported, the wobble is reproduced in the
simulation, and the measurement says what is wrong.

A ship is a station at a known offset and we roll. A rigid rotation of the
universe about us must keep the station at a constant distance. Ours does not:
with the station at (500, 0, 1500) rolling at the fastest rate, the xy-radius
over one full turn ranged 94.0 to 507.6, having started at 500. The radius
collapses to a fifth of its value, which a rotation cannot do - it is the
definition of a rotation that it preserves length. This is a spiral, and it is
the same at z=200 as at z=1500, so it is the rotation and not the depth.

A smaller version is visible in the first second, which is what a player sees:
after 300 frames the xy-radius is 434 where it started at 500, a drift of 13%
over six seconds. That is a body that visibly does not stay where it should as
the ship turns.

Both previous probes looked at the orientation - whether the render basis was
rigid, whether faces flickered - and were clean. This is the location, a
different vector, and it is the one that is broken.

Narrowed rather than fixed: the fault is in RotateLocationByOurPitchAndRoll,
which uses two-byte coordinates and writes the third byte as a sign, and in
Mvt6, which supplies the sign handling. The planet and sun take a separate
24-bit path and were not tested here, which is the next measurement to take.
271 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: State the objective's requirements against what is demonstrated, at round 129
events.message:
State the objective's requirements against what is demonstrated, at round 129

The goal has run for 129 rounds, so the roadmap now records what is
demonstrated against what was asked for: .NET 10 and MonoGame, the universe
with its canonical values checked, the mechanics read from the source, the
blueprints verified byte for byte against the assembled binary, the widescreen
HUD at both size extremes, all ten of the disc's SFX entries defined and played,
five projects and 147 commits.

One thing is not demonstrated, and it is the same thing it has been for thirty
rounds: the reported wobble. Two faults that could account for it are fixed and
the measurements say the frame is rigid and the slots draw, but they cannot say
the picture is right, and two independent probes have failed to reproduce it -
which is evidence about the probes rather than about the wobble.

So the goal stays active, not because work is outstanding that I can name, but
because there is one question the project has been asked and has not answered.
Marking it complete would assert something measured around rather than through.
271 tests pass.

events.title: Read the startup and flight log in full, after last round's fault came from it
events.message:
Read the startup and flight log in full, after last round's fault came from it

Last round's fault was found by reading the startup output rather than by any
test, so the log was read in full and followed for longer.

The arrival state is right: Lave's sun at -327680 is (s1_hi & 7 | 1) << 16, the
source's "the sun is behind us at a distance of 1 to 7", with the planet at
262144 ahead and the station 3000 ahead. The sun's distance being exactly a
power-of-two multiple is the encoding working rather than a clamp, because the
original's sign byte carries the top bits of the coordinate.

Every scene runs: the market, both charts and the jump all start without a fault
and report sensible state. Frame cost is unchanged after thirty rounds of
changes - 2.29 ms update plus 4.52 ms draw, 6.81 ms against a 20 ms budget.

Reading the log has produced a fault in each of the last two rounds where
several rounds of auditing produced none. That is not an argument against
auditing; it is an argument that the log is a different instrument and was being
ignored. It reports state no test asserts and no audit inspects, and it is
generated free on every run. 271 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: log: the IO trace carries the emulated time of each access
events.message:
log: the IO trace carries the emulated time of each access

The firmware's order says nothing about how far apart two writes are, and that distance was the question:
how long after the C64 comes out of reset does the firmware strobe its CPU speed. Each `--log io` line now
ends in `t=seconds`, the emulated clock of the access to the 10 ns tick.

Answered with it, three resets at 16 MHz, firmware 3.15:

    C64::reset()          W C64_MODE = 0x08 (UNRESET)        t=6.89741810
    setCpuSpeed()         W C64_SPEED_UPDATE = 0x01          t=6.89787014

452 us, 445 C64 cycles, identical on all three -- the speed is strobed long before the KERNAL decides between
PAL and NTSC, so a model that waits for the firmware's next strobe to speed the machine up never slows the boot.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012ZrJ7fdcGMeQu8svPU5Xan
events.author: Jondalar

events.title: Make a silent sound effect stop the current sound rather than do nothing
events.message:
Make a silent sound effect stop the current sound rather than do nothing

Wiring the last sounds left a loose end that only shows at runtime: the game
reports "Loaded 9 sounds" where the table has ten. SoundBank.Load renders each
effect and skips any that produces no samples, and entry 72 produces none, so
it was absent from the map and Play(EcmOff) did nothing.

That looked harmless and was not. Entry 72's four zero bytes are not an
unfinished sound; they are the original's way of silencing a channel, which is
how ECMOF cuts off the E.C.M.'s continuous tone. Ours renders that tone from
entry 64 with a duration of 255 ticks - nearly thirteen seconds - where the
field itself lasts sixty frames. With the switch-off treated as nothing, the
tone outlived the E.C.M. by a wide margin.

Play now treats an effect with no samples as "stop what is playing", and Stop
is public so the intent is nameable.

The lesson is about the shape of the check. Render already had the comment "a
sound with no duration, such as the E.C.M. switching off" - the case was known,
named, and returned an empty array, and the emptiness then propagated into a
silent no-op two layers away. A well-documented special case is not the same as
a handled one, and the documentation is what made it look handled. It was found
by reading the startup log, not by any test or audit. 271 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Guard the sound table against the disc's SFX data
events.message:
Guard the sound table against the disc's SFX data

The ship-type constants drifted silently because nothing compared them to the
data, and the sound table is the same kind of table: ten entries of four bytes
each, copied out of the source, where a wrong pitch still plays and is only
wrong beside the original.

The test checks every entry against the disc's SFX data, including the effect's
number being its offset in that table - which is how the original addresses a
sound and which a reordering would break - and checks that the E.C.M.'s
switch-off entry is deliberately silent. That second part is the one worth
pinning: it looks like an unfinished entry, it is the obvious thing to
"correct", and it is exactly right, because zeroing the sound buffer is how the
original stops the field's continuous tone. A test covering only the nine
audible entries would leave the one that invites a wrong fix unguarded.

Verified capable of failing: changing one byte of the low beep's pitch fails it.

Three tables have now had this treatment - the ship types, the ship data
block's offsets, and the sounds - and the question was the same each time: is
there anything here that a wrong value would not announce? 271 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Wire the last two sound effects, and confirm the E.C.M.'s zero entry
events.message:
Wire the last two sound effects, and confirm the E.C.M.'s zero entry

Last round left two effects unplayed rather than connecting them to the nearest
plausible thing. Both are now wired from the source's own call sites.

HitOrDeath plays when the commander dies: the table's labels are "We died 1 /
We made a hit or kill 2" and "We died 2 / We made a hit or kill 1", and
FlightSim.PlayerDied was being set and never read by the game, so the commander
died in silence.

Boop plays when the missile is unarmed: the disc's branch says "Call the NOISE
routine with A = 40 to make a low, long beep to indicate the missile is now
unarmed", which happens at the two points the lock is released. FlightSim now
raises a per-frame flag at both and the game sounds it.

And the E.C.M.'s switch-off entry is genuinely all zeros. I wired EcmOff last
round then doubted it, because a sound effect with no parameters looks like a
mistake - but it is what the original's SFX table holds, and ECMOF on the disc
really does call it. Zeroing the sound buffer is how the original stops the
E.C.M.'s continuous tone, so both the entry and the wiring are right. Our whole
table matches the source byte for byte.

Three effects had no caller and were three different things: a genuine gap in
our wiring, a state flag the core set and the game ignored, and an event the
core did not surface at all. They looked identical from outside. 269 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Play the E.C.M.'s switch-off sound, and record the two effects still unplayed
events.message:
Play the E.C.M.'s switch-off sound, and record the two effects still unplayed

Ten sound effects are defined with the original's own beep data and three
were never played anywhere.

The E.C.M. running down is now wired: the original has ECMOF for the moment the
field collapses, and we had the effect defined and the flag going false with
nothing connecting the two. FlightScene now plays EcmOn or EcmOff on a change
of state.

The first attempt at that was wrong in the same way as several faults before
it. I reused the pending flag to mean "it has just ended", but that flag is
also true before the first firing, so the E.C.M. would have made its
switch-off sound every frame of a session in which it was never used. A
previous-state field distinguishes the two and the flag is gone - the same trap
as the hostile bit and the station's refusal, a single boolean carrying two
meanings.

Two effects remain unplayed and are recorded rather than guessed at: HitOrDeath
and Boop both have correct beep data and no caller. Wiring them means deciding
which events correspond to the original's call sites, so they are listed as
open rather than connected to the nearest plausible thing. 269 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Check the ship data block's offsets against the source's own documentation
events.message:
Check the ship data block's offsets against the source's own documentation

The Thargon's type drifted from the data and the fix was to write the
comparison out. The ship data block's byte offsets are the same kind of
hand-written table - fifteen constants mirroring a layout the source documents
in prose - so they were checked next. All of them line up: coordinates at 0, 3
and 6 (the source's byte #2 is x_sign), orientation at 9, speed at 27 ("the
ship's speed byte #27"), then acceleration, both counters, flags, the AI flag
("the ship's byte #32"), scanner, explosion counter, energy, and the NEWB flags
at 36 ("the ship's NEWB flags from byte #36").

Nothing was wrong, which is the expected result for a table written off a
documented layout - but worth checking, because the Thargon's was also written
off something and was wrong, and a bad offset would corrupt a ship's state
rather than merely mis-name it.

Why this table is cheaper to trust than the ship types: its offsets are
confirmed by the routines that use them, so a constant that disagreed would
break MVEIT or ANGRY visibly, whereas a ship type constant that disagrees
breaks nothing until a specific thing is tried. The difference is not care but
whether anything would notice. 269 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Check every hardcoded ship type against the blueprints, and keep the check
events.message:
Check every hardcoded ship type against the blueprints, and keep the check

The Thargon's type was wrong - 20, the Adder's number - and the reason it
survived is that a constant which drifts from the data is invisible: it
type-checks, it reads correctly, and it silently names a different ship.
Nothing about Thargon = 20 looks wrong on the line it is written.

So all eighteen named ship types in the core were checked against the extracted
blueprints at once, and all are correct after the fix: the station, the
Constrictor, the Thargoid, the Thargon, the missile, the Anaconda, the Worm,
the Viper as the cop, the six junk types, and the two spawner bases.

The check is now a test, which is the point: this is the third round in a row
where the answer came from writing the comparison out rather than from reading
the code. It is the cheapest kind of test - eighteen assertions, no setup - and
it covers the one class of fault that reading cannot catch, because the wrong
value looks exactly like the right one. Putting the Thargon back to 20 fails it
immediately, which was checked.

269 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix the Thargon's type, and correct my own wrong scoop claims
events.message:
Fix the Thargon's type, and correct my own wrong scoop claims

Chasing the Thargon's scoop item meant reading all three scoopable ships'
comments in full, and one contradicts what the last two rounds asserted: the
splinter's says "Market item when scooped = 11 + 1 = 12 (minerals)". Round 119
says in the roadmap that it gives furs, and I changed the fallback from 12 to
11 to match that belief - wrong, on no better evidence than my own arithmetic.
The constant is back at 12 and the test is SplintersScoopAsMinerals again.

All three are now confirmed by the source's own words rather than by
inference: escape pod item 3 slaves, splinter item 12 minerals, thargon item 16
alien items. And the value passes through unchanged - the original's item
numbering doubles as the hold's slot numbering, so there is no minus one
anywhere, which is what round 119 got wrong in the other direction.

The real bug was Debris.Thargon = 20, which is the Adder, so Thargons were not
scoopable at all. That is fixed.

Three rounds on one five-line rule with two wrong turns, and the difference is
evidence: I inferred twice from arithmetic and a half-remembered comment, and
got it wrong both times; the three comments taken together state it outright.
A comment that names a value is evidence, and arithmetic about what a value
ought to be is not. 268 tests pass.

events.title: Check every index space against the source's own numbering
events.message:
Check every index space against the source's own numbering

Last round's fault was a one-based number used as a zero-based index, so every
crossing between the game's index spaces was checked the same way: the galaxy
system number (zero-based, as RUPLA names Lave 7 and Teorge 211), the market
items (one-based, so index = item - 1), the cargo hold (zero-based QQ20 slots),
the equipment list (the original's item 0 is fuel, selected straight from the
digit keys) and the two-letter name tokens (masked to 0-31, against a 32-entry
table).

Five spaces, one conversion that was wrong, and it is the only one where two
numbering schemes meet without a named boundary - which is what last round's
commit gave it.

The loop still flies: the suite passes, the extractor verifies byte for byte,
and a run reports 6 objects in the bubble and 52 triangles at 9.08 ms a frame -
110 fps against a 50 Hz simulation, our own work inside a fifth of the 20 ms
budget. That number has not been taken since round 65.

The pattern is the cheapest kind of verification: not a new test but the same
question asked of every place two systems meet. It found nothing, which after
last round is the answer to hope for. 268 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Convert the blueprint's market item to a hold index when scooping
events.message:
Convert the blueprint's market item to a hold index when scooping

The blueprint gives a one-based market item - "add 1 to the high nibble to
get the market item" - and the extractor's +1 is right. But the original then
uses that value directly to index the hold, whose QQ20 slots are zero-based. So
the number means both "market item 3" and "hold slot 3", and those are
different commodities for everything except the first.

Ours passed the market item straight to AddCargo, so every scooped commodity
landed one slot late: escape pods gave radioactives rather than slaves,
splinters minerals rather than furs, thargons alien items rather than
gem-stones.

What caught it was the source's own comment, which had been in the roadmap for
a round: "the high nibble of byte #0 that scooping escape pods gives us
slaves". Escape pods paying radioactives contradicts that in plain English,
which is a stronger signal than any of the arithmetic around it.

The conversion now happens at the point of use: ScoopItemProvider hands over a
hold index and the game layer does the minus one, so the data keeps the
original's meaning and the hold keeps its own. Two tests asserted the old
behaviour and one was named for it - SplintersScoopAsMinerals is now
SplintersScoopAsFurs.

The canister case is genuinely different: its scoop nibble is zero, so the
original skips the market-item path and gives a random commodity, which is why
zero cannot simply mean food. 268 tests pass.

events.title: update artefacts
events.message: update artefacts
events.author: fschuhi

events.title: Remove old attempts
events.message: Remove old attempts
events.author: Stephan

events.title: Record the scoop rule the extractor already had, having nearly changed it
events.message:
Record the scoop rule the extractor already had, having nearly changed it

The sweep reached the last two blueprint fields: the canister byte packs
how many canisters a ship leaves in its low nibble and what scooping it gives
you in its high nibble.

The escape pod reads as high nibble 2 and the source comment says scooping one
gives slaves, which is market item 3. Those do not agree on their face, so I
changed the extractor to use the high nibble directly - and the escape pod
started paying textiles. Wrong direction. The routine that does the conversion
is explicit: "Add 1 to the high nibble to get the market item". The extractor
was right and the change is reverted.

Twelfth diagnostic of mine to be wrong before the code was, and the most
expensive kind: I had the answer and talked myself out of it. The escape pod's
(2 << 4) and the comment saying slaves are consistent - 2 + 1 = 3, and slaves
is item 3 - and the reconciling arithmetic was two minutes away in a routine I
had not opened.

The mistake is a different shape from the previous eleven. Those were
mis-measurements: a wrong scale, a wrong encoding, a constant that never
varied, a decimal comma. This was mis-reasoning: I treated a disagreement
between two sources as evidence that one was wrong, when it is first of all
evidence that I have not found the rule that reconciles them. Three of the
twelve have been that shape and in all three the reconciling fact existed and
had not been looked for. 268 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Carry the targetable area and bounty, with readers for both
events.message:
Carry the targetable area and bounty, with readers for both

The search moved on to the remaining blueprint fields a ship needs, and two
more belonged in the same place: targetable area, which the original stores as
a squared radius and the hit test uses, and bounty, which is what a kill pays.

BlueprintDefaults now carries six fields and the two new ones have readers
rather than sitting in the table. TargetableAreaProvider defaults to the
blueprint instead of a constant 95 * 95 - the Cobra's value, so every ship in
a core-only session was exactly as easy to hit as a Cobra. BountyProvider
defaults to the blueprint instead of zero, so a session without the game is
paid for its kills.

Adding a field with no reader is the exact fault this session has spent five
rounds finding, and I came within one edit of doing it: the bounty went into
the table and the provider went on returning zero. What caught it was round
110's grep for the readers, applied to my own change in the same round rather
than several rounds later.

Verified by paying a kill in a core-only session: Sidewinder 50.0 credits,
Mamba 150.0, Thargoid 500.0, pirate Cobra 175.0, and a plain Cobra 0.0 - which
is the original's own data rather than a difficulty curve. 268 tests pass.

events.title: powermonger: PLAY RANDOM LAND reaches a world again (stops at the protection-check dialog)
events.message: powermonger: PLAY RANDOM LAND reaches a world again (stops at the protection-check dialog)
