events.title: Carry the rest of the blueprint defaults, and split broken from inconsistent
events.message:
Carry the rest of the blueprint defaults, and split broken from inconsistent

Round 114 found a spawned ship had no speed. The field next to it had the
same gap - no energy - so the same search was made across every blueprint
value a ship needs, and the four that matter are now in one place: speed, max
energy, max speed and visibility distance, carried by BlueprintDefaults.For
and applied by the spawner as NWSHP does. Four parallel tables became one
type, which is its own correction: I had been adding a table per symptom.

The two are not the same kind of fault and the roadmap should not claim they
are. The game layer stamps blueprint values on through FlightSim.ShipSpawned,
so in a real game the energy was being set - the gap was in the core, where
the tests live and where the spawner is used directly. Speed was different:
ApplyBlueprint sets it only when it is zero, so the core's zero carried into
the game and the ship never moved.

  speed:  a real game bug. A commander parked in a busy system was never shot
          at, because nothing the spawner produced could reach firing range.
  energy: a core inconsistency. Ships spawned outside the game arrived unable
          to absorb one hit; the game masked it, nothing else did.

Both fixed, and it matters which was which - a defect list that does not
distinguish them cannot be used to judge how much of the game was affected.
268 tests pass.

events.title: Test that the commander can fight back, completing the live pair
events.message:
Test that the commander can fight back, completing the live pair

Last round's check proved we are shot at; this one asks the opposite
question - whether a commander can shoot back and kill what the spawner sends
- and consumes the same real paths: Spawner makes the ship, the crosshair test
picks the target, and the kill goes through the destruction bookkeeping.

It passes, which is worth stating because it is the first thing in this area
to pass on the first attempt. Holding a spawned pirate in the crosshairs
destroys it.

Together the two live checks bracket the loop: one asserts only that damage
arrives, the other only that a target dies. Neither says anything about how a
ship is built, which is the property that lets them find faults in the thing
that builds them - three rounds of hand-built ships could not, and these two
found the missing hostile bit and the missing speed between them.

268 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Give spawned ships their blueprint speed, so they can reach us
events.message:
Give spawned ships their blueprint speed, so they can reach us

Round 113's lesson says to stop building inputs by hand and consume the real
path, so this round's check lets Spawner make the ships and asks only whether
the commander is ever hit. It was not, in twenty thousand frames.

Two faults, and the second was the one that mattered. The first was round
113's: no hostile bit. The second was speed - a spawned ship arrived with
Speed = 0 and stayed at the spawn distance, so it never came within the
8192-unit firing range and never fired. Ten hostile ships in the sky, at 9728
units, motionless. The original's NWSHP takes the new ship's speed from byte
#15 of its blueprint; ours left that to the game layer, so anything spawned in
the core was stationary.

Spawner.SpeedFor now carries the blueprint's speed per type and the spawner
uses it, the same shape as NewbFlagsFor - a small table in the core, checked
against the extractor's output, because the core has no dependency on the data
files.

Why the hand-built tests could not see this: every tactics test places its
enemy inside firing range, because that is what such a test is about. So the
range check never mattered, the speed never mattered, and a spawner producing
motionless ships passed all of them.

Two rounds running, flying the game found what the suite could not, and both
times the tests supplied the very thing that was broken. The test added here
asserts nothing about ships and only asks whether the commander takes damage.
266 tests pass, 267 with it.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Mark spawned ships hostile, which round 109 made necessary
events.message:
Mark spawned ships hostile, which round 109 made necessary

Two rounds after making the NEWB hostile bit decide whether a ship fights,
flying the live simulation showed every ship the spawner produced arriving
with newb=0x00 - not hostile. With the fight gated on hostility, nothing the
spawner created could attack at all: pirates and bounty hunters arrived
aggressive and peaceful at the same time.

The cause is the other half of the same seam. The original sets bit 2 of NEWB
before either spawn branch - "set bit 2 of the NEWB flags ... so the ship we
are about to spawn is hostile" - and our spawner set only the AI flag. That
was invisible while WantsToAttack read the AI flag alone, which is why it
survived until the gate was added; the moment the gate existed, the gap it
exposed was total.

The test suite had nothing to say about it. The spawner's own test checked
which ship type it chose and every tactics test built its enemies by hand with
the flags it wanted, so a change that made the entire game peaceful passed 264
tests. The new test asserts a spawned pirate is hostile and aggressive, with
the second half separate because aggressive alone is not enough; restoring the
bug fails it.

What this says about the last three rounds: 109 added the gate and verified it
with hand-built ships, 110 audited the bits for readers, 112 audited
parameters for defaults - and none looked at what the spawner produces, which
is the path every ship in a real game arrives through. A check that constructs
its own inputs cannot find a fault in the thing that constructs them. 266
tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Take the shield side from the attacker for missiles and collisions too
events.message:
Take the shield side from the attacker for missiles and collisions too

The rule from last round says a value crossing a boundary is a seam; there is
a third question it did not name, and the sweep found it: whether the value
can even be determined at the call site.

Combat.TakeDamage takes a fromBehind and uses it to choose the fore or aft
shield, and the original reads it from the attacker's own z_sign - "fetch byte
#8 (z_sign) for the ship attacking us... if A is negative, then we got hit in
the rear". The laser path does exactly that, but two other call sites passed
fromBehind: false as a constant: the missile that goes off on us, and a ship
we ram. So every missile took the forward shield however it arrived, and
ramming from behind took the forward shield too.

Both now read the attacker's own position. There are no hardcoded shield
sides left in the simulation.

This seam is a little different: the value was not merely unread or
overloaded, it was available and passed as a constant anyway, because the call
sites were written where all the other arguments were to hand. That is the
shape to watch for - a parameter a caller has to compute is the one most
likely to be defaulted, because defaulting it is the only way to make the call
compile without thinking about it. 265 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Stop the station's refusal being read as a collision
events.message:
Stop the station's refusal being read as a collision

Applying last round's audit to round 90's rule - that shooting an innocent
turns the station hostile - turned up two faults in the same seam, and the
second is worse than a no-op.

The caller hardcoded the answer: FlightScene passed stationHostile: false as
a constant, so the check could never fire whatever the station's flags said.

And the refusal shared a result with a collision. Docking.Check returned
DockingResult.Collision for a hostile station and the caller treats a
collision as fatal, so a commander who had annoyed a station was destroyed on
the approach rather than turned away. The check fired correctly and the caller
read it as having flown into the hull.

Both fixed: the caller passes ship.AiFlag >= 0x80, and DockingResult has a
Hostile value of its own which the scene handles by refusing the request and
saying so, as the original does.

The test that covered it was asserting the bug - AHostileStationWillNotLetUsIn
expected Collision, which is what the code did. It now expects Hostile and
asserts the two are different, which is the part that matters: the fault was
never that a hostile station was mishandled, it was that being refused and
being killed were the same value.

Four faults in this family. The rule for the remaining work: a boolean or enum
shared between two different outcomes is a seam, and the seam is where the
faults are. Whether the value is read at all, and whether it means one thing
or two, are the two questions to ask of any flag that crosses a boundary. 265
tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Audit every NEWB bit for a reader, and test the hostile link end to end
events.message:
Audit every NEWB bit for a reader, and test the hostile link end to end

Applying last round's rule rather than only stating it: every NEWB bit was
checked for a reader. Trader, bounty hunter, hostile, innocent and cop all
have one, which was not true a round ago, when the hostile bit was written
and nothing read it.

The link now has a test that can fail. AHostileShipEngagesUsAndANonHostileOne
DoesNot flies both cases - a ship lined up on us with the hostile bit and the
same ship without it - and requires damage in the first and none in the
second. Restoring the bug makes it fail, which was checked rather than
assumed.

The test flies the thing rather than asserting the flags, because neither
half looks wrong on its own: the role rules set the bit correctly and the
attack rule reads the AI flag correctly, and the fault was entirely in the
gap between them. That is the shape of all three faults in this family - the
escape pod's fuel, the Anaconda's callback, the hostile bit. A test against
either half passes; only one that exercises the seam finds them. 265 tests
pass.

events.title: Make the hostile bit decide whether a ship fights
events.message:
Make the hostile bit decide whether a ship fights

Round 108 implemented the trader-to-pirate rule and tested its rates; the
last check was whether anything read the bit it sets, and nothing did.

DecideRole set NewbHostile for a trader that turned out to be a pirate and
for a bounty hunter once we were wanted, while WantsToAttack decided whether
to fight from the ship's AI flag alone. So a trader that "became a pirate"
went on behaving like a trader while its own flags said otherwise: a flag
written and never read.

The fix is the link rather than a new rule. WantsToAttack now requires the
ship to be hostile as well as aggressive, which is the route the original
takes: TACTICS branches on the hostile bit and sends a non-hostile ship off
towards the planet rather than into a fight. Four tests needed their enemies
marking hostile, which is itself evidence that the flag decides - they had
been relying on an AI flag alone and passing.

Verified by flying it: a hostile pirate lined up on us and a non-hostile
trader beside it, four hundred frames, 374 damage taken. The harness's first
run took no damage because LaserPowerProvider defaults to zero, so neither
ship had a laser - the eleventh diagnostic of mine to be wrong before the
code was, caught in one run because the output said what it meant.

Three of the recent faults have been state written by one part and not read
by the part that should use it: the escape pod's fuel, the Anaconda's spawn
callback, and now the hostile bit. The way to tell an unconnected rule from
an unimplemented one is to ask who reads it whenever state is written. 264
tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Implement the trader-to-pirate rule from the NEWB flags
events.message:
Implement the trader-to-pirate rule from the NEWB flags

The item recorded as open in round 94 is in. Tactics.DecideRole reads a
ship's role from its NEWB flags before the tactics decide what to do with it,
and rewrites those flags as play goes on.

Bit 0 is a trader, which rolls against #100 and turns out to be a pirate on
the 39% of rolls below it - the source gives 39% here against 20% in the
advanced versions. Once hostile it stays hostile, because the flag is
rewritten rather than re-rolled. Bit 1 is a bounty hunter, which goes hostile
only once our legal status reaches 40, where 50 is a fugitive, so the ships
that exist to hunt the wanted leave a clean commander alone.

That second half is what the spawn-table model could not express: the
original chooses attackers from the state of our own record, so a bounty
hunter is a consequence of being wanted rather than an independent event.

The test measures the rates - ten thousand rolls at 39%, and a bounty hunter
checked at status 0 against 40 - rather than asserting the constants. The
Anaconda's roll was written the wrong way round once already and only a
measured rate caught it; a test asserting the threshold would have passed
with the comparison inverted.

Also checked: token 198, recovered by the traversal fix, is genuinely empty in
the source, so an empty token there is correct rather than a second fault.
264 tests pass.

events.title: Sweep every description and hint for completeness, and catch a false positive
events.message:
Sweep every description and hint for completeness, and catch a false positive

The traversal fault was found by looking at output rather than code, so
both text paths were swept the same way.

Descriptions: 1024 systems across four galaxies, 0 empty and 0 unstable on
a re-read. Fifty-one are under thirty characters, the shortest being "Sori
is a tedious world." - the original's own terse descriptions, not
truncation.

Hints: every hint of the first three galaxies, 25 hints and 20 distinct
renderings, 0 unstable. The twenty is the number that matters: the tables
hold 25 but five are random-element phrases, so twenty distinct outputs is
what confirms the random element varies rather than collapsing.

One false positive of my own detector: it flagged four hints as truncated
for ending in " TO" when the text is "TRY ERRIUS" and the " TO" comes from
the body. The tenth diagnostic of mine to be wrong, and the cheapest - it
cost one look, because the check printed what it flagged rather than only
how many. A counter alone would have sent the next round hunting a fault
that does not exist. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Correct the record: token 209 is literal text, not a placeholder
events.message:
Correct the record: token 209 is literal text, not a placeholder

Last round's note said every hint reads "APPEARED AT ERRIUS" because
token 209 is a placeholder and the original substitutes the system name.
That is wrong. The source is explicit - token 209 is ECHR ' ', ETWO 'E','R',
ECHR 'R', ECHR 'I', ETWO 'U','S' - the literal string " ERRIUS", with no
control code in it. The original's own decoded comment for token 106 reads
"I HEAR A [130-134] LOOKING SHIP APPEARED AT ERRIUS": the word is in the
text.

And ERRIUS is a real system - galaxy 1, index 253, at (184,149), which is one
of the mission trail's own hint systems. The phrase names a place a player
can be sent to.

So the hints are correct and complete and there is no follow-up. The lesson
is about the last step of a fix rather than the first: having repaired a
genuine traversal fault, I saw output that looked unfinished and wrote down
a plausible next step without checking it. A note promising work that does
not exist costs whoever reads it next, and four lines of source would have
settled it. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Restore the missing token: the hint walk only looked in the hint table
events.message:
Restore the missing token: the hint walk only looked in the hint table

Two causes, and the second was the real one. The hint walk's queue carries
tokens from both tables - a hint refers to main-table tokens, and those refer
to more of their own - but the lookup was only in the hint table. Tokens 106
to 110 are main-table tokens, so the lookup failed for every one and the
continue skipped them along with everything they referenced. Token 209 hangs
off token 106, so it was never reached.

It now falls back to the main table, and the traversal recovers token 209 and
two more: 209 tokens to 211, 141,431 bytes to 141,872. Thirteen hints that
read "APPEARED AT" now read "I HEAR A FUNNY LOOKING SHIP APPEARED AT ERRIUS",
and all five phrases the random element can pick are reachable.

Still wrong, and cosmetic rather than structural: every one ends in "ERRIUS",
because token 209's stored text is a placeholder. The original substitutes the
real system name for that control code when it prints and we print the table's
text, so the hint now has a name but not the system's. That is the next step
and is a substitution rather than a traversal, so much smaller.

The method note: this took two rounds because the first round's two fixes
were real but not the cause. What found it was tracing the queue's visits
rather than reasoning about the walk - the trace showed hint 10 visiting, its
five candidates pushed, and then nothing, which located the continue at once.
263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix two real bugs in the token reachability walk, which do not fix token 209
events.message:
Fix two real bugs in the token reachability walk, which do not fix token 209

Found while chasing the missing token 209, and both worth keeping whatever
else turns out to be true.

`if (element.Kind is "ETOK" or "EREC" && tokens.ContainsKey(...) && ...)`
- && binds to the second alternative only, so a plain ETOK skipped the whole
condition. Python's `a or b and c` trap, written by hand in C#.

And `reachable.Add(x) && queue.Push(x)` never queues a token that an earlier
walk already marked, so its own references are never followed: only the
marking is idempotent, and the visit must not be conditional on it. Both are
split now, and the main walk's early return given the same treatment.

The fix did not change the output - the file is byte-identical and token 209
is still absent, so there is a second cause. Traced as far as this: the
hints' random element does resolve to candidates 106 to 110, they are already
marked reachable when the hint walk sees them, and with the queue no longer
conditional token 106 should be visited and its trailing ETOK 209 followed.
It is not appearing, so something earlier is not what the trace suggested.

The walk fixes go in on their own merit and are labelled as not having fixed
it. 263 tests pass.

events.title: release: a C64 boots at 1 MHz — v0.8.6
events.message:
release: a C64 boots at 1 MHz — v0.8.6

The Ultimate's preferred turbo speed was treated as a state of the machine, so every reset
handed the KERNAL a CPU running at it. The KERNAL works out whether it is a PAL or an NTSC
machine by racing the CPU against the raster, and from 16 MHz up it won a race it must
lose: CIA 1 Timer A got the NTSC latch and a PAL machine ran its jiffy clock at 57.8/s.

Real hardware boots its C64 at 1 MHz and the firmware applies the turbo afterwards. A reset
now drops the C64 to 1 MHz and a speed takes effect when something applies it — a $D031
write or the firmware's strobe. No timing constant.

events.message:
Expose PrintToken, and record that token 209 is missing from the data

Sweeping the _DISC_DOCKED branches turned up the disc's Anreer
description override, which we have right, and then something larger:
thirteen mission hints are truncated.

Hints 10 to 22 all print as "I HEAR A FUNNY LOOKING SHIP APPEARED AT"
with no system name. Token 106 is "I HEAR A [130-134] LOOKING SHIP
APPEARED AT ERRIUS", whose trailing system name is token 209, which is

The hint's random element picks one of tokens 106 to 110, so two of the five
phrases lose their system name and the hint names no system at all - which,
for a trail hint whose whole purpose is to say where the Constrictor was
seen, means it says nothing useful.

The extractor does start token 209, traced, so the loss is downstream of
parsing; the output is a reachability walk rather than the whole table,
which is where to look next. Nothing was changed to paper over it: the
missing name is a symptom, and guessing at the walk would risk dropping
more tokens than it recovered.

PrintToken was added to DescriptionData while checking this, so a
main-table token can be printed on its own. That is what made the five
phrases visible individually and the truncation obvious. 263 tests pass.

events.title: fix(851): a C64 boots at 1 MHz, whatever speed the firmware prefers
events.message:
fix(851): a C64 boots at 1 MHz, whatever speed the firmware prefers

851 treated the Ultimate's preferred speed as a state of the machine: `u64_d031()` fell
back to `u64_speed_prefer` whenever `$D031` had not been written, and a reset clears
exactly that flag — so every reset handed the KERNAL a turbo CPU.

That is not a cosmetic ordering question. The KERNAL works out whether it is a PAL or an
NTSC machine by racing the CPU against the raster: `$FF5E` sets the raster compare to line
311 — a line only a PAL frame has — polls `$D012` until its low byte reads 0, and asks
whether the sticky latch fired in between. A C64 that boots at 16 MHz or faster reaches
line 256 before the raster has crossed 311, reads a clear latch, and `$FDDD` programs CIA 1
Timer A with the NTSC latch $4295. 57.8 jiffies per second on a PAL machine, for the rest
of the session.

Real hardware never does this, at any speed, five runs per step. It boots its C64 at 1 MHz
and the firmware applies the turbo afterwards — measured on the owner's device in a single
run: one program, one boot, work right after the reset exactly as slow at 64 MHz as at
1 MHz, then a factor of 71 in the same boot, changeover 2.62 s after the first instruction.
The CPU is still 56x for everything after, which is what UPic needs and what Gideon's own
REU test reports.

So: `vic.u64_speed_applied`, cleared by every reset, set when the speed is APPLIED — a
`$D031` write, or the firmware's strobe through `set_u64_turbo`. While clear the machine is
a 1 MHz 6510 whatever the setting says.

NO TIMING CONSTANT. The device's ~4.5 s is one observation of one firmware on one machine
and stays in the bug report. What is modelled is the architecture: a reset drops the C64 to
1 MHz, and a speed takes effect when something applies it. 851's own "the divider refreshed
at each instruction boundary" was a convenience with no source and it cost this project
half a picture last week; this is not another one.

One caller needed the firmware's half. `cia_alarm_check_gate` boots ROMs, so its `@64`
workload would have booted AND run at 1 MHz — a gate for the alarm check at 64 MHz quietly
no longer testing 64 MHz. It re-strobes after the boot now, and its digest is BIT-IDENTICAL
to the one recorded before this change. That is the evidence that a turbo machine still
behaves exactly as it did and only the moment the speed arrives has moved.

Gate: `u64_boot_speed_gate.rs`, 4 tests, all four red without the fix. 350 lib tests, 88
across the six U64 and turbo gates.

Found by the UE2 emulator session as "the C64 runs 3.3% slow under turbo". It was not a
clock, not a lost cycle and not a wrong constant — the machine was being told it lived on
another continent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01UsAKqeRcLNVeoQDfVY6QWa

events.title: Record the wobble investigation: what is ruled out, and two more probe errors
events.message:
Record the wobble investigation: what is ruled out, and two more probe errors

Three rounds of hunting the reported wobble have eliminated every
mechanism I can measure - model geometry, projection, near-plane clipping,
forced face culling, a non-rigid basis, boundary flicker, and the missing
docking slot. The last two of those were real faults and are fixed; the
rest are ruled out with measurements.

Two more probe errors of mine, taking the count to nine. The first was
structural: I called Mvs5 with vector offsets where its parameters take a
component offset, so my "x" and "y" were the nose and roof vectors, and the
numbers it produced looked exactly like a rotation fault while being an
artefact of the call. The second was reading a step printed as 93,583 as
ninety-three when the same program's filtered list showed nothing above 7.9.

Both were caught by cross-checking one measurement against another rather
than by care, which is now the ninth instance and stable enough to state as
a rule: a probe that has not been checked against a second, independent view
of the same quantity is not evidence. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Test the flicker mechanism for the reported wobble, and find none
events.message:
Test the flicker mechanism for the reported wobble, and find none

The reported wobble is the one thing only a player can settle, so the next
best move is to test the mechanism that would cause a changing shape: faces
flipping visibility at boundary angles.

Counting faces turns out to be the wrong instrument and even looks
alarming - the Coriolis's drawn-face count jumps by two at a time, 6 to 4 at
thirty degrees. For a body with parallel faces that is expected, and the
count says nothing about the screen, because a back-facing face contributes
no pixels whether it was culled or not.

So the image was measured instead: rendered every two degrees from 26 to 40
and counted differing pixels between consecutive frames. The differences run
270, 308, 322, 318, 312, 334, 322 - smooth across the face-count jump, so
the faces appearing there were behind the ones facing us and never reached
the screen. A flicker would have shown as one step several times its
neighbours.

That eliminates the one mechanism that would produce a changing shape as
opposed to a static inaccuracy. The instrument lesson is the same one a
level up: measuring a feature means measuring what the player sees, which
for a renderer is pixels. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Verify the whole game loop again at round 100
events.message:
Verify the whole game loop again at round 100

A hundred rounds in, the cheapest useful thing is to fly the game end to
end, since so much has changed under it: the market, the missions, the
legal status, the galaxy, and the visibility scale for every ship. Thirteen
checks, all passing - starts at Lave in flight, docks with a 17-item
market, buys cargo, does not restock the market when selling, survives ten
jumps and dockings, pays a pirate's bounty, stays clean for a pirate and
becomes an offender for an innocent, and takes a galactic jump with the
chart following it.

Nothing was found, which is the right result for a round like this.

The ships whose detail was suppressed are also confirmed drawing: the
visibility fault hid detail on every ship with visibility above 7, not only
the stations, so the ones with the most were rendered - the Cobra Mk III's
fourteen, the Viper's six, the Krait's ten, the Mamba's twenty.

Still open, and the only item that matters to a player: whether the reported
wobble is gone. Only someone looking at the screen can say. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record why the ship visibility distance is not masked, having nearly masked it
events.message:
Record why the ship visibility distance is not masked, having nearly masked it

Following last round's scale error I went looking for its siblings and found
AND #%00011111 a few lines away in the per-face path, concluded the
ship-level comparison was missing it, and changed it. That was wrong: it
would have masked the Coriolis's 120 down to 24 and collapsed a station to a
dot five times too early. Reverted, with the reasoning left in a comment.

They are two different scales and the source says so. A face wears its
visibility in bits 0-4 of its own byte, which is why the mask is there; a
ship's visibility distance is the whole of byte #13, which the blueprint
comments confirm by giving the Anaconda 50 on this build - and 50 cannot
survive a 0x1F mask.

Seventh probe of mine to be wrong before the code was, and the most
instructive: the evidence was genuinely ambiguous, the same phrase in two
places with a mask in one and not the other. What settled it was the
comments rather than the code. When two things share a name, find a value
that can only belong to one of them before changing either. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Check every ship's detail edges are reachable, and record my own false alarm
events.message:
Check every ship's detail edges are reachable, and record my own false alarm

The docking-slot fault was a whole feature culled at every distance, so the
follow-up is to ask whether any other detail edge is unreachable. All
twenty-two ships with detail edges were swept across four headings and
three pitches, counting the blueprint's detail edges against the most that
ever queue. Nothing is unreachable; the counts below the total are cases of
viewing - only detail on faces pointing at us can be drawn - and adding the
pitch axis is what brought the Shuttle, Fer-de-Lance and Mamba up.

One apparent fault was mine. The Constrictor reported 6 detail edges and 0
queued at every heading, which looked like the slot fault repeating. All six
decorate face 9, whose normal is (0,-27,0) - straight down - so they are on
the hull's underside and only visible from below; a negative pitch queues
all six. The face's normal points outward and the check was right.

That is the sixth probe of mine to be wrong before the code was, and the
same mistake as the docking slot from the other direction: last time I
measured the outline and missed a hole in the middle, this time one axis of
the camera and missed a hemisphere. Both were fixed by asking what the
measurement cannot see. 263 tests pass.

benchmark: Refine the sampled 68882 frequency calibration

Use 90 net cycles per iteration after subtracting integer-loop
costs. The previous factor implied 89.533 cycles and measured
24.87-24.88 MHz on a 25 MHz A3000 with the correct PAL oscillator.

Apply the empirical calibration across CPU models and cache settings.

events.message:
benchmark: Stabilize CPU and FPU frequency sampling

Require at least 1 ms of net loop work within 2 ms samples. Increase
the loop-count limit and avoid overflow when normalizing timings.

Subtract an established baseline loop to cancel fixed costs that
a tiny loop may miss. Keep balanced sample order and varying counts;
report the tiny-baseline comparison and estimated bias in DEBUG.

events.title: main: Find the bundled Identify library when LIBS: misses it

main: Find the bundled Identify library when LIBS: misses it

Launching from a floppy under an existing Workbench can miss Identify
because LIBS: still points at the boot disk. Fall back to the program's
Libs directory after the normal library lookup fails.

Use PROGDIR: on AmigaOS 2.0 and later. On Kickstart 1.3, derive an
absolute path from the Workbench startup lock or CLI program name,
then restore the current directory and release temporary locks.
Log library lookup attempts and the opened version in DEBUG mode.

hardware: Preserve 68040 identity when an FPU is present

Emulators can provide a 68040 FPU without implementing its MMU.
Keep the detected CPU as 68040 in both MMU detection paths instead
of relabeling it EC040 and suppressing its FPU frequency.

MMU availability remains independent of the CPU classification.

events.title: benchmark: Measure Dhrystone in interrupt-disabled chunks
events.message:
benchmark: Measure Dhrystone in interrupt-disabled chunks

Calibrate with interrupts enabled, then target 75 ms chunks with a
90 ms rejection limit. Let pending interrupts run between chunks
while keeping task switching disabled and Dhrystone state intact.

events.message:
gui: Add explicit PAL and NTSC display tooltypes

Add DISPLAY=PAL and DISPLAY=NTSC to open a separate HIRES screen with
an explicit monitor ID and matching height. This lets users bypass
AmigaOS Mode Promotion for xSysInfo while keeping their system setting.

Preserve AUTO, WINDOW, and SCREEN behavior. On Kickstart 1.3, the new

Require 50 us of loop work, limit measured samples to 200 us, and

benchmark: Use 18-cycle timing for 68000 Fast RAM samples

Use the documented eight-cycle SUBQ.L and ten-cycle taken branch
for differential 68000/68010 frequency samples in Fast RAM. The old

gui: Use dashes for unavailable processor frequencies

events.title: hardware: Decode every Gayle ID bit from bit 7
events.message:
hardware: Decode every Gayle ID bit from bit 7

Gayle supplies each serial ID bit in bit 7. Mask that fixed bit
before shifting it into position; shifting the mask discarded
later bits and displayed 80 instead of D0 or D1.

Protect the serial ID sequence with Forbid/Permit and balance both
early returns. Leave Amiga model detection unchanged.
events.author: reinauer

events.title: Fix the visibility scale that stopped docking slots being drawn
events.message:
Fix the visibility scale that stopped docking slots being drawn

Every visibility byte in the blueprints is on a 0-31 scale, which is the
same scale the original uses for a ship's distance: LL9 part 2 takes z_hi
and shifts it right three more times, so XX4 = z_hi >> 3. Ours divided the
scaled distance by 512 and clamped it to 0-7, which is eight times too
steep.

No detail edge could survive its own gate unless its visibility was 7 or
less, so every detail above that was culled at every distance - including
the Coriolis docking slot, which carries 30, and the Dodo's. The station
now draws 4 slot edges at the heading where the slot faces us, where it
queued exactly 0 before.

This is very likely the reported wobble: a slot appearing and vanishing
changes what the station looks like as it turns, and a missing slot is far
more visible than a two-percent shear.

The method note matters more than the fix. Two rounds went into a shear I
could not show was visible, while a whole missing feature was one line away
in the same file. A silhouette's bounding box is blind to a hole in the
middle of the shape; measuring a feature means measuring the thing the
feature is. The "queued detail edges" count found it in one line, having
been printed all along. 263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Move the frame rebuild into Core and prove it with a test that can fail
events.message:
Move the frame rebuild into Core and prove it with a test that can fail

Last round committed the basis fix as unproven because the station's silhouette
measured identically before and after. That conclusion was wrong: the ship
viewer auto-frames, so the station renders at the same size whatever
--viewer-distance is passed, and every before/after pair I compared was of a
constant. I was measuring my own scaling rather than the shear.

The rebuild moved into Core.Maths.RigidFrame, where tests can reach it, and
RigidFrameTests rolls a ship for 480 frames through the real Mvs5 and Tidy and
checks after every tidy that the vectors are unit length, mutually
perpendicular, and have determinant 1.

The test is known to be capable of failing: restoring the old behaviour -
normalising each vector independently - makes two of its three cases fail
immediately. Measured before: lengths 0.90 to 1.00, angles out by 2.3%,
determinant 0.82 to 0.98. After: all exactly 1.

The defence that works is not care but a control. The screenshot comparison
would have been caught at once by asking what it was supposed to differ from.
263 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Make the render basis rigid by Gram-Schmidt
events.message:
Make the render basis rigid by Gram-Schmidt

Measured over 96 frames of rolling, the basis the renderer builds from a
ship's orientation vectors is not orthonormal: |nose| swings between 0.91
and 1.00, |side| between 0.90 and 1.00, and the determinant between 0.82
and 0.98. A basis like that is not a rotation, and the transform it defines
shears the whole body differently as the ship rolls.

The original's TIDY normalises by NORM, which divides by an approximated
square root, so its basis is not exactly rigid either - which it can afford
because it draws a wireframe. Filling the faces exposes it.

FromEliteOrientation now puts the vectors through Gram-Schmidt: the nose
is kept as the reference direction and its length is the scale, the roof is
made perpendicular to it, and the side is their cross product.

What is not claimed: I could not demonstrate a visible difference. The
station's silhouette area and bounding box measure the same to the pixel
before and after, so whatever the shear was doing is below what these
measurements resolve and I have not confirmed it is what the player is
seeing. The defect is real and measured; the improvement is reasoned and
unproven, and committed on that basis rather than described as a fix for
the reported symptom. 260 tests pass.

events.title: Record the trader-to-pirate rule as a subsystem, not an adjustment
events.message:
Record the trader-to-pirate rule as a subsystem, not an adjustment

The comment sweep found a rule that is not a constant to correct but a
piece of the AI we do not have, and it is written up with the code quoted
rather than implemented this round.

TACTICS reads a ship's behaviour from its NEWB flags and rewrites them
during play: bit 0 is a trader, which becomes a pirate on a 39% roll per
frame where the advanced versions use 20%; bit 1 is a bounty hunter, which
only turns on us if our legal status is 40 or more. Everything else the
sweep found was a threshold or a branch; this decides what a ship is.

Getting it right means the roles come from the NEWB flags rather than the
spawn table, a "trader" becomes a much smaller category than our spawner
assumes - only the Shuttle and the Transporter carry the bit - the
per-frame roll needs the care the Anaconda's did, including a comparison
direction I got wrong there and only a rate-measuring test caught, and it
interacts with the legal status. A wrong rate here would change what every
ship in the sky does, so it is left for a round that can give it that kind
of test. 260 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Use the disc's docking cone and the source's own ratios
events.message:
Use the disc's docking cone and the source's own ratios

The comment sweep found a threshold that is version-specific and we had
the wrong version: the disc tests CMP #86 for a 26.3 degree safe cone of
approach where every other version tests CMP #89 for 22.0. Ours was
0.9272, the cosine of 22.0 - the other versions' value, in a hand-written
constant whose comment named the wrong angle.

The level check was wrong the same way. The original tests
|roofv_x_hi| >= 80 against vectors whose unit is 128, so the threshold is
80/128; ours was 0.8028, commented as 36.6 degrees and near neither the
constant nor the angle. Both are now the source's own ratios.

The lesson is how the constants were derived. A cosine of an angle looks
like a faithful port and reads like one, but it is a step removed from
what the original tests, and that step is where the error came in - twice,
in adjacent constants in the same file. The original's own unit is the
thing to encode, because it can be checked against the source character for
character.

Eighteenth fault of the session, and both were found by reading the
source's comments rather than its instructions. 260 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Close the disc-only sweep: the asteroid fix is in our variant
events.message:
Close the disc-only sweep: the asteroid fix is in our variant

The last disc-only branch, and the one where the question was which disc
we follow rather than what the code says. The Stairway to Hell disc - the
_VARIANT=2 this port follows - takes the NOP branch, patching out the
development jump that forced traders to spawn, so the code falls through
to the path that spawns rocks. Asteroids do appear in the build we port,
and they appear in ours: ChooseJunk rolls them at the original's rates and
FlightSim checks for junk before ships, as the original does.

So there was nothing to change, which closes the sweep with no open items.
Every IF _DISC_FLIGHT branch in the shared library is now read and
classified: three rules we already had, six we were missing, four pieces of
platform plumbing, and this one variant question.

Six faults from one systematic read, after three rounds in which the same
faults arrived one at a time from symptoms. When a project has a
conditionally-compiled source, the set of branches for your build is
enumerable, and enumerating it beats waiting for each one to bite. 260
tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Release a Worm when an Anaconda is hit by the tactics roll
events.message:
Release a Worm when an Anaconda is hit by the tactics roll

The next disc-only behavioural branch, and a rule we did not have at
all. CMP #ANA / BNE TN7 then JSR DORND / CMP #200 / BCC TN7, and a Worm:
on this build always a Worm, with no second roll, because the disc's
branch is the narrow one - "in the disc version, Anacondas can only spawn
Worms, while in the advanced versions they can also spawn Sidewinders".

It runs on every frame the tactics do, so an Anaconda that survives a
while fills the sky with Worms, which is what the source's own 22%
describes. The released ship gets an AI flag of %11110001 from the shared
TN6 path.

The branch direction was a trap: writing the roll as < 200 rather than
>= 200 - reading "BCC skips" as "below the threshold is the interesting
case" - the test caught it by measuring 77% instead of 22%. On this
codebase the direction of a comparison is as easy to get wrong as the
condition around it, and the defence is to measure the rate.

Also notes the remaining disc-only branch as open: a bug fix for the first
version of disc Elite in which asteroids never appeared, where whether the
Stairway to Hell variant includes the fix is the thing to establish.
Seventeenth fault of the session. 260 tests pass.

they are about how a 1982 machine with two banks of memory works rather

docked overlay, and hyp branches on the current view. A branch being

events.title: Protect the Constrictor, and turn the station hostile when we shoot an innocent
events.message:
Protect the Constrictor, and turn the station hostile when we shoot an innocent

Listing every IF _DISC_FLIGHT branch turned up two missing rules in the
laser code.

The Constrictor can only be harmed by a military laser, and then for a
quarter of the damage - the disc's branch says so outright. Ours took full
damage from any laser, which made the mission's target an ordinary fight
and the military laser pointless for the only enemy it exists for.

Shooting an innocent makes the station hostile. The original's ANGRY tests
bit 5 of the ship's NEWB flags and calls AN2 when it is set. We had no such
rule, so shooting traders was free: the station went on letting us dock.
It now turns hostile with a speed of 10 and an AI flag of %11111000, and a
hostile station refuses us. ANGRY also switches the target's own AI on and
raises its acceleration to 2, so a trader that survives a shot stops being
a bystander.

This is the rule the E% flags were extracted for: bit 5 decides it, so the
flags now do two jobs - the legal status and the station's temper.

Checked and already right: the Constrictor's AI flag is %11111001, matching
ours byte for byte. Fifteenth fault of the session. 257 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Resolve where the disc's bounty hunters get their AI flag
events.message:
Resolve where the disc's bounty hunters get their AI flag

The answer is a clean negative that explains itself. Every STA INWK+32 in
the spawn code is guarded away from the disc: walking the conditional stack
at each of the five, the only one that runs on this build is the
Constrictor's. So the disc's lone bounty hunter is spawned by TYA / JSR
NWSHP with no AI flag store at all - the line that sets it in every other
version is simply not assembled, exactly as the E.C.M. chance is not. The
value therefore comes from whatever the ship's slot already held;
reproducing that faithfully means modelling the ship-slot workspace rather
than the spawn, which is noted rather than guessed at.

The one store that does run is a check on our own data: the Constrictor is
given %11111001, E.C.M. and an aggression of 60 out of 63, and our
Missions.ConstrictorAiFlag is 0b1111_1001 - the same byte. Nothing had
checked that value against the source and it is right.

Three faults in a row have been version-guard faults, so the rule is now
recorded: read the IF above a suspicious instruction before changing
anything, because on this build the guard is evidence. 255 tests pass.

Take the E.C.M. off disc bounty hunters

The 22% chance of a lone bounty hunter carrying E.C.M. is guarded by
every version except this one, and the source says so in as many words:
"Lone bounty hunters in the disc version don't have E.C.M., while in the
other versions they have a 22% chance of having E.C.M." Ours had the
chance, which is the cassette behaviour. An E.C.M. is not a small thing on
a bounty hunter: it is a second health bar that shrugs off missiles.

The guard is the lesson. The line that mattered was not the instruction
but the IF above it, and reading the instruction alone gives the wrong
answer - the same shape as the Transporter's BEQ TT222 and the enhanced
AI flag, which makes three faults that were each a correct reading of a
line and a wrong reading of the version it belongs to.

disc's own. 255 tests pass.

events.title: Drive the legal status from the E% flags, as the original does
events.message:
Drive the legal status from the E% flags, as the original does

The table extracted last round is wired in. Ship carries its NewbFlags,
the game stamps each ship with its type's flags from the disc's E% table as
it spawns, and the flight loop tests bit 6 for a cop and bit 5 for an
innocent - the original's rule, replacing the AiFlag < 0x80 heuristic that
had been standing in for it.

The flags make sense of ships we knew: the Shuttle is a trader innocent,
the Transporter is a trader innocent cop, the Cobra and Python are
innocents carrying escape pods, and the Viper is a bounty hunter cop. The
Krait and Constrictor are hostile pirates with no innocent bit, which is
the case the old heuristic got right for the wrong reason: it treated
every hostile ship as fair game, so it could not tell a hostile pirate from
a hostile cop. A Viper that comes after us and a Krait that does are now
treated differently.

Tests cover both halves: one cop makes us a fugitive at once, an innocent
is worth one point, and a hostile ship with neither flag changes nothing
however hostile it is. 255 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Read the cop flags from the disc's E% table
events.message:
Read the cop flags from the disc's E% table

The cop flag comes from bit 6 of a ship's NEWB flags, whose defaults are
the disc's E% table - which is in the docked segment only, so the
extractor now reads it out of the assembled docked code into ships.json.

Where the table starts was decided by the ship registry rather than by the
listing: trying every candidate offset and asking which one puts the
source's own flag values on the type numbers xx21.asm registers them at
gives exactly one answer, at 0x445A - Shuttle 9, Transporter 10, Cobra 11,
Python 12, Viper 16, Krait 19, Constrictor 31 all together, which no
neighbouring offset does. It agrees with the disc's own COPS symbol for
the Viper.

So the cops are the Transporter and the Viper, where the previous
approximation had only the Viper: right about the ship that comes after
you, wrong about the other.

The listing's labels really are offset from its values - the row saying
"Transporter" carries the Shuttle's flags - so reading labels gives one
answer and reading values another, and they agreed with our type numbers
on different entries. Neither is trustworthy; the registry arbitrates.
254 tests pass.

events.title: Halve the legal status on every arrival, as SOLAR does
events.message:
Halve the legal status on every arrival, as SOLAR does

The other half of the legal status, and the half that was missing
entirely. SOLAR halves FIST with an LSR on every arrival, in the source's
own words "making us less bad... so every time we arrive in a new system,
our legal status improves a bit". Bit 0 is shifted out, so a status of 1
becomes 0 after a single jump.

Ours never decayed, which made a record permanent: a commander who became
a fugitive once could never be clean again, however far he flew. With last
round's fix to the rate, the whole arc is now the original's - one point an
innocent, fifty to be a fugitive, one cop to be a fugitive outright, and
half of it back per jump away.

The E% extraction stays open and the roadmap now records exactly where it
stands: the table's named entries sit at 0, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 15, 18 and
30, which is not one byte per ship type, and the two readings of the
listing agree with our type numbers on different entries, so they cannot
both be right. Settling it wants the disc image or the loader's ROM_E%,
not a guess at the alignment. 254 tests pass.

events.title: Fix the legal status threshold and the rate it rises at
events.message:
Fix the legal status threshold and the rate it rises at

Two faults in becoming wanted, both found by reading STATUS and the flight
loop.

The threshold is 50, not 24: STATUS prints Clean for 0 and chooses on
CPY #50, so 1 to 49 is an offender and 50 and up is a fugitive. Our
mapping was also dead in the middle - both the < 24 and < 48 branches led
to "Fugitive" - so a commander became a fugitive at half the legal status
the original needs.

The increase is not a flat 4. The original adds exactly 1 for an ordinary
innocent, so fifty of them make a fugitive by degrees, and killing a cop
sets the status to at least 64 with an ORA, making us a fugitive outright.
Ours made every kill worth four: too fast for traders and too slow for
police, with no notion of a cop at all.

One part is approximated and recorded as open. The cop flag comes from bit
6 of the ship's NEWB flags, from an E% table we do not extract, so the cop
is identified by type and only the Viper is marked. Extracting E% would be
the faithful fix and wants its own round, because the table's indexing is
not a simple one-byte-per-type list.

Thirteenth fault of the session. The test that pinned the old threshold
now checks the boundary at 49 and 50 exactly. 253 tests pass.

events.title: Rebuild the missions when a commander is loaded
events.message:
Rebuild the missions when a commander is loaded

CommanderSave carries MissionStatus and writes it on every save, and the
constructor rebuilds the missions from it - but Load, the path that runs
when a save is read, rebuilt the commander, the flight model and the market
and left the missions empty. A commander who saved while carrying the plans
or partway through hunting the Constrictor loaded with no mission at all:
the offer would come round again from the start and OfferMission2 would
refuse. The four bits a save had been writing all along were never read.

A test loads a commander mid-mission-2 and checks all four bits come back.

Setting that test up took three attempts, and each mistake was the same
shape: building the state by hand instead of letting the methods build it.
The first set CarryingPlans directly, which left the mission-2 bit set and
produced %1110 where the game produces %1010; the second tried docking,
which rebuilds the missions from the status byte and discarded the setup.
Going through PickUpPlans at Ceerdi gave the right state first time.

Twelfth fault of the session found by reading the source against passing
code. 253 tests pass.

Map the whole mission trail and record it

After two rounds of finding mission faults, the entire trail was mapped
from the data and checked against the source rather than spot-checked.
All twenty-five hints resolve to the systems the source names: four in the
first galaxy, eighteen in the second, the Constrictor at Orarra in the

The one thing that had to be checked rather than inferred is the Thargoid
intercept token, which sits at Xeveon (198,205) - a different system in the
third galaxy, where "the third galaxy" would have been the natural guess.

Checked and found correct alongside: the mission gating at 256 kills and
galaxies 0 and 1, the intercept chance of 56/256 while carrying the plans,
the delivery reward of 10,000 tenths, and that the data screen asks for the
hint at the system the commander is docked at rather than the one the
charts point at. No faults this round. 252 tests pass.

events.title: Put mission 2's plans and delivery where the original does
events.message:
Put mission 2's plans and delivery where the original does

Both of mission 2's systems were wrong, in a way that made the mission
impossible rather than merely inaccurate.

The plans are at (215,84) in the third galaxy - Ceerdi, index 83 - which
is what DOENTRY checks with CMP #2, CMP #215 and CMP #84. The code reused
the Constrictor's system instead, which is Orarra at index 193 of the
second galaxy: a different galaxy and a different system, so the pickup
condition could never hold anywhere.

The delivery is at (63,72) in the third galaxy - Birera, index 36, the
system the mission text names - which is what DEBRIEF2 tests. The code
delivered to Lave in the first galaxy, so the delivery could never be made
either.

Between them the whole of mission 2 was unreachable. The chain now runs:
status byte 6 on the way, 10 carrying the plans, 2 once delivered, with
the Thargoid intercept chance at 56/256 while carrying them.

Eleventh fault of the session. The tests covered PickUpPlans and
DeliverPlans as functions and did so correctly, but every one passed them
the Constrictor's system with the Constrictor's galaxy, so the predicate
was never asked about the place it was for. 252 tests pass.
