events.title: Pay the Constrictor mission at the debriefing, and award its kill points
events.message:
Pay the Constrictor mission at the debriefing, and award its kill points

KILLSHP does one thing when the Constrictor dies: it sets bit 1 of TP to
mark mission 1 as completed. Everything else happens in DEBRIEF the next
time a debriefing is attended at a station - it clears bit 0, awards 256
kill points with INC TALLY+1, pays 50000 tenths through MCASH, and prints
the thank you token.

Ours paid the 5,000 credits at the kill and never awarded the 256 kill
points at all. The points matter more than they look: 256 is exactly the
threshold that makes a commander Competent, so the debrief is what
qualifies him for the next mission's offer, and the chain could not have
advanced correctly for a commander who was not already Competent.

It also explains the status byte. KILLSHP sets only bit 1, so between the
kill and the debriefing the missions read %11 - objective done, mission
still in progress - where ours jumped straight to %10.

Checked and found correct while reading: the reward is 50,000 tenths,
which is the 5,000.0 Cr the comment gives, and the rating thresholds
match the documented table exactly - 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 2560,
6400. Tenth fault of the session found by reading the source against
passing code. 252 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Require the galaxy for a mission hint with bit 7 set
events.message:
Require the galaxy for a mission hint with bit 7 set

PDESC's criteria test has an order. It matches the system number, then
requires bits 0-6 of RUGAL to equal the current galaxy, and only then looks
at bit 7. So bit 7 means "no mission needed yet", not "any galaxy" - and
ours read it as a shortcut past the galaxy test, returning the hint before
checking the galaxy at all.

Three hints carry the bit and the fault showed on two: Teorge is in the
first galaxy, which is where a commander starts, so checking it there
passes either way; Arredi and Anreer are in the third galaxy and need no
mission, so they were appearing in every galaxy at systems 100 and 41,
which in most galaxies are ordinary systems with nothing to do with the
Constrictor.

The test checks each of the three in its own galaxy and in one it does not
belong to, and that the mission's own trail still requires the mission.

Ninth fault of the session found by reading the source against passing
code. Like the stock gate, no test went near the disagreement: the hint
tests covered the trail systems, which all need the mission, and the one
always-bit hint they covered was Teorge in galaxy 0. 252 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Make the equipment stock gate the original's jump, not a clamp
events.message:
Make the equipment stock gate the original's jump, not a clamp

EQSHP adds three to the tech level and compares against #12, setting the
count to fourteen if it is at least that - a jump, not a cap. So a tech
level of 9 stocks fourteen items rather than twelve, and 10 stocks
fourteen rather than thirteen: the two levels before the cap stock the
whole list, lasers included. Tech levels 0 to 8 agree with a smooth
clamp, which is nine of the fifteen and why the clamp looked right.

A test now walks every tech level, checking the count and that the gate
agrees with it - the nth item stocked and the one after not - and pins
the step itself by checking that tech 9 sells military and mining lasers
where tech 8 does not.

Eighth fault of the session found by reading the source against code that
already passed its tests. This one had no test of its own: the gate was
only exercised incidentally, by tests that happened to use tech levels 4
and 8, both of which agree. 251 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Set the large cargo bay to 37 tonnes, as EQSHP does
events.message:
Set the large cargo bay to 37 tonnes, as EQSHP does

EQSHP sets CRGO to 37 for a large cargo bay and says so in its own
comment. Ours set 35 and checked for 35 when deciding whether one was
already fitted, so the hold was two tonnes short of the original's and a
commander with a genuine bay could have been sold a second one.

Checked at the same time and found correct: the starting capacity of 22
(the commander template is EQUB 22 + (15 AND Q%), and Q% is zero for the
Cobra, so a bay is worth fifteen tonnes), the four-missile rack, the
energy unit doubling the recharge rate rather than raising a maximum,
100.0 credits and a full tank to start. The energy unit is worth noting
because the obvious guess - that it raises maximum energy - is wrong: it
sets ENGY, and the banks recharge at ENGY + 1, so it doubles the rate.

Seventh fault of the session found by reading the source against code
that already passed its tests, and this one had a test asserting 35 -
the same fault written from the code. 250 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Give the escape pod the whole of the original's rescue
events.message:
Give the escape pod the whole of the original's rescue

The original's ESCAPE routine empties the cargo hold, clears the
criminal record, spends the pod and delivers a replacement ship with a
full tank. Ours emptied the hold and spent the pod only.

The fuel is the one that matters: being picked up with an empty tank and
no cargo leaves a commander unable to jump anywhere and with nothing to
trade, which is a dead end the original's rescue deliberately avoids.
Clearing the record is the other half of a fresh start and is what stops
the rescuing station being hostile.

Two tests cover it, and neither existed before, which is why nothing had
noticed. Sixth of the session's faults found by reading the source
against code that already passed its tests. 250 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: fix multiple status flag returns in new codegens
events.message: fix multiple status flag returns in new codegens
events.author: irmen

events.title: Stop selling from restocking the market
events.message:
Stop selling from restocking the market

Every reference to the original's availability table, checked rather
than remembered: tt219 subtracts what you buy, var zeroes the alien items
on its way past, and tt219 and tt151 read it. The only code anywhere in
the library that adds to availability is in the NES version's own sell
path, so on the BBC disc what you sell is gone - it does not come back on
the market, and the cash is the whole of what you get for it.

Ours added it back, which let a commander buy a system's stock out, sell
it back and repeat, and made a market's availability drift upwards the
more you traded in it.

A fifth test was asserting it: SellingReturnsCreditsAndRestocksTheMarket
did what its name said and passed because the code did too. It now
asserts the original's behaviour and also pins what availability is after
buying, which nothing had checked.

Five tests this session have been found encoding a fault rather than
catching one, and every one was written from the code as it stood. The
tests that have caught things were written after reading the source. The
distinction is order, not diligence. 248 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add game-loop tests, which found that redocking rerolled the market
events.message:
Add game-loop tests, which found that redocking rerolled the market

Turning the last two rounds' habit - fly the game, then write down what
flying found - into tests paid for itself on the first run.

GameLoopTests covers the whole loop: dock, trade, jump, arrive, dock,
sell; that each system has its own market and the chart agrees about
which galaxy we are in; that a galactic jump moves the galaxy number,
system, market and chart together and lands at the nearest system to
(96,96); that eight jumps return to the first galaxy; and that the jump
refuses a system beyond the tank.

It found that docking rebuilt the market. The original's GVL has exactly
one caller in the whole source - the arrival after a hyperspace jump -
and the market screen prices from what that left behind, so the market is
fixed while you are in the system. Ours let a commander reroll the prices
by launching and redocking, which the original does not offer.

A test was asserting it: DockingChangesTheMarketAndLaunchingKeepsIt did
what its name said and passed because the code did too. It now asserts
the original's behaviour. That is the fourth test this session found to
be encoding a fault rather than catching one, and each was written from
the code rather than from the source - which is what a test is supposed
to prevent. 248 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Rebuild the sky after a galactic jump
events.message:
Rebuild the sky after a galactic jump

Flying a session through a galactic jump showed the numbers were right -
new system, market, next jump - but the sky was not rebuilt.
UseGalacticHyperdrive changes the session's system and nothing else, so
the planet, the sun and the station of the galaxy just left stayed where
they were. No test covered the transition and every screenshot of a
galactic jump showed a system that was correct on paper.

The status screen fires the drive, so it now rebuilds the flight scene's
system and bubble when the jump succeeds; ResetBubble became public for
it, which is the honest shape since the sky belongs to the flight scene.

A false alarm is recorded too. The same probe seemed to show the chart
stuck on galaxy 1 after jumping to galaxy 2, which looked like the
previous round's bug returning. It was the probe's comment that was
wrong: GalaxyNumber is zero-based, so 1 is the second galaxy, whose
systems begin at Ausis with Orarra at index 193 exactly as RUPLA says.
Checked before changing anything. 243 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix the galactic hyperdrive, which rotated the wrong seeds
events.message:
Fix the galactic hyperdrive, which rotated the wrong seeds

The original's GHY rotates the galaxy's seed table one bit to the left,
raises the galaxy number and finds the nearest system to (96, 96), which
is where it always arrives. Ours rotated the current system's seeds and
kept the same system number - an unrelated operation, so the system it
landed on was arbitrary. Rotating a system's seeds is not rotating the
galaxy's, the same confusion the charts had.

Measured after the fix, jumping from Lave: galaxy 2 gives ORORRA at
(96,95), galaxy 3 XEINES, galaxy 4 SOENISTI, each the nearest system to
the arrival point.

Two tests were pinning the bug - the third time this session a test has
encoded the fault rather than caught it. One asserted arrival at the same
system number, which was the fault written up as the specification; the
other asserted eight jumps return to the starting system, where the seeds
do return after eight bits but the commander lands at (96,96) every time
and so should end elsewhere. Both now assert the original's behaviour.

A verification script of mine was wrong too: checking the mission hints
against RUPLA's comments I had two systems in the wrong galaxy and read
the mismatch as a data fault. They are in galaxy 2, as the table and the
extracted criteria agree. 243 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Resolve the galaxy from the commander, not from the current system
events.message:
Resolve the galaxy from the commander, not from the current system

Flying the whole loop end to end turned up a bug the tests could not
have caught, because the one case they exercised is the one case where it
does not show.

Galaxy.GenerateGalaxy takes galaxy seeds and the callers were handing it
a system's. Measured: from system 0's seeds the generated galaxy matches
the real one in all 256 systems, but from system 7's, 100's or 255's it
differs in all 256. System 0's seeds are the galaxy's own, and every chart
screenshot the session had taken was of system 0, where the two coincide.

Once the commander has jumped anywhere, the short and long-range charts
drew a galaxy that does not exist, and the nearest-reachable-system search
- which is what H jumps to - picked its destination from that same
invented galaxy.

GameSession.SystemsInGalaxy resolves it from the commander's galaxy
number and the three call sites ask it. The name is not Galaxy, which
would shadow the class inside the session and did exactly that when first
written. Two tests pin it on the session, where the mistake was made:
four different systems must report the same 256, and from Lave the real
Lave at (20,173) with Diso and Leesti alongside. 242 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Start Coleco ADAM target architecture
events.message: Start Coleco ADAM target architecture
events.author: amypurple

events.title: Sweep every ship model, and give the hint-fitting rule tests
events.message:
Sweep every ship model, and give the hint-fitting rule tests

All 31 blueprints rendered in the ship viewer at a fixed heading and
pitch, laid out as a contact sheet and looked at, after the docked
screens' sweep turned up a fault. There is nothing to report: every
blueprint draws as a solid body, none is blank, inverted or collapsed,
and the sizes vary the way the blueprints do. It is a weak check - a
contact sheet cannot judge fine geometry - but it is the one that would
catch a blueprint whose faces had stopped reconstructing, which is what
the mesh builder is most exposed to.

The scaling rule behind last round's footer fix moved from the renderer
into EliteRemake.Core.Text.HintLine, where it can be tested, with four
tests covering a hint that fits, one that is scaled down, one that
cannot fit at any scale and degenerate inputs. The floor of one is
recorded where the rule lives: a line too small to read is worse than one
that is cut off, so the real answer to a hint that does not fit is a
shorter hint. 240 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Sweep every docked screen at a small window, and fix the footer hints
events.message:
Sweep every docked screen at a small window, and fix the footer hints

The settings screen's two faults only showed at 640x480, so every other
docked screen was rendered at that size and looked at. All seven were
laid out soundly - heading, data and footer inside the view, and the
short-range chart's fuel circle scaling with the window as it should.

One fault was shared: every screen's footer of key hints ran off the
right edge, because this remake's hints are longer than the original's.
The market's ran to eighty-four characters, which cannot be drawn legibly
at 640 pixels at any scale, so a scaling helper alone would have shrunk
it to unreadable rather than fixing it. The hints are now as terse as the
original's own - "F1-F3 SCREENS" rather than naming each screen - and
TextRenderer.DrawHintLine scales one down if it still overruns. The terse
text is what fixes it; the helper stops a future long hint clipping
silently.

The O CONTROLS hint was also missing from the status screen's footer,
which is how the settings screen is reached. 236 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix two settings-screen faults found by looking at it
events.message:
Fix two settings-screen faults found by looking at it

The rebinding would not have worked. SceneFactory.CreateFlightScene
loaded its own Settings and EliteGame loaded another for the settings
screen, so a rebind changed the screen's copy and left the flight scene
reading the old one - which looks exactly like rebinding silently doing
nothing. There is one instance now, owned by the shell and passed to
both.

The screen also ran off the top of a small window: the list began at a
fixed offset below the middle of the view, so at 640x480 the title and
first binding were above the top edge. It is laid out from the view now
and scaled to fit.

That second fix took two passes. The first chose a scale from a line
height, and the glyphs then did not fit inside the line height chosen;
the line height now follows from the scale instead. Both faults were
caught by rendering the screen at 640x480 and looking at it, which is the
only way either would have been noticed. 236 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add rebindable controls and a settings screen
events.message:
Add rebindable controls and a settings screen

The last piece of the agreed scope: the brief asked for a gamepad and
an authentic keyboard layout, the layout was in and rebinding was not.

Nothing here is a port - the original's keys were fixed - but the
defaults are the original's own keys, so a player who never opens the
screen gets the 1984 layout. The screen is reached from the status
screen rather than taking a red function key, so the original's own
screens keep the keys they had, and it walks the twelve bindings, rebinds
on ENTER, resets on R, saves on CTRL-S and leaves on ESCAPE. Escape
during a rebind cancels rather than binding Escape.

Bindings are held as key names and saved as JSON beside the commander
file, so the file is readable and a binding survives a key being added to
the enum. Anything unreadable gives the defaults back, and a binding
naming a key this build lacks falls back per binding. The arrow keys and
gamepad stay alongside the bound keys, because the original has two keys
for each direction and the arrows are one of them.

236 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Measure the frame cost, and separate it from the display's
events.message:
Measure the frame cost, and separate it from the display's

The first attempts at a frame rate gave 835 ms a frame and 1.2 fps,
which is a display that is not completing its swaps rather than anything
about the code. The report now times our own Update and Draw separately
from the wall-clock frame and prints both.

The budget is the simulation's own rate: 50 Hz, so 20 ms a frame. Our
work measures under 6 ms - 2.45 ms update plus 3.39 ms draw - and a
second run at 1920x1200 with twelve ships in the bubble came to 4.97 ms.
Roughly a quarter of the budget, with the remaining 747 ms of the frame
being the display.

--stress fills the bubble with ships so the worst case can be reached
rather than measured on a quiet system. The limit on the figure is
recorded: the stress run had only 122 triangles on screen, so the drawing
half is measured on a quiet view, though the simulation half is not.
236 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Wire the manual mis-jump, and test what witchspace holds
events.message:
Wire the manual mis-jump, and test what witchspace holds

Holding CTRL with the jump key now forces the jump to go wrong, ahead
of the random roll, which is how TT18 reaches MJP by two routes. The
original gates that key behind the author-names flag so its competition
code could record whether the feature had been used - an anti-cheat
measure for a 1984 contest, not a game rule - so the remake offers it.

The ambush moved from FlightScene into FlightSim.ArriveInWitchspace,
where it belongs and where it can be tested. A test checks that
witchspace holds four Thargoids and four Thargons and nothing else, with
no planet or sun, and whatever was in the bubble cleared away.

The one fault found was in the test: ForceMisjump is set before a jump
begins and consumed when the countdown ends, so clearing it part-way
through made the jump ordinary again. It is now asserted to be a
one-shot. 236 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Make the hyperspace tunnel visible, and record why it was not
events.message:
Make the hyperspace tunnel visible, and record why it was not

The rings were being drawn correctly all along. The fault was when the
screenshot was taken: HyperspaceCountdown is in simulation steps and the
shell takes up to ten of those per drawn frame, so a twenty-step
countdown begun at frame zero is over long before the frame-six
screenshot. Every marker placed inside the countdown branch vanished for
that reason, which is what several rounds of them eventually showed:

  - three bands drawn unconditionally all appeared, so the batch reaches
    the back buffer
  - a marker inside the countdown branch did not
  - forcing the condition to true made it appear

The harness fix is FlightScene.ShowTunnelFrames, which holds the tunnel
open for a given number of drawn frames; --jump sets it. The tunnel is
visible in screenshots/hyperspace.png and reads like the original's:
concentric rings crowded at the centre and opening out to the edge.

The ring spacing was also wrong for a dot rendering - a fixed count per
ring merges into a blob where the rings crowd - so the dots are spaced by
pixels instead, which keeps the inner rings readable. 234 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Port the hyperspace tunnel's ring layout, and add --jump
events.message:
Port the hyperspace tunnel's ring layout, and add --jump

HFS2's shape is ported: eight sets of rings, each ring twice the
radius of the one before, starting at 8 to 15 depending on the set and
stopping once a radius reaches 160. The rings are all on screen together
- a tunnel seen down its length rather than one ring animating - and are
drawn every frame of the countdown.

--jump starts a jump from the command line, so the effect can be looked
at without flying to the charts first, and the flight scene draws the
tunnel in place of the space view while the countdown runs.

It does not appear on screen yet. The countdown runs and the drawing
code is reached - traced - but none of its output survives to the saved
frame, and neither does a deliberate forty-pixel red block drawn from
the same place. That rules out the ring arithmetic and points at the
drawing itself; the Begin/End pair and the early return in
FlightScene.Draw are the places to look next. Recorded as it stands
rather than left as an unexplained absence. 234 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: [libromdata] WiiUPackage: Fix icon thumbnailing for packages extracted from a Wii U MLC.
events.message:
[libromdata] WiiUPackage: Fix icon thumbnailing for packages extracted from a Wii U MLC.

The TMD is sometimes not present in code/, and we were checking if the
TMD format version is 1 or higher. If there's no TMD, we can't check
this. Instead, check if "/meta/iconTex.tga" exists.

host_system_filename(): New function to construct a host system filename
for extracted packages.

open(): Use host_system_filename() for extracted packages.

file_exists(): New function to check if a file exists in the package.
events.author: GerbilSoft

events.title: Add witchspace: the mis-jump and the Thargoid ambush
events.message:
Add witchspace: the mis-jump and the Thargoid ambush

Witchspace was missing entirely. The disc version mis-jumps on a
random byte of 253 or more - TT18's CMP #253, which its comment gives
as a 0.78% chance, three rolls in 256 - and MJP then loads the Thargoid
blueprints, shows the tunnel again, resets the flight variables, sets
its MJ flag and spawns four Thargoids each with a Thargon in attendance.
There is no planet and no sun.

GameSession gains InWitchspace and the threshold with an IsMisjump test,
and CompleteHyperspace rolls for it: a mis-jump leaves the commander
where he was and still spends the fuel, because the jump happened and
simply did not arrive. FlightScene.ArriveInWitchspace clears the bubble,
suppresses the station and spawns the ambush through a new
FlightSim.SpawnAhead.

The disc's spawn loop is LDA #3 / CMP MANY+THG / BCS, so it keeps going
until there are four Thargoids, where the Master settles for three.

Two tests pin the threshold's boundaries and the 3-in-256 chance across
the whole byte range, so the rule cannot drift into an approximation.
234 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: [win32] RP_XAttrView: Disable hCboZAlg if the file system doesn't support compression.
events.message:
[win32] RP_XAttrView: Disable hCboZAlg if the file system doesn't support compression.

The checkbox was already disabled, but the dropdown was not.
events.author: GerbilSoft

events.title: Pin the combat and spawn constants after auditing them
events.message:
Pin the combat and spawn constants after auditing them

Audited every combat and spawn figure against the disc's own sources.
All were correct, and the readings are now recorded and pinned by a
test so they cannot drift to another version's the way seven equipment
prices had.

Checked: the four laser powers (POW 15, beam 15 with bit 7, Armlas 151
masked to 23, Mlas 50), heat 8 a shot and cooling 1 a frame from LASLI
and the main game loop, overheat at 242, one energy a shot, the bomb's
eight frames, and the spawn figures - 47% from the disc's CMP #120
against 90 elsewhere, 61% from CMP #100, z_hi 38 and an EV delay of 64.

The OOPS chain is right down to its corner case: a hit takes the shield
on the side the attacker's z_sign names, the remainder comes off the
energy banks, and the original's BEQ/BCS pair means energy reaching
exactly zero is death as well as going below it. TakeDamage reproduces
that with Energy > damage rather than >=.

The spawn thresholds were literals in the decision code; they are named
constants now, which is what let them be pinned. 232 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Make alien items unbuyable, as the original's var routine does
events.message:
Make alien items unbuyable, as the original's var routine does

Auditing the market against its source: the seventeen commodities match
the disc's QQ23 exactly in base price, economic factor, unit, base
quantity and mask, and both TT151's price and GVL's availability are
right, including the sign rule where a positive economic factor subtracts
the economy's effect on availability.

One rule was missing. The original's var routine, which both formulas
call, sets AVL+16 to zero on its way past, so alien items are never
available to buy in any system whatever the economy and random byte work
out to. They are what a Thargoid leaves behind and can only be scooped,
which is why the original always shows a dash against them. We were
computing their availability like any other commodity.

The test sweeps every economy and a spread of random bytes, because for
some of those the computed figure would otherwise be non-zero - so it
tests the rule rather than an accident. 231 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Use the disc version's equipment prices, not Elite-A's
events.message:
Use the disc version's equipment prices, not Elite-A's

Seven of the fourteen prices were the Elite-A table's. The disc's PRXS
gives the escape pod at 1000.0 Cr against our 100.0, the energy bomb at
900.0 against 90.0, the energy unit at 1500.0 against 700.0, the docking
computer at 1000.0 against 700.0, the galactic hyperdrive at 5000.0
against 3000.0, military lasers at 6000.0 against 1900.0 and mining
lasers at 800.0 against 250.0.

The two tables agree on the first seven items and on the last two names,
which is what made it easy to miss. Fuel is not a price at all: PRXS
holds a 1 there because EQSHP computes it as twice the light years, and
that doubling is what produces the table's tenths.

The test that should have caught this asserted the wrong numbers, in a
sample of eight that happened to include four of the seven. It now pins
the entire table by number, name and price, so another platform's table
cannot slip in again. 230 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Resolve the Constrictor's system from the galaxy's seeds, not a system's
events.message:
Resolve the Constrictor's system from the galaxy's seeds, not a system's

SceneFactory set sim.GalaxySeeds from Commander.CurrentSystem.Seeds,
which are a system's own seeds where ConstrictorTarget expects a
galaxy's. Measured in galaxy 1, the galaxy's seeds resolve Orarra as
system 193 and a system's seeds resolve the same Orarra as system 93 -
the right system by coincidence, in a galaxy a different length.

Missions.IsConstrictorSystem had the same confusion, passing a system's
seeds into ConstrictorTarget and so comparing a system against a target
resolved from itself; it now resolves from its galaxyNumber, with a
second overload for callers holding seeds already. FlightSim.SpawnMissionShip
duplicated the comparison by hand and now asks the predicate, so the two
cannot drift apart.

The new test drives the flight simulation rather than the decision: in
the Constrictor's system with the mission running it appears, and
elsewhere or with no mission it does not. 230 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Evaluate platform guards when reading RUPLA and RUGAL
events.message:
Evaluate platform guards when reading RUPLA and RUGAL

The hint overrun had a cause worth fixing rather than filtering
downstream: ParseMtin collected every EQUB in the file regardless of the
conditional branch it sat in, where ParseTokens alongside it had always
evaluated the guards. The extractor now returns 25 hints against 26
tokens - token 0 being the empty one - which is the disc's own table, and
the defensive filter added in the previous commit is removed so the
extractor is the single source of truth again.

An audit of the extractor's conditional handling, recorded in the
roadmap: the ship extractor uses a real assembler with expression
evaluation and is verified byte-for-byte against D.MOA-D.MOP, which is
why gating errors there cannot survive; the token extractor is a
hand-written parser and its two readers disagreed. The token text was
gated correctly all along - token 113 is empty in the disc because its
content is guarded away from us, and the Elite-A "CARGO VALUE:" text is
correctly not ours - so only the numeric tables were affected.

229 tests pass, extraction is deterministic, ship verification unchanged.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Seed system descriptions from their own seeds, and stop a hint overrunning RUTOK
events.message:
Seed system descriptions from their own seeds, and stop a hint overrunning RUTOK

PDESC reseeds the random generator from a system's s1 and s2 before
printing its extended description, "so we get the same extended
description for each system every time we call PDESC". Sharing one
running generator instead made every system read alike, because each
screen advanced it to a different point. EliteRandom gains a byte-wise
Reseed and the Data screen seeds it from the system's own seeds.

Lave was showing "ANCIENT" instead of a description because its hint
lookup returned token 26, and the disc's RUTOK has no token 26: the
Lave and Riedquat overrides sit inside the 6502SP and Executive platform
guards, so they are not in the BBC disc at all. The extractor reads those
tables without evaluating the guards and picked up 29 hints for 26
tokens. The hint list now keeps only entries the disc has a token for.

Recorded en route: the disc version only shows extended descriptions
when docked, because PDESC is not in the flight code at all - "due to
memory restrictions" - which our docked-only screen already satisfies.

229 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Port the AI's close-range disengage and nroll's graded turn
events.message:
Port the AI's close-range disengage and nroll's graded turn

The close-range rule the open-items list had been unable to find is at
the head of TACTICS part 7, at TA4. The original tests z_hi >= 3 and,
failing that, x_hi OR y_hi with bit 0 cleared, so a ship with z under
3 * 256 and both x and y under 2 * 256 heads away from us whatever its
aggression says. It shares the TA15 branch with the peaceful-ship case,
which is why searching for a separate routine missed it.

Without it a fight became a series of collisions, because an aggressive
ship kept flying straight through us.

Reading that part properly turned up a second gap: the disc version calls
nroll for its turn counters rather than setting a flat RAT. nroll doubles
the dot product and compares it against RAT2, leaving the counter with no
magnitude below the threshold so a ship does not twitch at an aim it is
already close to, and the full RAT at or above it. CounterFor does the
same, scaling the normalised float direction back into the original's
units where a unit vector's component is 96.

The test places a ship beside us facing along +x, so turning towards us
and turning away are distinguishable: its nose ends up at +0.91 close in
against -0.99 further out. 229 tests pass.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix MVT6's arithmetic, and the docking computer docks from every angle
events.message:
Fix MVT6's arithmetic, and the docking computer docks from every angle

Mvt6 ignored bit 7 of its A argument and got the small inputs wrong:
adding -62 to a coordinate of 0 came out as -319, and the wrapping cases
came out as 0, 1 and 514 where they should be -255, -256 and -257. It now
computes the low 16 bits as one value, subtracts with a borrow into bit
16, and takes the sign from whichever operand is larger - which is the
source's own convention: bit 7 of A is the delta's sign and the return is
the result's sign with A's bits 0-6 preserved.

The visible symptom was that one direction of a roll turned 18.54 degrees
and the other 3.55, where both should be the 1/16 radian MVS5 applies.
The two directions are now mirrored at 3.50 and -3.55. It affected every
world rotation in the game.

The callers needed no change after all: the alp2 ^ 0x80 I had taken for
compensation is the original's own pre-complemented ALP2+1, which MVEIT
part 5 genuinely uses for that one call and not the others.

With the rotation symmetric the faithful counter scale works too, so
StepsPerCounter is 16 - a counter of m is m frames of MVS5's fixed step -
and the deliberate sixteen-times-small departure recorded two rounds ago
is gone. The test that pinned the departure now pins the faithful
behaviour.

Docking, nine approaches of ten: every case that used to fly away for
ever or park a hundred units off the slot axis now docks, and the ones
that already worked dock in a third of the frames. The tenth arrives
perfectly - one unit of lateral offset - and collides on a 0.9% margin
because the station is mid-roll and its slot faces us at 0.890 against
the 0.8988 the check wants.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record that MVT6 ignores the sign it is given
events.message:
Record that MVT6 ignores the sign it is given

Probed at byte level: with a coordinate of zero, Mvt6 returns the same
result whichever sign A carries, and for the 0x80 case a magnitude of 319
where the delta was 62. The visible symptom is that one direction of a
roll turns 18.54 degrees and the other 3.55, where both should be 3.55;
the underflow path is reached only when the angle and the coordinate have
opposite signs. It affects every world rotation in the game.

A correct 16-bit implementation was written and verified in isolation -
it returns the exact magnitudes, including the 255/256/257 wrap cases -
but it cannot land on its own: the three call sites compensate for the
present behaviour with their own sign juggling, so fixing Mvt6 alone
reverses every turn and breaks the missile, counter-direction and docking
tests together. The roadmap records the three ordered steps the real fix
needs and the tests that will catch it.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Settle the energy bomb's exemptions, and add a frame-rate harness
events.message:
Settle the energy bomb's exemptions, and add a frame-rate harness

The energy bomb question is closed from the source rather than from a
grep. In main_flight_loop_part_5_of_16 the disc version's exemption list
is exactly one entry - the space station - and the Thargoid and
Constrictor exemptions sit inside _MASTER_VERSION/_C64/_APPLE/_NES and
_6502SP/_C64/_APPLE/_MASTER/_NES blocks, so neither is assembled into the
disc version. The code was already right: Thargoids and the Constrictor
are as vulnerable here as anything else.

Performance now has a harness: the game prints how long its frames
actually took when it exits after --exit-after frames. No number yet -
on this display it never reaches 200 drawn frames in 100 seconds, which
is not representative of a real session, so the figure has to be taken
interactively. That limitation is recorded rather than the item being
left as an unqualified "never measured".
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Measure the counter scale to the bottom, and keep the working one
events.message:
Measure the counter scale to the bottom, and keep the working one

A counter is a number of frames of MVS5's fixed 1/16 radian step, so the
faithful turn for a counter of m is m * 16 world-rotation units - one
step is exactly 1/(16*256) of a radian in that unit. Tried, and it fits
the source's own numbers: counters of 1 and 2 turned the world 3.55 and
6.95 degrees against the 3.58 and 7.16 the source implies.

It also cannot work as things stand. The angle has to come back through
RollAngle, whose rate is a byte: the deviation from the centre of 128
cannot exceed 127 and the routine divides by four, so the angle never
exceeds 31, about 6.93 degrees. The measured turn duly saturates at 6.95
for counters of 2, 4 and 8 alike. Turning further needs the world
rotation applied once per step, as MVS5 applies it to the orientation
vectors, rather than asked for one big angle.

With the faithful scale the autopilot's fixed +/-2 counters are sixteen
times more powerful than its control loop expects, and docking regressed
from three successes in five to one in five. The smaller scale is kept
deliberately - a docking computer that cannot dock is worse than a
counter scale that is numerically wrong - and a test now pins it so the
departure stays a decision. The measurements and the shape of the real
fix are in docs/ROADMAP.md.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record what the counter magnitude really is, and where docking still fails
events.message:
Record what the counter magnitude really is, and where docking still fails

A counter is a number of frames of turning, not an angle: MVEIT part 8
calls MVS5 once for each frame the counter is non-zero, and MVS5 turns
by a fixed 1/16 radian. SetCounters reads the magnitude as the angle,
which is right for DOCKIT's counters of 2 and wrong for large ones.

Also records the measured shape of the remaining off-axis failure: the
refine logic's deadband is RAT2 = 6, and a station 107 units off the slot
axis is only rollA = 3 off centre, so the autopilot corrects nothing and
arrives with a lateral offset the docking check will not accept. Offsets
up to 80 units dock; 100-300 reach the station and collide.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Make the docking computer's counters actually steer the ship
events.message:
Make the docking computer's counters actually steer the ship

The autopilot could only dock when the station was dead ahead, and flew
away for ever otherwise. Four faults, three of them in the flight model:

The counters DOCKIT writes are now applied as counters: a counter's
magnitude is the number of frames of the original's fixed 1/16 radian
step, so the world turns by that many angle units, instead of being fed
through the keyboard rate path where a small counter rounds away to no
turn at all.

The counter signs are not all the same way round. Measured on a station
above the centre line: roll 0x82 moves it left, roll 0x02 moves it right,
pitch 0x82 moves it down to the centre, pitch 0x02 moves it up and away.
The pitch counter is inverted relative to the roll counter, and assuming
one convention for both sent the autopilot into a diverging spiral. A
zero-magnitude counter is also no turn whatever its sign bit says, and
DOCKIT uses 128 - sign set, magnitude zero - as its "no turn" roll.

The sights threshold was out by six: RAT2 is 6/96 of a unit vector, not
six whole units, so the old test cancelled the controls for every target
that was not already centred.

And braking from rest wrapped the speed byte. The original's DEC/BNE/INC
tests the speed after the decrement; testing it before let a stopped ship
brake from zero to 255 and fire off at full speed. The autopilot brakes
every frame while lining up, so this alone made it shoot past the very
station it was docking with.

Six approaches tested: dead ahead docks, two more now dock from off to
one side, and the remaining four reach the station within 240 units
before hitting it. 227 tests pass.

events.title: Show the station's docking slot, and make the dashboard follow the window
events.message:
Show the station's docking slot, and make the dashboard follow the window

The slot was invisible for two separate reasons, and only the second of
them was a rendering fault.

The Coriolis blueprint draws its slot as four extra edges whose records
name face 0 twice. That is how the original says "this line belongs to
face 0" without describing an outline, and LL9 draws such an edge
whenever that face is visible - the Cobra Mk III uses the same trick for
its engine outline. A renderer that fills faces instead of drawing lines
paints straight over them. ShipMesh now finds those edges and
MeshRenderer draws them as a later layer than the faces, because no
depth sort can separate a slot from the face it is cut into.

The visibility rule was also wrong and was hiding the slot: LL9 reduces
the ship's z-distance to 0-7, not 0-31, so a station's slot (visibility
30) was culled until the station was nearly on top of us.

The second fault was that the station was created facing the wrong way.
The blueprint puts the slot in the station's +z face, and the original's
NWSPS turns the station right around as it creates it, so that the slot -
and not the blank rear - faces the player it has just been placed ahead
of. We never did, so the slot pointed off into space and could never be
seen or flown into. SystemArrival.CreateStation now does what NWSPS does,
and the whole thing is under test.

The dashboard had cached its layout at construction, so maximising the
window left it small and in the top-left corner; it now reads the layout
every frame, and its right-hand labels stop short of the screen edge
rather than being clipped.

The station's spin is unchanged: the original turns it by a fixed 1/16
radian a frame whenever its roll counter is non-zero, so no counter value
would slow it down. Measured at 3.58 degrees a frame, and pinned by a
test.

events.title: M68000: fire MFP Timer A again; zero divide stacks the next PC (120th)
events.message:
M68000: fire MFP Timer A again; zero divide stacks the next PC (120th)

Two regressions that stopped every PowerMonger world build:

- RaiseTimerA read TACR from mfpRegisters, but since the 105th pass TACR
  writes go to the tacr field, so Timer A never raised. PowerMonger's world
  build waits in $1ae40 for a flag its Timer A handler clears.
- DIVU/DIVS divide-by-zero stacked the instruction's own address (112th).
  Hatari's 68000 path stacks the next instruction (gencpu.c incpc before
  exception_cpu(5); exception_oldpc is only for the 68020+ tables), and
  PowerMonger's vector-5 handler is a bare rte, so it re-ran the divide
  forever. Restored PC + 2 + extension bytes. The one SingleStepTests
  zero-divisor vector (80ef) was already skipped for its flags.

Selftest 1000051 pass / 0 wrong / 9 skip; verify 5000000 passes; PowerMonger
differential gates (repro93-97, diff_pm98/99, diff_4bc8, kind2) all pass.

events.title: Find the docking fault: the counters go through the wrong path
events.message:
Find the docking fault: the counters go through the wrong path

Two measurements together identify it, and it is not in DOCKIT at all but in
how the counters reach the flight model.

The roll works: a counter of 100 moves a target's x from 3000 to 754. But the
rate-to-angle conversion — the original's own, dividing the distance from the
centre of the rate range by four and halving again below eight — gives an angle
of zero for a rate of 126, which is what a counter of 2 produces. The table says
so directly: rate 128 gives 0, rate 126 gives 0, rate 100 gives 3, rate 1 gives
31.

So every turn the docking computer asks for, in PH1 and PH3 alike, is rounded to
nothing and the ship never turns. That is the whole of the off-axis failure: the
autopilot is not mis-steering, it is not steering.

The cause is that the counters go into the wrong path. That conversion belongs
to the keyboard: MVEIT part 5 turns the universe by the rates the keys produce.
DOCKIT's counters are not key rates — the original writes them into the ship's
data block at INWK+29 and INWK+30, which MVEIT part 8 applies, turning the ship
about its own axes by the counter's magnitude directly. Part 8 is a different
calculation, and a counter of 2 through part 8 is a real, if small, rotation.

The fix is therefore in FlightSim.SetRotationCounters rather than in
DockingComputer: rotate the universe by the counter magnitudes as MVEIT part 8
does, instead of translating them into rates for the keyboard path. The roadmap
records that as the next change, aimed by two measurements rather than by
reasoning.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix the docking pitch sign, measured rather than reasoned
events.message:
Fix the docking pitch sign, measured rather than reasoned

The measurement the last note asked for: setting a counter by hand and watching
where a target to the right and above actually goes.

  pitch 2, clockwise (bit 7 set)  rate 126  y 3000 -> 2960  to the centre
  pitch 2, anticlockwise          rate 130  y 3000 -> 3000  unmoved
  roll 2, clockwise               rate 126  x unmoved
  roll 2, anticlockwise           rate 130  x unmoved

The pitch sign was inverted: a clockwise counter is a rate below the centre of
the rate range, and with the world turning around a fixed ship that brings a
target above the centre line down to it. The previous round reasoned its way to
the same conclusion and reverted it for lack of evidence; this is the same
change with the evidence, and the test suite still passes.

The surprise is the second result. The roll moved the target's x by nothing at
all, under either direction. A counter of 2 is the slowest turn the original
has — the pitch moved only forty units over the same forty frames — so it may
be too small to measure, or the roll may not be reaching the world. The next
measurement is the same one with a large roll counter, which separates the two.

Re-running the docking harness: dead ahead still docks at frame 507, off to one
side still does not, so the pitch sign was a real fault and not the whole of it.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record the docking sign question, and revert the unverified change
events.message:
Record the docking sign question, and revert the unverified change

The direction the autopilot turns is decided by the sign of the counter it sets,
and the probes establish that RollRight drives the rate below 128 with PullUp
doing the same for pitch. On that reasoning the sign tests in Steer looked
inverted. Flipping both was tried and the harness behaved no better, so the
change was reverted rather than committed: it could not be shown to improve
anything, and this one loop has now seen several sign changes made on reasoning
alone.

The roadmap records the reasoning, the negative result, and what to do instead:
a trace of the turn itself, logging the roll and pitch rates and the angles they
produce each frame, to see whether the world rotates the way the counters ask.
If it does, the fault is in the aim PH1 builds; if not, it is in the counter to
rate conversion. Reasoning is not evidence, and the loop needs a measurable step
before the next change to it.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Make PH1 head for the ideal docking position, not just match the roll
events.message:
Make PH1 head for the ideal docking position, not just match the roll

Reading PH1 rather than guessing at it: it works the ideal docking position
out, normalises and negates the vector, sets the roll counter to 127 to match
the space station's roll, and then falls through into the same turning code the
other phases use — TN13, which heads the ship in the direction of the vector it
has just built. So PH1 does two things and this did only the first, matching
the roll while never pitching towards the ideal position. That is what left the
ship circling the station for ever.

The second half is now in. It has not made the off-axis approach dock in the
harness, so the roadmap records where the remaining suspect is: not PH1's own
logic but the shared turning code it falls into, whose sign convention is the
next thing to check.

Every piece of the docking computer is now the original's own code rather than
an invention, which is the state worth handing over: it docks dead ahead, it
does not from off to one side, and the fault is a translation error in the
turning rather than a missing algorithm.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Anchor the scanner wedge at the centre and keep it inside the ellipse
events.message:
Anchor the scanner wedge at the centre and keep it inside the ellipse

The wedge started at the bottom of the scanner and its arms ran past the
ellipse. It now opens upwards from the centre, which is where the ship is, at
about 35 degrees either side of straight ahead, and each arm runs only as far
as the point where it meets the ellipse: the reach is solved from the ellipse
equation along the arm's direction, so the wedge can never leave the scanner
however the dashboard is scaled.

events.title: Port RefineApproach, which is the disc version's own PH3 code
events.message:
Port RefineApproach, which is the disc version's own PH3 code

RefineApproach lives in the demo library, and the note above it says it was
copied from the disc version, where the code at PH3 has been extracted into it
so it can serve both the enemy target and the planet or station. So this is the
disc's own algorithm, and it does three things:

- it zeroes the pitch counter and sets RAT2 to 0, so roll and pitch are always
  applied while refining
- it rolls towards the target using the sign of -x * y, a quadrant test on the
  target's position in the ship's own frame rather than the x component alone,
  which is how the ship knows which way to roll to bring the target round
- it gives up if the target is more than six units off the centre line, letting
  the caller slow right down, because refining is a fine adjustment and getting
  roughly lined up is PH1's job

All three replace the x-component rule and the invented dead band. An approach
from off to one side still does not dock, and since PH3 is now the disc's own
code the remaining fault is in PH1 or in the handover between the phases, which
the roadmap records along with the phase trace that shows it.

events.message:
Put the forward view wedge on the scanner, where it belongs

corners. It belongs on the scanner: two lines from the bottom of the ellipse
fanning up and out, so you can see at a glance which contacts are in front of
you. Forward is up the scanner, so the wedge opens upward from the point the
ship occupies.

The space-view lines are gone. The roadmap's list of presentation departures now
describes the wedge where it actually is.

events.title: Correct the docking diagnosis: the counters of two are the original's
events.message:
Correct the docking diagnosis: the counters of two are the original's

Reading PH3 closely changes the picture from the last trace. The original
really does set a roll and pitch counter of two in PH3 — LDA #2, STA INWK+29,
then the same for INWK+30 — so the fixed counter here is not a fault, it is the
original's own value. The previous round's conclusion that it was the cause is
wrong, and this note corrects it rather than leaving it to mislead the next
attempt.

Two other things follow. There is a ±12 sight limit that is missing here: the
original stops manoeuvring when the station is more than 12 off the crosshairs,
because it is not worth turning towards something that far out of the window.
And RefineApproach is a separate routine that PH3 calls to work out the pitch;
it is called from dockit.asm but is not defined there, and it is not in the
common library under that name. Finding it is the next step, since it decides
the pitch and is probably where the real answer is.

Draw the view frustum

Two lines fanning from the gunsight to the bottom corners of the space view,

rather than the disc version's own rendering: the only cones in the disc
sources are the docking approach tests, and its space view is stars, ships and
the gunsight. Like the dotted scanner, it comes from the NES version's
dashboard.

The roadmap now lists the presentation departures together — the dotted scanner
and the frustum — so neither can be mistaken for disc fidelity later. Everything
else in the dashboard, the instrument set and its arrangement, the scanner's
projection and height sticks, and the compass dot, is the disc version's own.

events.title: Trace the docking computer's phases, and name the cause
events.message:
Trace the docking computer's phases, and name the cause

Tracing which phase is entered on an approach from off to one side gives the
answer, and it is the same failure mode as before: a simplification standing in
for an original routine.

The refine phase turns with counters of 2, the smallest the original has, and
holds them for hundreds of frames. The lateral offset never shrinks — it is
still (400, 300) all the way in — so the approach angle degrades from -1.00 to
-0.62 as the distance closes, until the ship is no longer squarely facing the
slot, at which point it falls into PH1, matches the station's roll and circles
for ever without closing.

The cause is that PH3 does not use the original's RefineApproach routine, which
works out how far off the aim is and sets the counters accordingly. This sets a
fixed counter of 2 whenever the aim is off by more than the dead band, which is
a simplification invented here, and small constant turns cannot correct a
500-unit lateral offset in the time available.

So the next step is not another trace: it is to port RefineApproach and its
helpers, as DOCKIT itself was ported, and delete the fixed-counter
simplification. DockingComputer now reports the phase it used, which is what
made the trace possible and will make the next one readable.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Correct the docking computer's branch test, and keep the compass inside the scanner
events.message:
Correct the docking computer's branch test, and keep the compass inside the scanner

The branch test was reversed. DOCKIT's dot product is the station's slot against
the line to us; this implementation's runs the other way, so the comparison has
to be reversed with it. Getting it wrong made PH1 the default branch, which
left the ship rolling to match the station's roll for ever rather than ever
refining its approach. The instrumented trace showed it plainly: the station sat
behind the ship at approach +0.99 with the slot facing it perfectly, and the
autopilot held roll counter 191 — the station's own roll — for thousands of
frames. A first attempt at the fix inverted the sign the other way and two
tests caught it immediately, which is the tests doing their job.

A docking dead ahead still completes at frame 507 and an approach from off to
one side still does not, so the remaining fault is elsewhere in DOCKIT's phases
and the roadmap says to trace the phase actually entered rather than guess
again.

Also: the compass now sits inside the scanner's right edge rather than on it,
and the panels have a wider gap, so neither overlaps the scanner.

Draw the scanner with dots

The ellipse and the blips are drawn as dots rather than a hairline outline and
blocks, which is the style the dashboard is being taken to and reads better at

Recorded in the roadmap as a deliberate departure rather than an oversight: the

CIRCLE routine, and marks ships with dashes rather than dots — CPIX2 is 'draw a
single-height dash on the dashboard' and CPIX4 is 'draw a double-height dot'.

also has the $ ELITE panel along the top. If strict disc parity is wanted here
the change is localised to DrawEllipse and the blip size.

Size the instrument panels from the scanner

what let them crowd the scanner and squeeze it into a sliver. They now stop a

than the other way round: making it wider or the window larger moves the panels

The left-hand bars and the scanner are now cleanly separated. The EN and SP
labels still sit at the left edge of the right-hand panel, right against the
scanner, and moving them to the outer side of their bars is the obvious fix —
recorded in the roadmap as not yet done rather than overlooked.

events.title: Give the scanner room, and draw its outline as a line
events.message:
Give the scanner room, and draw its outline as a line

The scanner's ellipse was drawn as a ring of thick little blocks, which is what
looked wrong. It is now a thin continuous outline, joined line segment to line
segment, and it keeps the original's shape: 128 by 52 in a 256-wide dashboard,
a little over twice as wide as it is tall.

The instrument bars are narrower than they were, so the scanner has room
between the two panels, which is closer to the original's arrangement than the
crowded centre it had before. The compass dot sits inside the scanner's right
edge, as the original's does.

Still imperfect and recorded: the EN and SP labels sit very close to the
scanner's right edge, and a proper layout pass would space the panels from the
scanner rather than from fixed fractions of the dashboard width.

events.title: Write down the open items and what the session taught
events.message:
Write down the open items and what the session taught

Six open items, each saying what was checked and what was not, so none of them
can be mistaken for finished work: the AI's close-range disengage, which
TACTICS has not given up yet; the docking computer's off-axis approach; the
station's rendering, which may be right but has not been checked against the
blueprint; the energy bomb's exemptions, read from a grep rather than a careful
read; rebinding and a settings screen; and performance, which has never been
measured.

Also recorded: four bugs were found by looking at the game rather than by any
audit — the missing scanner, missing ship collisions, a station that never
rotated, and an invisible planet — and a fifth, the compass drawn as a ring
instead of a dot, survived an audit that checked which instruments existed
rather than whether they looked right. Five invented numbers or algorithms have
been replaced by the original's own, each found by reading the source after
writing the invention.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Draw the compass the original's way, and drop the ring
events.message:
Draw the compass the original's way, and drop the ring

The compass was a large circle in the middle of the dashboard, which is not
what the original has and is the ring that looked wrong. The original's SP2
works the dot's position out by dividing the planet's or station's x and y
coordinates by ten, giving a value from -9 to +9, and places the dot at
(195 + x, 204 - y) on its dashboard. So the compass is a small fixed circle
just inside the right edge of the scanner with a dot moving inside it, and
there is no large ring at all.

The scanner's height sticks were already drawn from the original's SCAN — a
blip's y is its row less half the ship's height in high bytes, with a stick
joining it to the centre line — and they now stand out against the dashboard
without the ring across them.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Scoop by the blueprint's nibble, as the disc version does
events.message:
Scoop by the blueprint's nibble, as the disc version does

The cassette version decides what a canister holds with hard-coded conditions,
but the disc version reads the high nibble of the first byte of a ship's
blueprint: it says both whether the ship can be scooped and what it gives when
it is. This now takes that nibble as the authority rather than a hand-written
list of types, so the original's commodities fall out of the data:

  escape pod  item 3   slaves
  splinter    item 12  minerals
  Thargon     item 16  alien items
  one other   item 9
  31 others   item 0   not scoopable, which is how the disc version says so

The fallback for when no blueprint is available keeps the Core usable on its
own: a splinter scoops as minerals, an escape pod as slaves and a Thargon as
alien items.

Three tests needed correcting rather than the code: they passed a market item
of zero for a canister and expected food, but zero is precisely how the disc
version marks a ship as not scoopable. A Cobra Mk III cannot be scooped, and
now the tests say so.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Check the scanner empirically, and use the original's bubble range
events.message:
Check the scanner empirically, and use the original's bubble range

Flying for a while and listing what the simulation holds against what the
scanner projects showed three blips for the three ships in range and seven
ships beyond it. That is the original's behaviour rather than a bug: FAROF sets
A = 224 and compares it with x_hi, y_hi and z_hi, so a ship leaves the bubble
only once it is more than 224 in the high byte, which is 57,344 units — well
past the scanner's 16,384. The bubble therefore holds ships the scanner does
not show, exactly as the original does, and the scanner was right all along.

The bubble range itself was an invented 32,768 and is now the original's
224 << 8, so ships stay a little longer than they did.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add the planet and sun altitude check
events.message:
Add the planet and sun altitude check

The original checks our altitude every 32 iterations of its main loop, on
iteration 10, and the algorithm is its own:

- the m routine ORs the top bytes of the body's three coordinates together, and
  only if they are all zero — meaning we are within 65535 units — is the rest
  of the check worth doing, because only then do the coordinates fit in the
  high bytes the check squares
- the squares of the high bytes are totalled, divided by 256 so the result fits
  in a byte, and compared against the planet's radius
- the planet's radius is 96 in the original's 8-bit units, and 96 * 96 / 256 is
  36, which is the figure the check uses; the original subtracts 37 so the
  surface itself counts

The division by 256 is easy to miss and the test caught it at once: without it
the radius comes out as 9216 and nothing ever crashes. Flying into a planet is
now fatal, which it was not before.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Draw the planet as a disc rather than a square
events.message:
Draw the planet as a disc rather than a square

The disc texture stored plain white with an alpha channel, but the sprite
batch's default blend state expects premultiplied colours, so the corners drew
opaque and the planet came out as a square. Storing the colour multiplied by
its alpha fixes it.

Worth noting how this survived: the planet was invisible until the visibility
cull was fixed a round earlier, so the texture had been wrong all along behind
a bug that stopped anyone from seeing it. Fixing one bug exposed the next,
which is the argument for looking at the game after every fix rather than
trusting that the fix was the last one.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Fix the planet and sun, which were never visible
events.message:
Fix the planet and sun, which were never visible

Two bugs hid them, and neither was where it looked:

The visibility test. The original hides a body once z_sign reaches 48 — and z_sign is the sign
byte, the top byte of a 24-bit coordinate, so the test is on z >> 16. The renderer divided z by
256 instead, which for Lave's planet gives 1024, well past 48, so every planet and sun in the
game was culled. This is the one that actually made them invisible.

The placement. The original works the planet's distance out from s0_hi and stores it in the
z sign byte, then puts the same value in the x and y sign bytes — so the planet sits ahead of
us and only slightly to one side, because the sign byte carries the top bits of the coordinate
and a small value there is a small offset. This placed the planet half its distance to the side
instead, which threw it off the corner of the screen before the cull even mattered. The sun is
behind us, also with small sign-byte offsets, as the original has it.

Lave's planet now fills the view on arrival, with the station in front of it.

events.author: ataribaby42

events.title: Make 'use the original algorithms' a project rule
events.message:
Make 'use the original algorithms' a project rule

Every behaviour comes from the original's routines where one exists, and the
routine is named in the code and the commit. Where an invention has crept in it
is a bug to be replaced, not a variation to be kept.

The rule records the three things built by hand here and later replaced by the
original's own algorithm, as a reminder of the failure mode: an invented PD
controller for the docking computer, where DOCKIT has three phases and matches
the station's roll; key presses for rotation, where DOCKIT writes INWK+29 and
INWK+30; and a constant station roll of 6, where the main game loop gives the
station a random clockwise roll. Each was found by reading the source after
writing the invention, which is the wrong order.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add collisions with other ships
events.message:
Add collisions with other ships

Station collision existed on its own, driven by the docking checks, and there
was nothing for the ordinary case of flying into another ship. The original's
main flight loop part 10 handles it, and this now does the same: we take 128
damage with OOPS, the ship we hit takes 64 with n_hit, and it is made angry.
The range test is the original's too, within 256 units on every axis.

Two cases keep their own paths, as they should: the space station, which has
the docking checks and is fatal to hit anywhere but the slot, and missiles,
where the missile reaching us is a detonation rather than a collision and the
missile code already handles it.

Verified by test: flying into a Sidewinder costs us 128 off the shields and
costs it 64, it turns hostile, a ship far away is not a collision, and a weak
ship is destroyed by the impact.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Give the space station the roll the original gives it
events.message:
Give the space station the roll the original gives it

The station's rotation was invented — a constant roll of 6 — and the
original's formula is in the main game loop where the station is created: a
random value with bit 7 cleared, which is a clockwise roll of random magnitude
with a 1 in 127 chance of having no damping. MVEIT spends a counter as it uses
it, so the station's roll is renewed from the value it was created with, which
is what keeps the Coriolis turning for as long as it is there.

That removes another invented number, and it is the mechanism the docking
computer's roll matching is for: the slot's orientation changes as the station
turns, so lining up means turning with it. Docking still succeeds for a
well-placed approach and still overshoots from off to one side, so the
remaining fault is in the approach geometry rather than the station — with the
station 6000 units away and 2000 to one side, about 18 degrees off, the
autopilot does not turn onto the slot before it arrives. Which of DOCKIT's
three branches it should be taking at that point is the next question, and the
harness to answer it is in place.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Let the docking computer set rotation counters, as DOCKIT does
events.message:
Let the docking computer set rotation counters, as DOCKIT does

The simulation now accepts rotation counters set directly, which is what the
original's docking computer actually does: DOCKIT writes INWK+29 and INWK+30
and lets MVEIT fly the ship, rather than holding keys down. A counter says how
far to turn this frame, so it is converted into the rate the rest of the
simulation flies with — the centre is 128, and a larger counter is a faster
turn.

This was the blocker identified last round, and it was a change of shape
rather than more tuning: the docking computer now completes a docking when the
station is straight ahead, at frame 507 in the harness. Its phases fly as
written — the ideal docking position eight nose vectors out, the roll match,
the 157-unit turn-away, the refine, and the docking speed cap of 22.

An approach from off to one side still overshoots, and the likely cause is
recorded: the Coriolis does not turn in this implementation, while in the
original it rolls continuously, which is exactly what PH1's roll matching
matches. A station that never rolls gives the matching nothing to match, so
the ship's roll drifts and the approach misses the slot. The station now at
least carries a roll counter, so that is the thread to pull next.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Replace the invented docking controller with a port of DOCKIT
events.message:
Replace the invented docking controller with a port of DOCKIT

The hand-written controller is gone, replaced by the original's algorithm: the
three phases (fly for the ideal docking position and match the station's roll,
turn away when too close and badly placed, or refine the approach), the ideal
docking position eight nose vectors out as DCS1 and PH1 work it out, the roll
matching read from the station's own roll counter, and the original's
thresholds — RAT 2, RAT2 6, 157 units, a dot product of 35, a docking speed of
22. The speed discipline is now the original's cap rather than an invented
glide slope.

It still does not dock, and the reason is now clear from reading DOCKIT
properly: it writes the ship's roll and pitch counters directly, with STA
INWK+29 and STA INWK+30, rather than holding the controls down. The original's
docking computer is not a pilot pressing keys — it sets the rotation rates and
lets MVEIT fly the ship. A FlightInput can only press keys, so it cannot
express what DOCKIT does, and the ship never turns at the rate the algorithm
asks for.

The fix is therefore a small change of shape rather than more tuning: let the
simulation accept a counter override for the docking computer, as the
original's key logger's manoeuvring code does, and the phases will then fly as
written. That is recorded in the roadmap along with the routines still to
port.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record what porting DOCKIT actually involves
events.message:
Record what porting DOCKIT actually involves

The docking computer here is a hand-written controller, and the project's own
rule is that maths is ported rather than reinvented. DOCKIT is the original's
algorithm, in the enhanced library, reached from the key logger's manoeuvring
code: it sets up a scratch ship looking along +z at our speed, calls DOCKIT to
work out the moves, and writes the answer into the key logger, so the docking
computer flies the ship through the same path as the keyboard.

The roadmap now records its structure and thresholds (RAT 2, RAT2 6, CNT2 29,
the speed capped at 22), its three cases — fly to the ideal docking position
in front of the slot, turn away if too close and badly placed, or refine the
approach while the station is within 12 units of the crosshairs — and the
routines it needs: TA2, TAS2, TAS3, TAS4, TAS6, TA151, VCSU1, DCS1 and GOPL.

Reading it also turned up the reason this implementation's autopilot arrives
off the slot's axis: PH1 rolls to match the space station's own roll, and PH3
rolls towards the station. The Coriolis rotates, so the slot's orientation
changes as you approach and the docking computer tracks it. A controller that
aims at a point and ignores the station's rotation cannot line up with a
rotating slot, which is exactly the failure observed.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Give the docking computer a control loop that settles
events.message:
Give the docking computer a control loop that settles

The autopilot held its controls at full deflection until the station was
centred, which overshot and swung past it. It now asks for a turn no faster
than the aim error warrants and lets go once the ship is turning at that rate,
reading the roll and pitch rates — whose centre is 128, and which rolling
right takes below it — so the turn eases off instead of reversing.

The approach also follows a glide slope now: the speed it allows itself falls
with the distance, so it cannot charge past the station. That mattered more
than it sounds, because the flight model has no yaw, so overshooting leaves
the station behind and no way to turn back. Before the glide slope the
autopilot ended up sixteen thousand units past the station and flying away
from it at full speed.

What still does not work, and is recorded rather than papered over: it arrives
a couple of hundred units off the slot's axis, just outside the 22 degree cone,
and collides instead of docking. The tests pin the control settling and the
glide slope — the parts that work — rather than a docking that does not happen
yet.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Record the dashboard audit
events.message:
Record the dashboard audit

Checked the dashboard element by element against the original's four DIALS
routines. It is complete for the disc version: the speed indicator, the pitch
and roll indicators, the four energy banks, and the shields, fuel, laser
temperature and cabin temperature of the last routine, plus the missile
indicators, the compass and the new 3D scanner.

The one element that could not be placed, an altitude indicator mentioned in
the fourth DIALS routine, is Apple II only. That makes three features this
remake has been asked to account for which the BBC disc version does not have
- the shipyard is Elite-A only, the docking music is Commodore 64 only, and
the altitude indicator is Apple II only - so the roadmap now says so in one
place.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add the 3D scanner
events.message:
Add the 3D scanner

Core:
- Scanner projects a ship onto the dashboard in the original's own coordinates:
  x = 123 + x_hi, and y = 220 - z_hi/4 - y_hi/2 clamped to the scanner's
  194..247 rows. Forward is therefore up the ellipse, and a ship's height
  lifts its blip off the centre line, with a stick joining the two — which is
  how the original's SCAN routine works
- Ships more than 16383 units away on any axis fall off the scanner, as the
  original tests bits 6 and 7 of the high bytes; the planet and the sun never
  appear; missiles are marked so they can be drawn in their own colour
- The sign of a coordinate lives in its own byte rather than in bit 7 of the
  high byte, so the magnitude and sign are read separately, exactly as SCAN
  does

Game: the HUD draws the ellipse, its centre line and every blip and stick,
scaled to fit the gap between the instrument panels

Verified by test: a ship straight ahead sits on the centre line above the
middle, left and right and up and down carry the original's signs, distant
ships fall off the scanner, the planet never shows, missiles are marked, and
the ellipse is widest across the middle.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Start the docking computer, and record where it falls short
events.message:
Start the docking computer, and record where it falls short

Core:
- DockingComputer produces a FlightInput rather than steering the ship
  directly, which is what the original does: its docking computer writes its
  manoeuvres into the key logger, so a person and the computer fly the ship
  with the same code. The autopilot aims for a point out along the slot's
  axis, rolls and pitches onto it, and closes

A modelling fact this turned up, and a bug it exposed: because this
implementation turns the universe around the player rather than the player
within it, our own axes are the fixed ones and we always face +z in the
world's terms. The docking checks were passing the player's stored
orientation as our facing, which never changes, so they were comparing the
wrong thing. They now pass +z, and the autopilot steers by the aim's world
components directly.

What does not work yet, and is recorded in the roadmap rather than papered
over: the autopilot's controls are full deflection or nothing, so it
overshoots and swings past the station instead of settling, and it cannot
dock. The fix is to read the rotation rates and ease off as the aim error
shrinks. The tests pin the steering sense, which is right, rather than a
docking that does not yet happen.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add the docking checks
events.message:
Add the docking checks

Core:
- Docking applies the original's ISDK tests before letting us in: the station
  must not be hostile, its slot must be facing us within about 26 degrees, we
  must be facing the station rather than away from it, we must be inside the
  slot's 22 degree cone of approach, and the slot must be roughly level. The
  station's nose vector is what defines the slot, and its roof vector says how
  level the slot is
- Anything else within contact range is a collision, and hitting the station
  is fatal: the original's ApplyStationCollision takes the shields and energy
  to nothing and kills us
- The tests are run within the original's 256-unit contact range, which is
  where its main flight loop considers docking, scooping and collisions

Game: the flight scene runs the checks each frame, docking when we fly
through the slot and dying when we hit the station anywhere else, with the
beep and the explosion to go with them

Two bugs of my own on the way, both about which way a vector points: the
parameter is the station's position in our frame rather than ours in the
station's, and the approach cone compares our position seen from the station
against the slot's axis. Getting the first one wrong made a perfectly aligned
approach read as a collision.
events.author: tkleisas

events.title: Add the energy bomb, and correct the parity list
events.message:
Add the energy bomb, and correct the parity list

Core:
- FlightSim.FireEnergyBomb follows the original's rules: the bomb must be
  fitted, it is consumed on use, and while it is going off every ship in the
  local bubble is destroyed except the space station. Its victims count
  towards the kill tally, which is what the main loop does as it reaches each
